chapters.title: The Lake That Walked
chapters.html:
The lake had moved in the night, which was ordinary. What was not ordinary was that Reet had known where it would go.

She sat the grey mare at the crest of the heath with the chain coiled over the saddle-bow and looked at the water the way a gambler looks at a coin that has come down on the called side. Yesterday Kuld Mere had lain east of Dry Cairn, a long brown sheet that went gold at sunset and had been named for it. This morning the east was bracken and a tumbled sheepfold, and the west, where yesterday there had been a drovers’ track and a hawthorn hedge, held half a mile of slate-coloured water, steaming in the cold. Mist lay on it in strips. A line of fence posts marched down the track and into the lake and carried on under the surface, like a sentence nobody had told to stop.

Plover blew out through her nose and declined to be impressed.

Reet got down. Her knees complained. She had been in the saddle since the third bell, riding out from the Hollow in the dark with a satchel of blank Sheet frames and a bag of empty vials knocking at her hip. She unhooked the chain. A chain was sixty-six feet and a hundred links, and most riders on the Seam’s edge used theirs, by late autumn, for tying up the horse. Reet used hers.

She began at the cairn, because everything began at the cairn. Dry Cairn was a heap of grey limestone as high as a man’s belt, put up by some dead Surveyor who had understood the value of a thing that stays where it is, and it carried a brass stud in its capstone for a datum. She set the first link against the stud, took her bearing, two degrees south of west, and sent the tally-tag out across the frost.

Pacing would have taken a third of the time. She knew her pace as she knew her own name; the Guild had checked it twice against a standard rod, and the Guild did not check twice for just anyone. But there were numbers you paced and numbers you chained, and the difference was whether you meant to be asked about them afterwards. Lay the chain, stick the pin, lift the chain, walk to the pin. The frost cracked under her boots like sugar. The heather snagged her cuffs. Ahead of her the water lay perfectly flat, as if it knew it was being measured and meant to behave.

At the fortieth pin the lake was still ahead, a dark lip fringed with rushes. She laid out the odd links. Eighteen. The brass tag on the last of them touched the first wet rush and sank a little, and the water closed over its edge with a small, ordinary sound.

Forty chains and eighteen links, two south of west. To the yard.

She did not write it down. Writing was for the Hollow and for Mihkel Org’s red pencil. She let the number go to the place where she kept numbers, which was large and orderly and had never lost anything in nineteen years, and she noticed, standing there with a wet cuff and a cold nose, that her hands were not quite steady and that it was not the cold.

Nine mornings ago she had said that number aloud. She had said it to a bowl of porridge in the riders’ mess, after reading the Correction Book the way she read it every Thirdday, front to back, because it was public and dull and she remembered what she read. Leaf 31, the clerk’s round hand had said. Kuld heath, lake basin re-inked. Tidy. Re-inking was what the Guild called the upkeep of the Atlas: vellum cracked and ink flaked, and every so often a leaf was gone over with a fresh pen, and the Book recorded it, one line at a time, for the sake of the audit. Nobody read it for pleasure. Reet had read it for four years, and twice in that time, in the privacy of her own head, where she could be as easy on herself as she liked, she had set a line from the Book beside a Shift in the ground nine nights later and called the match chance.

The third time she had not been easy. She had asked what a tidy hand would do with Kuld heath: where the lowest ground lay, where a lake could sit without drowning the drovers’ track or the Hallik fields, where a clerk with a ruler and a feeling for neatness would put the shore. Forty visits to this heath had told her. She had worked it out in the time it took the porridge to cool, and then, because she wanted to hear how it sounded, she had said it.

It sounded better out here.

“Hoy! Sallik!”

Pille Raud came down the heath from the east on the piebald mule she called Biscuit, because it was hard, dry and nobody could remember choosing it. Pille was twenty-three and built like a door, with a plait down her back like a tow-rope and a nose that burned in any weather. She had a way of leaning on a conversation as though it were a gate. She reined in at the shore and looked at the lake for some time with her mouth slightly open.

“Well,” she said. “That’s wet.”

“It’s forty chains and eighteen links from the cairn.”

“Is it. You’d know.” Pille dug in her coat and came out with a heel of bread, which she tore at with her teeth. “Guild bread. Baked Seventhday, issued Fourthday, like they do it to hurt us. You could build a wall with it. Want some?”

“No.”

“Wise. I’m eating mine as a penance.” She chewed, and her eyes went from the water to Reet and back again. “You said that. At breakfast, nine days back. I remember because you said it to your porridge and I told you the porridge couldn’t help.”

“Nine mornings.”

“And I said a week of my crusts against a week of yours that nobody could name where Kuld would land, not even you.”

“Then you owe me a week of crusts.”

“I owe you nothing. I haven’t measured it.” Pille swallowed. “Guess or luck?”

“Neither.”

“Those are the only two.”

“Forty chains, eighteen links, two degrees south of west,” Reet said. “The northern spit against the Saar hedge, the shore along the thirty-eight-foot contour. I said it nine mornings ago and I’m saying it now, and it’s the same number.”

She did not stammer. Pille listened for it with her head on one side. Everyone in the riders’ loft knew about Reet Sallik’s tongue, which was the only piece of gossip she had ever supplied them with, and they treated it as a sort of public weights-and-measures. She told a lie and it came out in pieces, and the pieces were how you knew. Nobody laughed at it. They checked their purses by it, and asked her whether the stew was fresh.

“Huh,” said Pille at last. “That’s the worst of it, then. If you’d stammered I could’ve gone on thinking you were a normal sort of liar.”

“I’m not any sort.”

“I know. It’s wearing.” Pille wheeled the mule. “Keep your crusts. I’ll do the south shore; the sheep have all gone there to be sad.” She went off down the margin, still chewing, and called back without turning her head, “Don’t tell Mihkel you called it. He’ll want it in triplicate!”

Reet turned north along the water with a Sheet frame on her knee.

She had gone twenty paces when she heard it: a dry grinding, like a cart wheel in a rut, from a place where nothing was driving a cart.

The Hallik stone was a block of grey granite as high as her ribs, shouldered into the track where the Hallik sheep-run met the Kuld commons, with an H cut into one face and a K into the other and a century of lichen to say it had never in its life gone anywhere. Now it was going. It slid across the turf behind a bow-wave of torn heather, a hand’s breadth at a time, toward the lake, and the ground around it did not stir. A yard of heath under the stone and a yard of heath behind it were on the move, and the rest of the world sat by and watched.

Reet stood very still, which was how she thought. Last night’s Shift had put the lake here. It had not put the stone anywhere; the stone had been left to find its own way, and the way it was finding ran, by her reckoning, eleven feet to the water and eleven minutes. When the lake closed over it the Hallik line would be a fiction, and in a season there would be a lawsuit and two families of cousins who didn’t speak. That was one way of looking at it. The other way was that something was pulling the stone, steadily, as a hand pulls on a rope, and she held that thought at arm’s length and looked at it and put it down again.

“That’s our stone!”

A woman was coming up the track from the farm at a run, in clogs and a sacking apron, with a milk pail swinging from one hand and her hair half pinned. She addressed herself to the heath at large. “Leelo Hallik, and that’s the Hallik stone, and it’s going in the lake!”

“Yes,” said Reet.

“My husband’s grandfather hauled that stone up from the quarry with two oxen and a quarrel. It’s the line. If it goes in the lake the Kulds’ll say the lake’s theirs and we’ll be at it till the Hollow freezes over.”

“I can hold it.”

“Then hold it, girl. Why are you stood there?”

“Because it holds for a night. It’s day-ink. One night, no more. Tomorrow it goes where the ground wants it.”

The woman looked at the stone, which was nine feet from the water now, and then at Reet. “One night’s more than that stone’s had in a hundred years,” she said. “Hold it.”

Reet knelt on the frost. She unhooked the horn cup from her belt, dipped it in the lake, which was cold enough to ache, and tipped into it a thimble of Ilves Black from the steel flask at her hip. Ilves Black was what the Guild bought by the barrel, and on its own it was only ink. Mixed with water from the ground it was meant to hold, it was something with a short temper and a long reach. She laid the pin-sheet on her knee, a hand’s breadth of stiff vellum, and took up the pen with her left. Her right, steadying the cup, was dyed to the wrist already; the left, which wrote, had ink only to the second knuckle, and a good deal of rider’s pride about it.

She drew the stone. A few lines: its top face, the slant of its flank, the track beside it, the nearest fence post for a reference, and the small tick of contour grammar that said falling toward water. It took less than a minute. The knack was to draw the thing as it was at that instant, with the stone in the middle of its stride; you did not draw where you wished it were. Then she stood, because you had to stand, that was the whole of it, with both boots on the turf and her shadow across the page, and said the words every rider learned in the first week and said a hundred times without hearing them.

“I stood here. I drew only what I saw.”

The grinding stopped.

It was the quiet that startled her, more than the noise had. The stone had been mid-lurch; it finished the lurch, rocked once on its base like a man caught by the sleeve, and was a stone again, with a furrow behind it and a hand’s breadth of dry heather ahead.

“Well,” said Leelo Hallik, after a time. “That’s all?”

“That’s all.”

“I’ll tell them at the Hollow they’re not all useless.”

“Thank you, I—”

Reet closed her eyes, as she did when she wanted to be sure. It was an old habit. She walked the heath in her head from the cairn outward, yard by yard, like a woman going down a passage of lit rooms. The cairn, with frost on the capstone. Forty chains of heather, every pin. The hedge, the posts, the rim of the lake. And at the stone, one room with no light in it. She knew the stone was there. She knew the track ran past it. But the yard of turf she had knelt on, the yard she had looked at with her own eyes not a minute ago, was not in the passage at all; there was only the place where it should have been, smooth and exact, like the gap where a tooth has been, and her thought went into it again and again and found nothing to bite.

She had never forgotten anything in her life. It had not occurred to her that this was a thing a person could lose.

She opened her eyes. Leelo Hallik was peering at her.

“You’ve gone the colour of tallow.”

“It’s the c— the cold.”

“Mm,” said the woman, and looked at Reet’s mouth for a while, as people did. “Sit on my wall and I’ll bring you something hot.”

She did not bring it, as it turned out. She stood beside the stone with her pail and patted it now and then, the way you would pat a dog that had come home, and Reet did not blame her.

Every other rider on the Seam’s edge pinned a yard or two before breakfast and thought nothing of it. Reet found she was thinking about that. They did it every morning and never noticed what it cost, because nobody remembers a yard. She walked down to the water, stepping where the heather was whole, and crouched at the new shore with her bag open.

The last duty of any Shift was a vial. Every rider drew one at every site: a thumb-length of thick green glass, filled from the place itself, corked, sealed with a drop of wax and labelled with the date and the name. They went to the assay shelf in the Hollow, where they stood in rows by leaf number among thousands of others, and she had never known anyone to take one down. The custom was older than the rule that required it. She held the glass under the surface until it stopped speaking, wiped it on her sleeve, sealed it, and wrote on the label in her small square hand: Kuld Mere, north shore, first light. Then she sat with it in her palm, a very small amount of lake, and did not feel like a woman who had just done something ordinary.

She rode north with the sun coming up on her right hand and the lake steaming behind her. Plover took the drovers’ track at a walk, and for once Reet let her. The Hollow’s rim stood ahead as a black ragged line, with a thread of lamp-smoke going up from it straight as a plumb-line, and she went over the matter as she went over everything, in order, from the first fact.

A leaf is re-inked when it has worn, or when it has gone wrong. That was what the Guild taught: the Atlas records. The ground moves, and the Atlas follows after, one line behind, like a clerk with a pen. Everyone knew the order of things. The ground first; the record second.

But the Book had said lake basin re-inked nine nights before there was a lake. A clerk who is one line behind does not arrive nine nights early. And the stone, this morning, had not been dragged by a clerk. Something had held it by the rope, and she had cut the rope with a thimble of ink and nine words, and the ground had listened to her because she had stood on it and the other thing had not.

She thought of the lake, laid so exactly in the lowest ground, with a neat straight shore along the fence. Tidy. The word had been written down by someone who knew what was coming.

Plover’s ears went back and then forward. Reet watched them.

“If the Book knew,” she said, “then someone drew it first.”

The mare walked on, which was perhaps the most sensible reply anyone had made all morning.

“Someone drew that lake,” Reet told her, “before it was there.”

Behind them, a long way off by now, the water went on being exactly where it was.

chapters.title: The Correction Book
chapters.html:
The lamp-boys were still at it when Reet came down into the Hollow, though it was past the fourth bell and the sky over the rim had gone the colour of clean slate. They went up and down the stairs in pairs with their hooked poles and oil-cans, trimming wicks on every landing, because a city built in a sinkhole saw the sun for four hours a day in winter and did not mean to spend the rest of it in the dark. The lamps burned all year. The whole Hollow smelled of them: lamp-oil and wet limestone and, under both, sharp and brown and everywhere, the oak-gall tang of Guild ink, which got into the plaster, the bread, the hair of the children and, in Reet’s case, every pore of her right hand.

She had left Plover at the rim livery and come down on foot, because there was no other way. There was the Guild stair, with its four hundred and nineteen steps to the floor, and there were the thousand unregistered ones that went everywhere else. She did not count the Guild stair. It counted itself.

“Sallik!” A lamp-boy hung from the rail of the eighth landing by one arm, eleven years old and all knees, soot to the elbow. “Mihkel’s looking for you.”

“Mihkel is always looking for me, Ants.”

“He’s got his waistcoat on.”

Reet stopped with one foot on the next step. “Which?”

“Mustard.”

“Oh, lovely,” she said, and gave him the sugar lump she had been keeping for Plover.

The mustard waistcoat was for audits, funerals and visits from the Assembly’s clerks, in that order of dread. She went the rest of the way down faster than she meant to.

The Guild House stood against the Hollow’s north wall, where the limestone was driest, a long pale building with too many windows, and the Day-book room sat at the top of its east wing, up four flights of a stair that had been designed by someone who disliked clerks. It was a long room under a skylight, full of slanting desks and ink-stained racks, and it had one cupboard at the back that was Reet’s. Inside were her copies: every Shift since she was fifteen, a fat ledger for each winter, the Sheets she had inked and the notes she had made at the edges of them. She had never needed to look anything up. She kept them for the same reason a man with a good memory for faces keeps a portrait of his mother.

She had the Kuld frame inked and set to dry on the rack when the door opened.

Mihkel Org was round, and bald as an egg except for a fringe dyed a walnut brown found in no living creature. He had been Master-Surveyor for nineteen years and had a face like a man holding in a sneeze. The mustard waistcoat strained at its buttons. There was a fine white dusting of sugar down one lapel.

“Sallik. Forty chains.”

“Yes, Master.”

“With the chain.”

“Yes.”

“Rule Fourteen. A rider’s hour belongs to the Sheet. The Sheet goes to the printers at the sixth bell, it is now a quarter to, and I am informed by a lamp-boy that you were seen strolling to the livery like a woman with an independent income.” He looked at the frame on the rack. It was done, it was dry and it was exact, and Reet watched him be disappointed by it, as a man is who has loaded a speech and finds there is no one to fire at. “Rule Eleven,” he said regardless. “The rider reports the ground. The interpretation of it belongs to the Keeper. Since you have enthusiasm to spare, you may spend it on the quarterly audit of the copy room: every tracing against the leaf it was taken from, pinholes, ticks and all. The stove wants its ash taken down. And Pille’s pencils.”

“What’s wrong with Pille’s pencils?”

“I am told they are a disgrace.” He turned for the door and put a hand, casually, over the pocket of the waistcoat, where something small and flaky crackled. “That will be all.”

Reet looked at the sugar on his lapel. She did not mention it, which was what made it worse for him.

She did the ash. She sharpened Pille’s pencils, and there were fourteen of them, and every one chewed. And then, because the Sheet had gone to the printers and nobody had said what she was to do with the rest of the day, she went to the cupboard at the back of the room and began taking out the ledgers.

She had meant to be quick. At the third ledger she stopped being quick. At the eighth she was on the floor with the long table cleared and the Sheets spread out along it like cards, and the afternoon had gone grey in the skylight, and she had not noticed.

The Correction Book lived on a lectern in the great hall, chained, and its old volumes in a rack beneath it, open to anyone who cared to read them. It was a public thing and a boring one. She had gone down at noon and read the last eight years of it in an hour and a half, not because she needed to take notes, but because Mihkel believed in paper the way other men believed in saints, and she wanted something to put in front of him. Now she copied it out, strip by strip, in the clerk’s round hand, onto slips as long as her palm. She laid each slip beside the Dawn Sheet for a day nine nights after.

Leaf 56, Tallow Moor, the north hill re-inked, minor. Nine nights on, the hill at Tallow Moor had got up in the dark and walked a quarter-mile east, and every rider in the loft had sworn at it for a week.

Leaf 71, Kask Ford, bend of the river re-inked. The river at Kask Ford had taken a new bend, to the great distress of a miller.

Leaf 88, Sora Crossing, the marsh drain re-inked. Last spring. Her mother had written: The drain’s moved, can you imagine, four hundred yards, overnight, and the whole street’s in a state. Reet had read the letter and thought: that’s a Shift. It had not occurred to her to look at what the Book said nine nights before.

She laid them down one by one. Fourteen. Fourteen entries, fourteen Shifts, and every one of the fourteen nine nights apart, to the night. The first was eight years old. Before it, in the Book’s earlier volumes, the re-inkings had been about damp and mice and a spilt inkwell in a wet March, and not one of them matched a thing on the ground. After it, they matched every time. Whoever had started doing this had not started cautiously.

She sat back on her heels. Her hands were cold, and the skylight above the table had gone the grey of old pewter.

“Sallik,” said a voice behind her. “Why is my floor covered in fish?”

“It’s not fish, Master. It’s Shifts.”

Mihkel stood in the door with a paper bag in one hand and the expression of a man who has come to eat something in private and found it occupied. He crossed to the table with his short quick steps and looked down at the row of Sheets and slips, and his eyes went along them, and she saw him add it up. He was not stupid. That was the thing people missed about Mihkel. He read from left to right and he got to the end.

“Fourteen,” she said. “Each of them nine nights after an entry in the Book. The leaf is re-inked, and nine nights later the ground does what the leaf says. All in the last eight years.”

“Re-inking is maintenance.”

“Then it’s maintenance that moves a river.”

“The Seam moves every night of the year. Take eight years of Shifts and eight years of anything, Sallik, and you will find fourteen of something that agrees with the price of onions.” He said it kindly, which was worse. “The Atlas records. When the ground changes, the Atlas is corrected to match it, and the Book makes a note. That is not a theory. It is Rule Three.”

“Then why is the Atlas nine nights early?”

“Clerks are meticulous.”

“Nine nights, fourteen times.”

“Rule Eleven,” said Mihkel, with some relief, as a man steps onto a good dry plank. “The rider reports. The Keeper interprets. You have reported, and I thank you, and I will mention it.” He looked at the slips for a moment longer, and the bag in his hand crackled, and she saw him decide something. “You have told me you can see the Atlas is not what it says. Very well. Choose a leaf for the audit. Any leaf. It will be traced under watch, as the Rules direct, and you may lay your hand on the vellum and see that ink is ink.”

“Eighty-eight.”

“Your own Sora.” He sighed through his nose. “Sentiment. Come.”

She had never been inside the vault, and she was not inside it now. She stood in the antechamber below the east wing, a bare stone passage with a lamp in a cage and an iron door at the end of it with three locks, and watched Mihkel take a key from a ribbon under the waistcoat. There were three keys, he said, without being asked: the Keeper’s, his own, and a third that lived in a sealed box in the Assembly’s strong-room. It took two to open the door. The Keeper’s had been left for him, as it was every quarter for the audit. He went in. The door closed on a smell of cold air and old vellum, and she counted forty seconds, and he came out with a flat case lined with felt, and handed it to her as one hands over an infant.

“Rule Nineteen,” he said. “Two gloves on vellum.” They were cotton, grey from other people’s hands. She put them on, and the left one, over the ink, felt like a bandage. “Tõnis.”

Tõnis was the vault porter, seventy-one and about as quick as a glacier, and he went up behind her with a lantern, watching her as a cat watches a bird it is too old to chase.

The copy room had a north window the size of a barn door and a long table of frosted glass, lit from underneath. She laid Leaf 88 on it and the room went quiet.

Sora Crossing was not large on the vellum. A marsh, a mill, a ford, a street, the green line of the drain, and a plum tree where her mother’s house stood, drawn by some hand a long time dead with a single curl of the pen. She had loved this leaf at seventeen. She had traced it herself two years ago, sitting where she sat now, and the tracing was in the file. She took it out and laid it over the leaf. The street matched. The mill matched. The drain was in the wrong place, as it should have been; the leaf had been corrected. And down in the lower margin, where the dividers had pivoted when the first hand drew it, the pinhole did not match.

The Guild’s dividers always went in five millimetres from the gutter. It was the oldest habit in the Atlas, a rule so old that no one remembered making it. The old tracing had its hole at five. The leaf in front of her had its hole at four.

She measured it twice with her steel rule. She did not need to. She knew it was four as she knew the date of her own birth.

A new hole was a new drawing. You did not redo a leaf and keep the old hole; you set the dividers down again and they pierced the vellum again, a little off, because no hand sets down twice in the same place. Somebody had redrawn Sora’s marsh. Somebody had redrawn it with dividers that sat down a millimetre wrong.

In the lower right corner, where the new ink had gone on, the black was glossy, as if it had not dried. The rest of the leaf had faded to brown over three hundred years. This corner shone like a beetle. Behind her, Tõnis breathed through his mouth and was, by the sound of it, asleep on his feet.

Reet slid the point of her pen-knife under the edge of the new ink and lifted a sliver the size of a grain of rice. It came away clean. She put it into the thumb of her glove and drew the cotton over it, and it was the first thing she had done in four years that was not in the Rules, and it took no time at all.

She made two tracings. One went in the file, as the Rules required. The second she made on onion-skin so thin it floated, and folded it small and put it inside her shirt. She did not need it. She could have drawn the leaf blind in a cellar. But a tracing was for everyone else; her own head was the one place in the Guild that nobody could be asked to trust.

The assay hall was on the ground floor, in a long vaulted gallery with green glass lamps, where the shelves rose to the ceiling and the vials stood in their thousands in racks, each corked and sealed and labelled with a place, a date and a name. It looked like a church built by a pharmacist. She had meant only to leave the Kuld vial in its row. Thirty-one, third rack. But on her way down the aisle her eye went along the numbers as it always did, and stopped.

Row 88 had held ninety-four vials in August. She knew; she had walked it. Now it held six at the far end, and where the rest had been the oak showed pale in rings, a long shelf of clean circles with a hand’s width of dust between them. She went on to 163. Palu’s valley had been a hundred and twelve vials, from every ford and well and bridge-foot, the careful work of eleven years of riders. The shelf was bare. It was as clean as a plate.

“Mistress Piret,” she said.

The assay-keeper looked up from a ledger and an ear-trumpet. “Mm?”

“Where is Palu’s row?”

“Breakage.”

“A hundred and twelve vials.”

“Glass,” said Piret, “is a terrible material.” She went back to her ledger. Reet stood with the Kuld vial in her hand, and then put it in its slot, and it looked very small and very alone.

There were nineteen other rows with gaps in them. She counted. She did not need to.

It was the lamp-lighting hour when she reached the great hall. The clerk had just finished his evening round, and was leaning on his stick with his spectacles pushed up, blotting. The Correction Book lay open on its lectern with the day’s last line still shining in the lamplight. She read it from three feet away, and then, because she had been taught to be sure, from one.

Leaf 163, Palu valley, re-inked.

Her stomach turned over, slowly, like a fish under ice. Palu had nine hundred people in it and forty rope bridges. She had inked its Sheet a dozen times. She knew the gorge and the church and the shape of the east ridge above it, bare as an egg. She stood there with the clerk coughing behind her, and the ordinary feet of the Guild going by, and she lifted her hands.

She counted on her fingers: the left bare now, the cotton gone, ticking off one finger at a time against the ink-dyed knuckles of the right. Tonight was none. Tomorrow was one. She went on down the days, through the ones that were Toomas Veskimae’s and Mihkel’s and the Keeper’s, and out the other end of her fingers, until the last one she had was a night with a number on it.

She stopped on the tenth.

chapters.title: A Binder in Tinta Row
chapters.html:
The thread was wrong again. Toomas Veskimae held it up to the lamp and watched it spin on its own twist, which good linen thread did not do, and told the empty shop what he had told it every Fifthday for forty years.

“Six-ply, waxed. Is that so much? Is a man asking for the moon, or for a thing that was in every shop on the Row when I was a boy?”

Nobody answered, because nobody was there. The shop answered in its own way: the press ticked as it cooled, the glue pot sighed, and the ledger on the sewing frame lay open on its cords with eleven years of herring in it, waiting. Lill & Sons, Smoked and Otherwise. The leaves smelled so strongly of fish that a cat had waited outside the door all afternoon in a spirit of faith. Toomas had been asked to make the thing look important. He had been trying for three days, with a bad needle, a worse thread and a right knee that had opinions about the stool.

He leaned on the frame and rubbed the knee. It was a good knee, as knees went, and it had served him for sixty-two years. It had also served him on the Guild stair, once, when it was not required to, and had never quite forgiven him. His chain-staff stood in the corner by the door. He used it to get about and not to measure, and he had not measured anything with it for twelve years.

The tea at his elbow had gone cold and grown a skin. He drank it anyway, on principle, the principle being that heating it would mean standing. Over the stove stood the two cups, where they stood every evening when he lit the lamp. He drank from one of them. The other stood mouth-down on its saucer all day, and he told nobody why. A man might lay a cup for a visitor who had never come; there was no law against it, though in Tinta Row, which was the street of ink-sellers and binders and had laws against most things, he sometimes looked for one.

No letter had come at Midwinter, either. His sister Helju wrote every Midwinter, one page, her cramped hand going downhill at the end of every line, to say that the bridges had held and Jaan’s boy had a cough. This year there had been nothing. The post was slow, he had told the second cup. It was a bad road, in the Seam.

The knock was three raps, a pause of exactly equal length, and three more.

Someone who counted. He felt it in the back of his neck before he had set the needle down.

“It’s open. It is always open. A binder who locks his door has something to bind.”

The girl who came in was five feet tall, with cropped dark hair that had been hacked at by survey shears, a notch in her right eyebrow and a satchel strapped across her like a bandolier. She was ink to the wrist on both hands, and there was a brass plumb-bob on a cord at her neck. She looked at him once, quickly, and then at the room, and he watched her take it in, from the press to the cups, and put it all somewhere. She did not look at his left eye. That was manners, or training.

“Master Veskimae?”

“Binder,” said Toomas. “Master of nothing since the year three hundred. Boards, spine, a title in gilt? I do not do love-letters.”

“I’m Reet Sallik.”

“I know who you are.”

She had not expected that, and he took a small mean pleasure in it, and put it away again. “You are the girl the Guild keeps in a drawer and takes out for the Assay Fair. They rang a little bell for every mistake. I stood at the back and counted the bell.”

“It didn’t ring.”

“No. That is why I counted.” He picked up the awl. “I am sewing herring, Rider. If you want something bound, I am at your service on Thirdday.”

“It’s about the Correction Book.”

The awl stopped.

“Fourteen entries in eight years,” she said. She had not sat; she stood with her satchel held in front of her, and her voice had gone quick and level, like something read from a slate. “Each a leaf re-inked. Tallow Moor, the north hill. Kask Ford, the river bend. Sora Crossing, the marsh drain. Kuld heath, the lake, yesterday morning. Nine nights after each entry, the ground moves to match what the leaf says. Nine nights, fourteen times. And yesterday evening the Book says Leaf 163, the Palu valley, re-inked.” She stopped for air. “Nine nights after yesterday.”

“Go away,” said Toomas.

“I haven’t—”

“You have said enough. Correction Book. Atlas leaves. Go away, Rider. I am a bookbinder and a bookbinder is a wall, and a wall remembers who leaned. I have leaned all I mean to.”

She did not go. She stood on his worn boards with the lamp on the side of her face, and the thing he noticed was that she did not look hurt. She looked as though someone had told her a number she could use.

“I know you were Keeper,” she said. “I know you were dismissed over a lost leaf. I know what the Guild says and I’ve never been able to find what’s true. So I’ll tell you something else, and you can throw me out after.” She closed her eyes. “Soo valley, from the last Dawn Sheet before the flood.”

He said, “Don’t.”

“The stream comes in at the north-east corner at the hundred-and-forty-foot contour and runs south-west in three bends. At the second bend there’s a ford of nine stepping stones, and the fourth stone is a different grey from the others. The mill’s on the west bank, forty yards off the stream, with a race cut from the first bend; the race has three sluices, and the middle sluice is drawn crooked. There are fourteen roofs below the mill, in a curve like a hand cupped, and the ash tree stands at the cupped place with a bench under it. Above the village the slope goes up in four steps. The first has a stone wall—”

“Stop.”

She stopped. She opened her eyes. Her mouth was slightly open, and she was a long way off, in a valley.

Toomas found that the awl was shaking in his fingers, the point jittering on the board like a bird’s foot. He laid it down very gently, where it would be less honest. He did not say what he knew. He had not said it in twelve years to anyone, and he did not say it now to a child with ink to her elbows who thought she was giving him a credential. But he could see it. She had drawn it back into his skull like a nail, the ash tree and the bench and the crooked sluice, and the worst was that she had it right. She had the fourth stone right.

“How old were you?” he said.

“Sixteen. It was in a bundle of waste Sheets in the Day-book cellar, lining the bottom of a drawer. They burned the rest.”

“Sixteen.” He drew a breath through his moustache. It rattled. “And you remember all of it.”

“I remember everything I’ve ever looked at.” She said it flatly, like a fact about the weather. “It isn’t an accomplishment. It’s an ear.”

He did not answer that. He took a pencil from behind his ear and a spoiled endpaper from the waste-basket, and turned it over to the plain side, and began to draw.

It was Palu. He did it from memory, which was a good memory, hung with the dust of twelve years: the gorge, the river at the bottom of it, the forty bridges strung across the gap like washing, the bell-tower, the long bare ridge on the east side where goats grazed. He drew fast, with the pencil held like a chisel, the way he had once drawn a hundred things a day for the Atlas, and as he drew he planted his mistakes. He put the sixth bridge on the wrong side of the bell. He gave the river an extra bend. He put fifty bridges where there were forty. He added a well where there had never been a well and left the mill off altogether, and when it was done he pushed the sheet across the bench without a word.

She read it the way he had seen a very good musician read a score, with her head still and her eyes going. “There are forty bridges,” she said. “You’ve fifty. That’s a flourish, I think. The sixth is on the north side of the tower, not the south. The river doesn’t have that bend, and the well is the old well, which was filled in after—” She frowned. “Eight years ago, I think. The mill’s on the third terrace. And the ridge.” She tapped the east side with her left forefinger. “You’ve drawn it bare. There’s a birch hanger on the north flank. It was planted nine years ago.”

“I did not plant it.”

“No. But it’s there.”

“And the tower?”

“The tower is what?”

“I left it as it was.” He heard his own voice. “I put it facing east.”

She looked at the sheet again. For the first time she looked uncertain. “It faces south. They rebuilt it. It was in the Sheet for—”

“I know it was.” He had not known. He took the paper back, and looked at his own tower, facing the wrong way, and the girl who had found the four mistakes he had put in and a fifth that he had not known was a mistake. A sensation went through him that he did not quite know what to do with. It was delight, at the plain, extravagant fact of her. And behind the delight, like the shadow of a wall behind a lamp, something else. He knew what the Guild did with instruments. He had been an officer of the Guild.

“Mm,” he said. “Say that shorter.”

“The Guild’s been using me as a party trick.”

“Better.”

She was the Atlas, he thought, if one cared to put it that way: a living leaf, in a satchel, with a notch in her eyebrow. He wished he did not.

She had gone to her satchel and was drawing out a folded piece of onion-skin so thin it clung to her fingers. “This is Leaf 88,” she said. “Sora Crossing, the lower margin. I traced it yesterday in the copy room.” She spread it on the bench. “Look at the pinhole. The dividers always go in five millimetres from the gutter. Always. When I traced this leaf two years ago it was five. On Leaf 88 yesterday it was four.”

He looked.

He found, to his considerable annoyance, that his eye went straight to the four and sat there, like a dog on a doorstep. A pinhole. A small circle of pricked vellum on a sheet of paper that weighed less than a breath. He had made a hundred thousand such holes, and had seen them go in, and had never in forty years thought of one as a signature.

A tool with one leg bent, he thought. It would not lie straight in its box. A girl he had trained, a quiet girl with quiet hands, who had dropped her dividers on the Guild stair in her first winter and refused to have them mended, because she said the slant suited her. He did not say the name. He did not say it even in his head, which he found took a good deal of effort, like holding a door shut against a wind.

“There’s more,” said Reet. “At Kuld, yesterday morning. There was a boundary stone moving, being dragged, as if there were a rope on it. I drew it in day-ink with the lake’s water and swore the oath, and it stopped. Dead.” She drew a hand across her eyes. “It cost me a yard.”

“A yard of what?”

“Of what I knew. I can’t remember it.” She said it very evenly. “I’ve never forgotten a thing in my life, Master Veskimae, and I have spent a day and a night walking round the place where one yard used to be.”

He did not move. He sat on the stool with the awl before him and the herring on his lap, and the lamp lit the side of his face where the eye was clear and the side where it was white, and he thought of a valley with nine hundred people in it. A town costs everything. Nobody had told her that. He was not going to be the one to tell her tonight.

“Then you have found it out already,” he said, slowly. “A far hand can only be beaten by a near one. Whatever is done at a distance, by a hand in a drawer, is only a rumour of the ground. A hand that has stood on it is a witness. A witness beats a rumour. Your stone knew it.” He rubbed his knee. “Someone must stand in Palu.”

“I told Mihkel Org.”

“And what did he say?”

“Rule Eleven.” She gave a short humourless breath. “The rider reports, the Keeper interprets. He said it twice. Then he went to find his pastry.”

“Ah.”

“There isn’t anyone else.” She said it to the floor, quickly, as if it were a debt. “There’s the Rules, and there’s him, and there’s the Keeper, and the Keeper is—” She did not finish it. She raised her grey eyes to him, and they were not a child’s. “I’ve nobody else to tell.”

Nine nights, he thought. Nine nights was a hand’s width of time, and a girl with a perfect memory and nowhere to put it, and a valley he knew better than he knew the back of his own hand. His sister’s valley. His sister, who had not written at Midwinter.

He got up. It took a moment; the knee had to be consulted. He went to the stove, and picked up the kettle, and found it light, as it had been for twelve years, and went on holding it.

“Nine nights,” he said. “Sit down. How many are left?”

Reet sat. She sat on the edge of the customers’ stool as if it might be taken from her, with the satchel on her knees, and her ink-dyed hands closed on the strap.

“Eight,” she said.

And Toomas Veskimae, for the first time in a very long while, filled the kettle at the jug and set it on the ring, and took the second cup from the shelf and turned it the right way up.

chapters.title: Naturally
chapters.html:
The Keeper’s summons came on a card the size of a playing card, carried by a lamp-boy who would not look at her, and said in a hand like a row of pins: Second bell. My rooms. Bring the draught.

Reet read it on the loft landing with the smell of last night’s frying still in the stairwell. She had not slept. She had lain in her bunk with her eyes open and Toomas Veskimae’s shop laid out in her head, the press, the two cups, the pencil moving over the back of the endpaper, and at some hour of the morning she had found that she could not remember what he had said to her at the door. She could remember the words. She could not remember whether he had meant them kindly. It was the first time she had been unable to put a face to a sentence, and she disliked it more than she could say.

What he had said was this. If they send for you, go, and say nothing about where you have been. If they send for you twice, run. There is a gate in the south wall where the wharves are. I am generally there at noon, feeding a duck.

She had not asked which duck.

The Keeper’s rooms lay along the vault antechamber, three small chambers in a row like beads on a string, with a door apiece into the passage. Reet knocked at the first. At the end of the passage the iron door with its three locks stood shut in the light of its caged lamp, and she did not look at it.

“Come.”

It was a low room with no window but a lightwell, a fire the size of a hat, and shelves of Guild ledgers bound in the same oxblood calf as far as the ceiling. On a table covered with green baize stood a tray: a silver pot, two cups so thin that the firelight came through them. Behind the tray, with her feet not quite reaching the floor, sat a very small woman.

Kaie Tammaru could not have been five feet tall. She was the smallest Keeper in the Guild’s history, and her hair, which was silver rather than grey, was plaited into one rope that came over her shoulder, lay across her lap and, when she stood, hung to her waist, thick as a wrist. Her face was thin and tired and kind, with the fine lines at the eyes of someone who had read by lamplight for thirty years. Her hands lay folded on the baize. They wore gloves: white kidskin, thin as a second skin, buttoned at the wrist with seed-pearl buttons.

“Reet Sallik. Come in, and sit, and take tea. You take tea, naturally.”

“Thank you, Keeper.”

“Kaie, in this room, if you will. The title is for the stairs.” She poured, with the gloved hands, and did not spill a drop. “You are looking at my gloves. It is a Keeper’s habit. The vellum is older than either of us, naturally, and skin is a poor thing to lay on it.”

The tea was black and smoky and had a pinch of salt in it, as they took it on the Pale Flats. Reet drank some to have something to do with her mouth.

“Master Org brought me your draught last night,” said Kaie. “He was a little alarmed. I told him that alarm is the correct response to good work. Your pin-sheet from Kuld came up with the frame as well. The Hallik stone.” She said it as she might have said the weather. “Day-ink on a stone that is already walking is a difficult thing, I am told. I have always admired riders who can do it.”

“It was only going into the lake.”

“And it stopped.”

“Yes.”

“Naturally,” said Kaie, and her gloved fingers closed on the edge of the baize and opened again. “Your draught, please.”

Reet took the sheet from her satchel. It was long and narrow, with fourteen columns ruled on it in her square left-handed script, and Kaie unfolded it on the baize and smoothed it flat with her palm, as if it were something that might wake. Then she reached to a roll of green baize at her elbow and took out a pair of brass dividers.

They were old. The pivot was worn bright where a thumb had turned it for years. And one leg had a knee in it, a little above the middle, so that when Kaie stood them point-down on the paper they leaned: one leg true and the other kicked out at an angle, like a dancer’s foot at rest.

Reet noticed the lean the way she noticed a wrong number, without wishing to, and put it away to look at later.

Kaie walked the dividers along the draught. She set the points on the first entry and then on the first Shift, and lifted, and set them on the next, and the steel tapped the paper with a small clean sound. “Nine nights,” she said. “And nine. And nine.” Each step landed on its mark. She went down all fourteen without a word, and at the end she laid the dividers on the baize, where they sat at their slant, and looked at Reet with great and genuine warmth.

“It is very exact,” she said. “May I ask what you believe it means?”

“I don’t know what it means. I know that it’s there.”

“That is an honest answer, naturally.” Kaie smiled. “You have found a rhythm in the Book that no one in this House has troubled to look for in eight years. Not Master Org, who audits it for tidiness. Not I. That is a gift, and I do not use the word loosely. The Guild’s habits are old and their reasons older, and a rota of re-inking kept by clerks who have long forgotten why—it is not impossible. I shall look into it myself.” She turned her cup a quarter-turn on its saucer. “I should be grateful if you would speak of it to no one in the meantime. A place like this lives on rumour, and the Hollow has forty thousand people who like to think the ground is steady.”

“Yes, Keeper.”

“Kaie.”

“Yes. Kaie.”

“Good.” She was still smoothing the draught with one gloved hand, in small even strokes. “May I ask you a different question? Have you spoken to Toomas Veskimae?”

It was asked so lightly that Reet had already begun to answer before she understood what she was answering.

“I— I— I have not.”

The words came out of her in pieces, one after another, like beads off a broken string. She heard each one land. In the lightwell a drip of water counted four. Kaie did not look surprised. She nodded slowly, once, as a woman nods at a figure in a column that has come out as expected, and took her hand from the paper.

“Thank you,” she said.

Reet’s face was hot. She could have said it again, steadily, and it would not have helped; the Guild knew about her tongue. Everyone knew. She had thought of that as a harmless peculiarity, like the notch in her eyebrow, and it had never occurred to her until this minute that a thing everyone knew could be used.

“He was my teacher,” Kaie said, to the teapot. “I think of him often. He was a very fine Keeper, until he was not, and I should hate to learn that anyone had been troubling him.”

“Is he in trouble?”

“Not from me.” She lifted her eyes. They were a pale brown, and there was nothing in them but concern. “Reet, you are tired. You have ridden every dawn for four years. A mind like yours is a lamp, and lamps are not meant to burn all day. I am giving you leave of absence, on full pay, for as long as it takes to rest. You will report to Master Org at the fourth bell each morning, so that I may be sure you are resting. And he will sit outside your door, for your protection.”

“From what?”

“From yourself, naturally. You are the sort who does not stop.”

“I don’t want leave.”

“No. Naturally you don’t.” Kaie rose, and the braid slid with her, and she was no taller standing than she had been sitting. “Leave the draught with me. It will be kept safe. You have extraordinary hands, Reet, and I should like to see them used well.”

At the door Reet looked back. The Keeper had sat down again. She was drawing the dividers toward her across the baize, in her gloved fingers, and they walked toward her slowly, one leg after the other, with the same lean, like something that had learned to move that way and would not be corrected.

Mihkel Org was sitting on a stool outside her room in the riders’ loft, with a copy of the Rules open on his knee and a sugar bun he was trying to eat with the book between it and the corridor. He half-rose, shut the Rules on the bun, and sat down again.

“Sallik. I am to—”

“I know.”

“Rule Ninety. A Surveyor on leave shall be watched for her own good.” He looked miserable. “I do not think it is a good Rule.”

“You could have said so.”

“I am a Master-Surveyor, I do not say so, I merely—” He stopped. “I am sorry for it. There. Rule One Hundred and Four, which I have just made up, says an apology is in order.”

She nearly liked him. That was the trouble with Mihkel.

“May I fetch clean linen, Master?” she said. “Rule Sixty.”

“Rule Sixty is the weight of Sheet-paper. Linen is Sixty-One.” He waved the bun. “Go on. It’s in the cupboard. Don’t be long.”

The linen cupboard stood beside her door, a tall closet of shelves and sheets that smelled of camphor and of lamp-oil, because its back wall had a hatch in it. She had known about the hatch since she was fifteen. Everyone in the loft did, and none of them admitted it. It gave on the lamp-boys’ stair, a spiral cut inside the Hollow’s wall, where the boys went up and down with their cans in the dark and nobody who mattered ever went at all.

She had packed the satchel before the Keeper’s card came, from an instinct she had not examined. It was on the bunk. The chain hung on its peg by the door. Under the pillow lay her mother’s last letter, the one about the drain, and she took that too, though she did not need it; she could have said it aloud from the date to the postscript about the plum tree. But a thing she could say was a thing only she could say, and she was beginning to understand that this was not the same as a thing being known. She took them all into the cupboard, among the sheets, and shut the door on Mihkel’s voice saying, “Fresh sheets, mind, not the good ones”; and she pressed the thin onion-skin tracing flat against her ribs under her shirt, where it crackled at her breastbone like a small dry animal, and put her shoulder to the hatch.

The stair was black and narrow and smelled of oil. Her feet found the steps by habit. Below her a can clanked; a small pale face looked up at her from a landing, soot-black to the eyes.

“Sallik?”

“Ants. You haven’t seen me.”

“Nobody sees anybody on this stair,” said Ants, comfortably. “That’s what it’s for. The Wharf Gate’s down and left, the third landing, and the step’s gone, jump it.”

She jumped it. She went down for what felt like a long time, past the thin slits of light where the stair opened on the terraces, and at each one the Hollow went by in a strip: a woman shaking a rug; a stack of barrels; a dog on a roof. She tested herself as she went. Cairn. Hedge. The Guild stair, four hundred and nineteen steps. All were present. It was only the yard at the stone that was missing, a smooth hole she could feel with her mind like a tongue feels a gap.

The Wharf Gate was a broad arch in the south wall, where the Cold Stream left the Hollow through a cut in the rock. Flat-bottomed barges lay along the wharf under a tide-mark of moss, and a flock of ducks went about the stone quay with the air of a committee. Beyond the arch the daylight lay white on the plain, and the road ran out into it. The gate-sergeant, a man with a pie, had looked at the chain on her shoulder and the satchel on her back as she came through the guard-room and said, “On leave, then?” She had said yes, which was true, and he had said, “Lucky,” and gone back to the pie, and she had walked on feeling that her face had been written on in large letters.

Toomas Veskimae sat on a bollard at the edge of the quay. He was in his boots, and he had a canvas bag at his feet that sagged on one side, and the chain-staff across his knees. He was breaking a crust into small pieces and dropping them to a duck, which regarded each piece as an insult.

“Bread,” he said, before she had asked. He nodded at the bag. “Only bread.”

“It’s very heavy bread.”

“It is a very good loaf.”

She stood in front of him on the wet stones. There was a place in her chest where something had been wound too tight for too long, and it began, quite without her permission, to come undone.

“I stammered,” said Reet.

Toomas did not look up from the duck. “I know,” he said. “I heard it from the next street.”

chapters.title: Ilves Black
chapters.html:
In the vat-house it was always night. The shutters had been nailed shut since Salme Ilves’s grandfather’s day, because daylight turned gall-liquor the colour of weak tea, so the lamps burned from the first bell to the last and the vats stood in their rows in the yellow dark, breathing sulphur. Toomas had smelled that breath from the corner of Tinta Row, as he had smelled it on the way to every dealing he had ever had with the Ilveses. It got into the back of the throat and stayed. It was the smell of forty years of Guild business, and it had not improved with keeping.

“Mind the third plank,” he said over his shoulder. “It has been loose since the Assembly last sat.”

Reet minded it. She walked behind him with her satchel held against her chest and her eyes going from vat to vat, counting, and he could have told her how many without looking: thirty-one, in four rows, each the height of a tall man and stoppered with a wooden lid on which some Ilves of the last century had burned the batch-date with a hot iron. There were no clerks. The vat-men had been sent home early, which in itself told him something, since Salme Ilves had never sent a man home in her life without being threatened first.

She was at the far end, with her sleeves pushed up and a long paddle in her fist, stirring a vat the colour of a bruise. She was short and wide and stood like a woman who has planted her feet and defied the floor to move them. Her forearms were blue-black to the elbow. Her grey hair was crammed under a leather cap, and in the corner of her mouth was a thin black cigar, burning at a pace that suggested a grievance.

“Veskimae,” she said, without turning. “I heard you’d died.”

“The reports were exaggerated.”

“Twelve years. I sent a wreath to the Row, and the florist said you hadn’t any need of it, you’d been seen buying thread.” She looked round then, and her small black eyes went over him, over the stained moustache and the white eye and the chain-staff, and over Reet, and came back. “You’ve brought me a child.”

“I have brought you a rider.”

“She’s the Sallik girl. With the head.” Salme put down the paddle. “Sit. Not there, that’s acid. Taavi!”

A noise came from behind the third row, a clink of glass, a thump, a sound of someone apologising to a shelf. A young man came round the vats at a half-run, holding a pestle like a candle. He was twenty and all angles, with a freckled face, ears that stood out like the handles of a jug, and fingertips stained the blue-grey of a pigeon’s wing. Across his chest crossed a bandolier, and in every loop of the bandolier sat a tiny stoppered vial, so that when he moved he rang softly, like a small and nervous church.

“Stand up straight,” said his mother. “You look like a question.” She seized him by the ears, which she could reach by holding them, and kissed him on the forehead with a smack that rang off the vats. “My son. Best nose on the Row. Worst taste in waistcoats. He can tell you which oak a gall grew on, and which side of the tree the wasp was on. Say hello, Taavi.”

“Hello,” said Taavi. “I’m so sorry. Technically I don’t know any of you.”

“You will,” said Toomas. “Reet, the sliver.”

She took it out of the thumb of her glove with great care. It was a speck smaller than a grain of rice, a fleck of black with a dull gleam on one side. Taavi took it on the blade of a spatula, and Toomas, watching his hands, saw the hands go still. He saw Salme not look at them.

“Where did it come from?” said Taavi.

“The lower corner of a leaf,” said Reet. “The new ink. It hadn’t dried.”

“Hadn’t dried.” He licked his lips. “That’s, technically, not possible. Iron-gall dries in an afternoon. Even Ilves Black. Unless it’s—” He stopped himself. He laid the sliver on a white tile, put one drop of water on it from a dropper, and watched the drop go dark, not at once, but in a slow spreading bloom, like smoke finding the edge of a room. Then he reached up to a shelf without looking and brought down a stoppered flask of tincture. He added a bead. The black went through a colour Toomas had not seen in twelve years, a clear violet that deepened and would not settle.

Taavi bent down. He put his nose to the tile, and then, the poor boy, his tongue to a speck on the end of his finger.

“It’s, technically, an iron-gall,” he said. “In the sense that it has iron and gall in it. Technically it isn’t ours. I mean, it isn’t anybody’s. It has, technically, the right sulphur in it, but there’s the salt as well, the Pale Flats salt, in proportion, and the lamp-black has been ground so fine that—” He stopped. He wiped his finger on his apron again and again. He had gone the colour of his own fingertips. “It isn’t Black,” he said, in an entirely different voice. “It’s Founding.”

The vat-house was very quiet. A lid ticked in the dark.

“Don’t be a goose,” said Salme.

“It’s Founding grade. Nobody has made it, Mother. Not for three hundred years. It’s in the book, Great-grandmother’s page, you showed me once as a joke, and nobody could make it up because the base wasn’t—” He stopped. “It was made by someone who knew. I’ve never smelled it in my life and I know it like a face.”

Toomas looked at the sliver on the tile and thought of a stoppered jar he had once emptied, to the lees, with a steady hand and a bad reason; and he put the thought where he put such thoughts, as a man puts a coin in a boot.

“There is more,” said Taavi, unhappily. He had bent over the tile again, because he could not help it. “It’s got water in it. It was mixed with water, and the water was local. It’s bog-iron. There’s sedge ash in it, and peat, and a bit of... here.” He held out the tile. “Smell.”

Reet smelled. She said at once, “That’s the drain behind Kalda’s mill.”

Taavi stared at her. “Is it?”

“Sora Crossing. It’s the marsh drain. I grew up two hundred yards from it.” Her voice was entirely level. “The leaf had been re-inked, and the ink was made with water from the place that was moved. It was made there, or the water was taken from there. Either way, the ink was made with Sora’s water, and you can taste it.”

“Don’t,” said Taavi. “Please. I don’t want to.”

Toomas turned his head. “Salme.”

The ink-mistress had taken the cigar from her mouth. It was a very small gesture. “Rubbish,” she said. “The boy has been at the sulphur. He does this. He once told me a barrel of Black was haunted.”

“It was haunted,” said Taavi faintly.

“I have sold the Guild forty-one barrels of Black a year for twenty-six years,” said Salme, “and not a pint short, and not a drop of anything else but, roughly, the odd cask of something special years back, that’s all, to a clerk, nothing like that. I’ve not made that stuff in my life. I couldn’t make it if I tried.” She put the cigar back in her mouth. “Who is the Sallik girl to tell me what I make?”

Toomas watched Taavi.

He did not know, afterwards, why he watched the boy and not the mother. It was an old habit, perhaps; in the Atlas a man learned to look for the thing that moved against the grain of the page. And Taavi had flinched. It was the smallest flinch, a tightening of the freckled face, as if a thread had been drawn through it. His mother said roughly, and years back, and the odd cask, and the boy’s eyes went to the floor, and Toomas understood that Salme Ilves, who loved precisely and counted exactly and had never in her son’s hearing said about, had lied. And that her son had heard it.

Taavi did not look up. He pressed the pestle to his chest. And Toomas saw him see it, and saw him decide to be a person who had not.

“Mm,” said Toomas, very softly, to nobody. “A wall remembers.”

The knock at the front of the works was three heavy blows.

“In the Guild’s name,” a man’s voice said, through the door and the vat-house and the thickness of the sulphur. “Open to the Surveyor’s office.”

Nobody moved. Then Salme took the cigar from her mouth and said, in an entirely different voice, quick and dry and without a trace of a joke, “Dye room. Taavi, the ladder. Veskimae, you’ll go over the plank, and mind your knee. Move.”

The dye room lay behind the vats, down three steps, a long low shed lit by one skylight set in the roof, with a copper vat running the length of it, as long as a boat and full of a green so deep it looked solid. A plank crossed it at the middle, and at the far side stood a ladder to the roof hatch. Toomas looked at the plank, and then at the green, and then at his knee.

“I will not be—”

Reet had him by the arm. “Plank,” she said. “Quickly.”

He took two steps. The plank, which had held generations of Ilves dyers and every sort of confidence, took exception to the third. It tipped. He went in to the thigh with a sound like a cow stepping off a cliff, and the green closed round him, warm and thick and smelling of vinegar and copper, and for a moment he stood in it with his chain-staff held over his head like a man fording the Pale. Reet hauled. He came out onto the far side dripping, green to the hip, with the boots squelching and his dignity somewhere in the vat.

At the dye-room door a man in a grey coat burst through from the back lane and stopped. He had a warrant in his hand. He had the look of a man who has been told this will be easy.

Salme Ilves was behind him with a bucket.

She flung it with the whole of her shoulder. The lamp-black went through the doorway in a single dense wave, took the watcher full in the face and chest, and left him a black pillar with two white eyes, standing perfectly still. “Rule Eighty-Four,” she said, “of the Ilves house: you don’t come in the back.” And she spat out her cigar and trod on it.

“Up,” she said to the others. “Up. The roof. Go.”

Reet went up the ladder like a squirrel. Toomas followed, one rung and one considered breath at a time, with the green running out of his trousers. The hatch opened on white sky, and a roof of slates, and a gutter, and then the next roof, and the next, tilting down the terraces toward the Wharf Gate like a staircase built for cats.

“Taavi!” Salme’s voice, from below. “Don’t be a—”

A clatter. The ladder shook. A pair of long arms arrived over the lip of the hatch, then a freckled face with its ears alight in the daylight, then the rest of him, ringing like a bell all the way out of the hatch with the bandolier tangled in his arm. He sat on the slates, panting.

“I’m so sorry,” said Taavi to the sky. “I took your brass funnel, Mother, and the good indigo. I’m sorry about the indigo. Technically they’re mine, the funnel was a present, but I should have—”

“Keep the funnel!” Salme shouted up from the dye room. “Keep it clean! Go!”

He looked at Reet, and at Toomas, who was green to the waist and was leaning on the chimney-pot, and Toomas saw that he did not know whether he was allowed. A boy who had waited twenty years for someone to say come, and who was too well brought up to ask.

“I’m not, technically, invited,” said Taavi.

“You are now,” said Reet.

They went down the roofs in the flat white light of early afternoon, across the terraces and along a ridge-tile and down a drainpipe that held, with the Hollow opening under them like a bowl of lamps. A watcher shouted in the lane. Nobody looked. At the bottom of the lane the Wharf Gate yawned, and the barges, and the ducks, and Salme Ilves herself, red-faced, standing at the quay with her hands on her hips, as if she had never left it.

“You went the long way,” she said, and she was hardly out of breath.

“Mother, how did you—”

“I know the back streets better than the Guild knows its own Rules, which is not hard.” She put her hand in the pocket of her apron and brought out a flask. It was small, stoneware, no longer than a hand, stoppered with a plug of wax and bound at the neck with red thread. She did not look at it. She pressed it into Taavi’s palm and closed his fingers over it with both her own, hard, so that her knuckles whitened. “Don’t drink it,” she said. “Don’t lose it. Don’t tell me where.”

“What is it?”

“A flask. Is a flask a conversation?”

“Mother—”

“Go and be useful.” She kissed him on the forehead, and then, swiftly, on each of his ears, and then she turned and walked back up the lane with her short wide stride and did not look round, and the green light of the arch swallowed her.

Taavi stood with the flask in his fist. His hand was shaking. “I need to do up the bandolier,” he said, to nobody, “I’ve lost a loop,” and he held the flask out to Toomas without looking, the way a person passes the baby while he ties a shoe.

Toomas took it.

It was warm. Not the warmth of a thing left in the sun, which comes from outside; it was warm all through, as the heart of a loaf is warm, and in the stone there was a faint living pulse of it, the warmth of a thing that had been held in a hand against the body for a very long time.

chapters.title: Oxen Named for Officials
chapters.html:
Forty wagons stood in the Salt Company yard in three ragged rows, and a very tall woman was reading their oxen aloud to them.

“Registrar. Deputy Registrar. Auditor, Assistant Auditor, and that one’s Auditor’s Cousin, he’s only on loan. Guildmaster, who stands in the middle of the road and makes everyone go round him. Quartermaster, Treasurer, the Speaker.” She had a voice that crossed a yard without being raised, and a long salt-hook slung across her back like a bishop’s crook. She was six foot two, with a shaved head and a red scarf wound three times round her neck, and when she grinned a front tooth was chipped in a small neat triangle. “Rule Forty. He sleeps all day, he’s against the wheel. And that one,” she said, pointing the hook, “is Mihkel.”

Reet looked. The ox was dun-coloured, deep in the body and heavy in the shoulder, with a pale belly like a mustard-yellow waistcoat.

She made a small noise, and put her hand over her mouth.

“You know him?” said the woman.

“I know someone very like him.”

“Everybody does.” She looked down at Reet with sharp, amused, assessing eyes, and then past her at Toomas, who had been dried by a barge-woman’s stove and was still faintly green below the knee, and at Taavi, who clinked. “Aino Rebane. Guard. I’ve thirty-six oxen and forty wagons, and I’ll tell you now the arithmetic is a matter of faith. Four of them tow, like ducklings. You’ll want to be pilgrims.”

“We are pilgrims,” said Toomas.

“To?”

“The Bridge at Palu. The Name-Day feast. We are going to tie a ribbon.”

“Nobody goes on pilgrimage to a bridge.” Aino folded her arms. “It’s six days of mud for a rope. The Company doesn’t care what you are. I care whether your boots are clean, because a pilgrim has dirty knees from praying, and yours are spotless.”

“We pray standing,” said Toomas.

She looked at him for a good five seconds. “That’s the worst lie I’ve heard this month,” she said, “and I’ve been in the Salt trade since I was fifteen. Nine marks for the three of you, and your own bread, and you walk when I say walk. I don’t want to know why.”

“Six.”

“Nine. The sick one’s cheaper.”

“I’m not sick,” said Taavi. “Technically I’m only apprehensive.”

“Eight, then,” said Aino, “and I’ll take the funny one at half.” And she stuck out a hand like a spade, and Toomas shook it, and counted eight silver marks into it from a purse that was clearly not going to survive the journey. When he offered to bind the Company’s ledgers for life as a supplement, she looked at him as if he had offered her a goat.

It was after the third afternoon bell when the yard began to move. The master of the train, Hendrik Loo, a man who wore his hat indoors and out and had not been seen without it since the spring, walked down the line shouting names at oxen. The oxen ignored him. Registrar leaned into his yoke with an air of pained dignity, and the wagon in front of Reet shuddered, creaked and began to roll. She walked beside it with her satchel, her chain over her shoulder and the tracing against her ribs, and did not look back at the Hollow, because she could not stand to see how little there was to see. A dark smudge of rim and a thread of smoke. Lamp-boys. Mihkel, on his stool, with a bun.

The wagons made a noise like a village moving house. Axles shrieked, harness chimed, and under it all went the slow wet tread of thirty-six pairs of hooves on the frozen ruts, steady as a clock. Everything smelled of salt: the sacks, the planks, the oxen’s flanks, the very air, so that every breath was faintly a preservative. Salt was the one cargo that did not mind where it woke up. A bale of wool could be ruined by a night in the wrong field, a cask of ink by a tilt of the road, but a block of salt weighed what it weighed in any country, and the Company had built a hundred years of trade on that dull fact. Reet, walking in the ruts with her chain clinking, thought it the most reassuring thing she had heard all week.

Aino fell in beside her at the third mile, with the hook over one shoulder.

“Right, rider,” she said. “You’re a Guild girl. I can see the ink. What’s at the Three Pines?”

“Three pines,” said Reet.

“Ha. Very good. What else?”

“A mile and a half south of the edge. One of the three was burned by lightning in the autumn of GY 308 and is black on its west side. The ford beyond it was shin-deep at the last Sheet. There’s a stone with a K cut into it at the north end that marks the Kesk boundary, and a dead heron in the second bend of the stream, or there was a month ago.”

“Is the heron still there?”

“I don’t know. It was a month ago.”

“Hm.” Aino walked in silence for a while. “Kesk’s well.”

“Eleven feet to the water. Stone-lined. A cracked lip on the east side.”

“What colour’s the handle?”

“There isn’t a handle. It’s a rope and a bucket. The bucket’s tin with a blue rim.”

“You’re guessing.”

“I don’t guess.”

“Then you’re mad,” said Aino, “or useful,” and she looked, to Reet’s surprise, quite put out. “I hate that. I was hoping you’d be useless, and I could be rude to you till Palu.”

“Both are possible.”

“Don’t be clever. It makes it worse.” But she was almost smiling, and the chipped tooth showed. Reet found, with an odd sideways drop of the stomach, that she wanted to go on being useful to her, and that this was a thing she had not wanted from anyone in four years.

They reached the Seam’s edge at sunset.

It was not a line. People imagined it as a line, a hedge, a river, and it was nothing of the kind; it was a thickening. Three miles from the Wharf Gate, where the Seam bellied north in a long belly that was a mile wider every year, the road ran on across heath exactly as it had before, and the heath looked exactly as it had, and the sky went tight. Reet could not have said how. It was as if the whole dome had been drawn up over a mast, and the air strained against it like canvas in a rising wind, with every sound she made coming back to her half a breath late. The light turned long and brass-coloured. The shadows of the wagons ran sideways, off the road, into the heather. The oxen put their ears forward, all thirty-six, and went on walking.

“Hold your hat,” said Aino, who wasn’t wearing one.

Nothing happened. That was the thing about the edge. Nothing happened, and you were in it.

They made camp in the first dusk, in a ring: forty wagons, thirty-six oxen, and a stew. The oxen were staked on long tethers outside the circle, each to an iron stake driven in with a mallet, and Aino went round them with a lantern, patting each flank and giving it a title. “Evening, Treasurer. Don’t look at me like that, you know what you did.”

Across the dark, a hundred yards off, another lantern swung. A voice came with it.

“Hoy the Salt! Who’s your north?”

“We are!” Aino bellowed back.

“No, who’s your northmost wagon?”

“We are, you ass, we’re all in a ring! You’re our north!”

“We’re not north, we’re east!”

“You’re a wool train. You don’t have an east!”

“We’ve an east and a west and a lost cousin! Who’s your Guildmaster?”

“He’s the one in the middle of the road!”

“We’ve one of those!”

“That’ll be ours! Give him back!”

This went on for some while, to the great pleasure of the camp. It was stake-and-ask, the custom of the road: a caravan staked its oxen at dusk, then asked its neighbour where it was, because after the Shift nobody would be sure. They were the Mägi wool train, said the voice at last, thirty wagons of fleece, and they were stationed, so far as anyone could tell, to the left of the Salt Company. “Which left?” shouted Aino. “The left that’s ours,” came the answer, with dignity; and Reet, sitting with her back against a wheel, found she was laughing, silently, for the first time in two days.

Aino told the story of the wagon that woke in a barn, over the stew.

“Real barn,” she said. “Hay, a cow, a farmer. This was a wagon-master I knew, Joosep, a decent man, and he’d gone to sleep on the Flats in the middle of nothing, and when he woke there was a roof. The cow was extremely upset. So was the farmer, who wanted rent for the night.” She dug a spoon into the pot. “Joosep paid. A bale of salt. He said it was the only time he’d ever got a better night’s sleep than he’d expected.”

“Where was the barn?” said Reet.

“Where it had been. They’d gone to it.” Aino laughed through her nose. “That’s the Seam. It doesn’t pick you up. It sets you down.” She stood, brushed off her knees, and picked up from beside the wheel a wicker basket with a cloth over it. She carried it the way another woman might carry an infant. “Hens,” she said. “I keep six. Best layers in the Seam. They sulk if I’m late.”

“They’re very quiet,” said Reet.

“They’re shy.” She went off past the last wagon, into the dark beyond the lantern light, where the ground was bare of heather and the sky was already pricked with stars.

Reet watched her go. She noticed the direction, because she noticed everything: away from the camp, north, toward the Hollow. She noticed that the basket was lifted, just once, high, as one lifts a bowl at a feast. She heard, or thought she heard, a small dry clatter, like a hand of cards being shaken. She filed the three of them with the other things she had not yet needed, and then Taavi, behind her, was sick over the wheel.

“Sorry,” said Taavi, from a distance. “I’m so sorry. It’s the, technically it’s the ground.”

“It isn’t moving,” said Reet.

“It feels as if it’s thinking of moving.” He sat down, very green himself. “Some people get it before. Like a man who feels the weather in his teeth.”

Toomas had come out of the dark with a twist of paper in his hand. He knelt beside the boy, which cost him, she saw, and she heard the knee crack like a stick. “Mint,” he said. “Chew, do not swallow. It is dried, from my own window, and it has never done anyone any harm except my guests.” He folded Taavi’s fingers around it. “Look at the horizon. At a fixed star, if you can find one. And breathe out longer than you breathe in.”

“Is that a proverb?”

“It is a remedy. The proverbs I keep for people who are not sick.”

He stayed with Taavi for an hour, talking about nothing, the best way to cut a mitre, the price of calf-skin, a quarrel between two binders in his youth over a monogram, and Reet sat with her back to the wheel and watched him. She watched him, once, look back over the dark, north, to where the sky above the Hollow glowed a faint dull orange on the underside of the cloud. He looked at it longer than at the south. He said nothing. His face was perfectly calm, in the lantern-light, and his hand on the boy’s back went on moving in small slow circles, and Reet thought: he is saying nothing about something, and it is very large. And she did what she did not often do. She let it alone.

Midnight arrived without any warning. It was quite dark. The fires had burned down. In the wagon above her someone was snoring in two keys. Reet, who had been lying on her back with her eyes open counting the stars she knew, found that she had stopped being able to hold the count.

The sound came first. It was not loud. It was low, so low that she felt it through the ground and into the base of her spine before it was a sound at all, and it came from the south, a long, deep, rolling roar like surf heard through a wall. All forty wagons shifted on their axles. Thirty-six oxen lifted their heads and lowed, one after another, down the line. The lantern on the wagon-tail guttered and leaned, and she saw the flame lie over sideways, pointing north, as if the whole world had tipped a degree on its keel.

And then she felt it. She had never been in the Seam at midnight. She had ridden out at dawn for four years to what the night had done. Now she was in it, and it was not like an earthquake, not like anything she knew; it was like standing on the deck of a ship that has begun, very gently, to turn. The stars slid. A black hill she had marked at dusk went by on her left, in no hurry, and a smell of wet stone, and cold, and brine came out of the dark; and all of it, the roaring, the turning, the sliding of the world, lasted perhaps the length of a long breath and went out.

Silence. A single ox, complaining.

Nobody spoke. Then Taavi, somewhere in the dark, said in a very small voice, “Oh, I’m going to be sick again,” and from the wagon above her somebody laughed, and the camp began to murmur, and lanterns came up one by one.

Reet lay still. She was shaking. She ran her mind back down the evening, the road, the Three Pines, the heron, and found them all, and the cairn and the hedge and the Guild stair, and the smooth hole at the stone. Nothing new was missing. She had not drawn anything. She held the thought carefully, as one holds a cup that is nearly full, and she lay on the ground that had turned, and did not know where she was.

Aino came by with a mallet and a stake. She did not say anything. She walked round the wagon-tail in the lantern-light, found a place by the near wheel, and drove the stake into the ground with three exact blows.

“What’s that for?” said Reet. “If it moves.”
