Aino leaned on the mallet and looked down at her, tall and black against the stars, with the red scarf pale at her throat.

“It’ll still move,” she said. “The stake’s just so we know where we woke up.”

chapters.title: The Road That Ended
chapters.html:
The road ended at breakfast, which Toomas thought rude of it.

He had woken with the knee. It did not wait for the Shift to be over to complain of it; it began at the first grey, a hot bar laid across the joint, and he lay under the wagon for some while doing his sums. A man of sixty-two who has slept on ground that moved in the night should be grateful to be lying in one piece. He tried gratitude. The knee did not accept it. So he crawled out into a morning the colour of skimmed milk, got the chain-staff under him and levered himself up, and found the whole camp standing at the edge of the world with its porridge going cold.

The wagons had come to rest in a ring, as they were meant to. That was the odd mercy of the Seam: it set you down in your own arrangement. But forty yards beyond the northmost wagon the heath stopped. It did not slope. It simply left off, in a clean raw lip of turf with the roots hanging out, and past the lip was air, and in the air a long way down was a river the width of a bootlace, lying in a gorge with a mist on it.

“Yesterday,” said Hendrik Loo, the Company’s master, “there was a road.”

“There was,” said Aino.

“With a ditch on the left and a milestone.”

“Eleven miles to Kesk’s well. I know. I looked at the milestone myself.” She held a bowl of porridge in one hand and her salt-hook in the other, and appeared to have forgotten which was which. “It’s gone, Hendrik. It’s down there somewhere, with the ditch.”

Master Loo did not remove his hat, because he never did, but he turned it a quarter-turn on his head, which in a man of his habits amounted to a scream. Behind him the wool-train’s mistress had come across from her own ring, a thin woman in a man’s coat called Mägi, as her train was, and she stood with her hands in her sleeves and said that the Seam had done the same to her grandmother at Tallow Moor and that grandmother had gone round.

“Round which way?” said Loo.

“She never said. She died before she’d got there.”

They argued for the better part of an hour. West, said Loo, because the Company’s charter named west in bad ground. East, said Mistress Mägi, because wool did not like to be wet and the western lip had a look of drizzle. Someone proposed lowering the wagons by rope, and was asked by whom, and into what. Toomas leaned on his staff and let it wash past him; he had sat through forty years of the Assembly, and he knew the sound of men arguing in order not to be the one who decided. It was the sound of a kettle that has been told it may not boil.

In the end the oxen decided. A beast called Auditor, who had stood at the edge looking down with the long patience of his office, turned his head, swung it west along the rim, and began to walk. The Guildmaster fell in behind him, and Treasurer behind that, and the whole line of them went off at the plodding pace of animals who know they are being watched, and the masters, seeing their cattle depart, found that they had reached an agreement.

“West,” said Loo, with dignity.

“I always said west,” said Mistress Mägi.

Toomas rode ahead on a pony called Clerk, which Aino had lent him on the grounds that Clerk reads nothing and carries everything. It was a mealy, short-legged animal with an expression of settled disappointment. Reet rode beside him on the Company’s second pony, sitting it as she did everything, upright and exactly, as if the saddle had been surveyed.

They went at a walk along the rim, a quarter-mile in front of the oxen. This was the work he had been trained for, once, and it surprised him how easily it came back, like a dance learned in youth. The ground in the Seam was a language that kept changing its nouns. You could not trust the nouns. You could trust the grammar.

“The rim runs west by north,” he said. “And the heath tilts toward it. Do you know why?”

“It’s been pulled,” said Reet. “The turf on this side is stretched. Look at the heather, it’s been combed toward the edge. Something heavy went over, and took the ground with it.” She did not turn her head. Her grey eyes were running along the lip as a finger runs along a column. “Four hundred and ten paces back we crossed a hawthorn that has its roots on the far side of a wall. It’s moved about seven yards from its wall. The wall hasn’t.”

“And so?”

“And so the slope is new, and it’s pitched about one in nine, and the lip isn’t going to give. I’d trust it to a pony. I wouldn’t trust it to a wagon.”

“Mm. Say that shorter.”

“The edge will hold you. It won’t hold the Company.”

“Better.” He looked down the slope with his good eye, and then with the bad one, which saw a glare and a smear and had the advantage of not being impressed. “The contour grammar would say we are on a convex slope, falling away, with the ticks pointing down and the lines crowding. A ledge, then, where the lines spread out. Do you see where the lines spread?”

“No.”

“Nor do I. That is why we are riding.”

It took them forty minutes. The ledge, when they found it, was a shelf of limestone twenty feet wide that ran out from the rim like a tongue from a mouth, and at the end of it, bright against the grey, was something that did not belong to the morning at all. It was red. It was a post of new red larch, as thick as a man’s thigh, driven into a crack in the rock and bound with tarred cord, and from the post a bridge went out over nothing.

Reet counted it. He watched her do it, her lips moving without sound. Ninety-two feet of rope and plank, hand-rails of twisted hemp, the planks laid crosswise and wired, and on the far side a second red post, small as a matchstick. It swayed in the wind of the gorge. Under it there was a thousand feet of morning.

“Someone built this last night,” she said.

“Mm. Someone who was caught on the same side of the same cliff as we were, with a quantity of rope and no sense of occasion.” He pointed at the near post, where a tin tag swung on a nail. She dismounted and read it aloud.

“’Kask and Daughters, salt, southbound. Left for the next. Mind the ninth plank.’” She looked up. “It’s the custom?”

“It is the custom. A caravan that is lucky leaves what it built. A caravan that is unlucky does not need anything.” He tapped the red wood. “I have always found that the road has better manners than the people who govern it.”

The Salt Company reached the ledge by noon and stood in a long and uneasy line along it, looking at the bridge as if it had said something about their mothers.

Aino did not say a word. That was how Toomas knew. She was a woman who narrated; she had named thirty-six oxen after men she disliked and addressed each of them daily, she had heckled a wool train across a hundred yards of dark. Now she stood at the near post with her scarf wound to the chin and looked at the planks, and all the colour went out of her except the chipped front tooth. She said nothing for a minute and a half. Then she said, in a voice that carried to the back of the line, “Well, it’s only rope.”

“Aino,” said Reet.

“It’s perfectly good rope. Look at it. Tarred. Somebody’s mother made that rope.” Her voice was climbing. “Hendrik, who’s first? Somebody’s first. Is it the oxen? It should be the oxen, they’ve no imagination. I’m only saying, I’m the guard, the guard goes last, it’s in the charter, somebody has to watch the rear—”

“Aino,” said Toomas.

“—and there’s no rear, there’s a very large hole—”

“Aino. Is the charter in the habit of saying that?”

She stopped. She looked at him, and for a moment she was very young and very tall and seemed to be standing on something that was already moving. “No,” she said, in her ordinary voice. “No, it isn’t. I made that up.”

“Ah.” He nodded. “Good. We have established it.”

Nobody said anything else about it, then or afterwards. Reet crossed first, on foot, leading Clerk, counting the planks aloud in a level voice that carried back to the ledge: “Seven, eight, nine, mind it, ten.” The bridge swung as the pony stepped, a long slow swing that went out and came back like a pendulum, and the wind took a plank and set it dancing, and Toomas, standing at the near post with his staff, thought that if he lived he would never again complain about a staircase. The first ox went over after her. The second. The line began to pour.

Taavi crossed with his eyes shut and one hand locked on the hemp. He got to the middle, where the bridge hung lowest and sang in the wind, and stopped, and leaned out over the side with great dignity and was sick into the gorge. “I’m so sorry,” he called, to nobody, to the whole sky. “Technically that’s below us, it should be fine, it should be miles before—”

“It is a thousand feet,” said Reet from the far end. “Four seconds. Keep walking.”

“Four seconds to where?”

“Keep walking.”

The trouble came at the eleventh ox. Registrar was a big, slate-coloured, aggrieved animal, the oldest in the Company, and he walked up to the first plank, and put one hoof on it, and took it off again. He looked at the gorge. He looked at the bridge. He sat down. It was a considerable sitting, and it took the whole line behind him by surprise; the oxen piled up on the ledge, and a wagon-man swore, and Registrar closed his eyes with the serenity of a creature that has refused petitions all his life and will not be hurried by a petition from rope.

“He’s got principles,” said Aino, who had come forward, grey in the face. “He’s been refusing everything since he was a calf. I named him well.”

It was then that Toomas saw the far post move.

It was not much. A hand’s breadth. The weight on the span had grown, and the red larch on the far side, set in a crack of rotten shale, leaned toward the gorge with a small dry crackle, and the whole bridge gave a lurch that sent two oxen into the rail. He heard Reet call something. He was already moving, as fast as the knee would let him, which was not fast, across the swaying planks with the chain-staff in his fist.

“What are you doing?” Aino shouted. “Veskimae!”

“Crossing, I believe!”

He reached the far end at a limp. The post was leaning, the guy-cord was singing, and the crack it stood in was widening at the lip in a thin trail of grit. He looked about him for ground that had stood a long time. Behind the post the rock was sound, grey, old, a ridge of it, running back into the heath. He took the chain-staff in both hands, set its iron shoe into the nearest seam, and leaned on it with the whole of his weight, which was considerable, and wedged it. Then he took the guy-cord, passed it twice about the shaft, and tied it off in a knot he had not used since he was twenty-three.

“There,” he said. “Do you know what the Keeper before me said about moustaches?”

“What?” said Reet, who was holding the post.

“He said that a man’s moustache is the only part of him that sees the future, because it arrives first. He had a very large one. There was a morning in the Assembly when a sparrow was found to have nested in it, and he would not allow it to be disturbed until the fledglings had flown, and so for nine days the Guild’s accounts were audited by a man who could not nod.” He gave the knot a final pull. “On the tenth day, the sparrows left. And the Keeper, being a man of regular habits, then took a pair of scissors to the whole thing, and has been clean-shaven ever since. Do you know why?”

“No.”

“Because he said that he had learned, from the sparrows, that a thing is only worth keeping if something can live in it.” He looked up. “I have never been able to decide whether he meant the moustache.”

On the bridge behind them, and this was what he had been aiming for, the sound had changed. Aino was laughing. It was a cracked, furious, terrified laugh that went on and on, and between the gusts of it she was saying “a sparrow, oh, Veskimae, you old liar, a sparrow,” and the planks under her were creaking with each step she took toward them. She did not look down. She came off the last plank on her hands and knees, in the shale, with the laugh still going out of her like air from a bellows, and Reet took her by the elbow.

“Not a word,” said Aino.

“I didn’t say anything.”

“You were going to. Not a word. Not one.” She stood, and wiped her face on the red scarf, and pointed with the salt-hook back along the line. “Somebody get that ox up.”

Registrar, as it turned out, crossed with Reet in front of him, walking backwards, counting aloud. He took one plank at a time, with the air of an animal conferring a favour.

By the middle of the afternoon the Company was over, wagon by wagon, hauled across with the oxen unhitched and the wheels roped, and the last of the wool train had begun to follow. The wind had dropped. Toomas sat on a boulder on the south side with the knee stretched in front of him and a tin mug of tea that Taavi had made him, and for the first time that day nobody wanted anything from him.

He looked at the land.

It was very beautiful in the daylight. That was always the cruelty of it. The gorge below ran away in a long blue haze, and the cliffs on the far side were striped in rose and cream, and a hawk went round and round in the clear air with its wings quite still. He knew this country. He had walked it at thirty, with a chain and a plumb-bob, under a Keeper who had made him measure every bend of a river to the link. There had been a ridge here, a modest one, with a stand of birch. There had been a ford. He could see it still, the way a man sees the face of someone he has quarrelled with, laid over the true one: the ford was there, in his head, as clear as ink.

And it was fifty feet to the left. All of it. The gorge, the rim, the ridge, the whole bearing of the country had slid fifty feet from where he had known it, and not a living soul had said a word. It had happened in the night, the way a house gets older.

He drank the tea. It was too sweet. Taavi, who was frightened of him, always put in too much.

A river, he thought. A long thin stroke of blue-black, drawn with a steady hand under a lamp, from the high ground down to the plain, and how quietly the nib had gone, and how it had hardly seemed—

He put the memory down. He put it down as one puts down a pan that has no handle, quickly and without looking at it, and shook the fingers that had held it. It lay where it fell. It would be there tonight. It was always there at night.

“Toomas?” said Reet. She had come up beside him, with her left hand ink-black to the wrist, and was watching him with the exact look she gave the ground. “You’ve gone white.”

“It is the tea,” he said. “Taavi has put in a quantity of sugar sufficient to embalm a registrar.”

“It’s not the tea.”

“Mm. Say that shorter.”

“It’s not the tea,” said Reet.

Neither of them said anything more. Behind them a wagon-man began to sing, badly. Down on the ledge across the gorge, the last two wool carts waited their turn, small as beetles.

Then Reet’s head came up.

He saw it a moment after she did: on the north rim, where they had come from, far across the gorge, a smear of tawny dust was rising into the clear air. It rose in a feather. Under the feather, as it thickened, he saw dark specks that were horses, and the glint of a bridle, and the specks were coming along the rim at a trot, in a bunch, and then in a line. Nobody on the ledge had noticed. Aino was shouting at an ox.

“How many?” said Reet quietly.

He counted them. He had counted a great many things in his life, and he did it as he always did, twice, to be certain. “Twelve,” he said. “Twelve riders.”

“Can you tell who?”

The Seam had given him a morning of bright, hard, cold light, and a white eye that saw nothing and a brown one that saw very well at a distance. At the head of the line, a good way in front of the rest, there was a rider on a heavy bay, round as a barrel in the saddle, and on his chest, plain across half a mile of air, was a small hard patch of colour like a button of mustard.

“Mm,” said Toomas, and set the tea down on the rock. “That would be Org.”

chapters.title: Rule Forty
chapters.html:
“Rule Forty,” said Mihkel Org, “reads as follows.”

He had not yet got down from his horse. He sat the heavy bay at the south mouth of the Gullet with his eleven riders drawn up behind him in grey coats, their mounts blowing, and he held up one finger in a buttery kid glove as if he meant to test the wind with it. Reet had known him for six years. She had never seen him out of doors. Away from the Guild House he looked like a pudding that had been put on a horse by someone with a grudge. The mustard waistcoat had been brushed, and there was a smear of dust across the front of it where he had plainly sat on a pastry.

“’No Surveyor sleeps unwatched in a shifting place.’” He let it ring. It rang rather well, in the cleft, and came back off the rock a moment later in a smaller voice that said shifting place. “You are in the Seam, Sallik. It is four hours to dusk. You are a Surveyor of the Guild, on leave, but a Surveyor, and the Rule does not distinguish. I am therefore obliged, as Master, to stop this caravan, and to see you to a held place, and to watch you there.”

“Master Org,” said Hendrik Loo, who had walked up with his hat on his head and his charter in his fist. “You’ll forgive me. This is a Salt Company train under Article Nine. No officer of the Guild may detain—”

“Article Nine is subordinate to Rule Forty.”

“It is not, sir. It is a different book.”

“Then,” said Mihkel, with perfect composure, “I invite you to raise it with the Assembly. In the meantime, would someone please move that animal?”

The animal was an ox. It had wandered up from the line to see what the noise was, a broad dun beast with a pale belly and a short, ill-tempered tail, and it had come to rest with its nose a foot from the bay’s. The bay looked at it. The ox looked at Mihkel. It was one of those long, mild, appraising looks that an ox can give, in which the whole history of a creature’s contempt for committees is held for an instant in the eye.

Aino arrived at a run, with the salt-hook over her shoulder. “Mihkel!” she bawled. “Come away from the gentleman!”

There was a silence.

“I beg your pardon?” said the Master-Surveyor.

“The ox, Master. His name’s Mihkel.” Aino’s face was perfectly grave. She stood with her hand on the dun neck. “Very common name, in the Seam. We’ve had him since he was a calf. He’s a good worker, mostly. A bit officious.”

“I,” said Mihkel, “see.”

“Is it a name you know?”

“It is a very common name,” said Mihkel, and Reet, who was standing in the dust with her satchel and the stained hand at her side, counted. She counted it because she could not help it; she counted four seconds of absolute rigid stillness in Aino Rebane’s face, with the chipped tooth showing, before the whole six feet two of her broke like a dropped plate and she had to turn away and put her forehead against the ox. Behind her, among the riders, someone coughed in a manner that was nearly a laugh and was converted at the last into a throat condition.

Mihkel’s ears went the colour of his waistcoat.

“Sallik,” he said. “Walk with me.”

They went a little way up the slope, where the track forked round a boulder and the wind had scoured the grass flat. Mihkel got down from the bay at last, with the effort of a man dismounting from a wardrobe, and stood with the reins over his arm. He did not look at her. He looked at the hills, and at the dust, and at the little rock-ringed pool beside the track where a seep of water came out of the mountain and lay black and still in a ring of ferns.

“You have been very foolish,” he said.

“Yes, Master.”

“You have left the Hollow without leave of absence being counted as departure. You have fallen in with a former Keeper who is, by the Assembly’s own minute, not to be consulted on matters of the Atlas. You have gone into the Seam with a salt caravan and a baker’s boy—”

“Ink-maker’s.”

“—and I am obliged by the Rules to bring you home.” He took off his hat. It was a tall black hat with a flat brim, and he held it before his chest like a man at a burying. The walnut fringe stood up in the wind. “I have been your Master for six years. I have never had a rider who was so often right and so rarely tidy.”

“Master,” said Reet. “Rule Eleven. Rider reports. Keeper interprets. I reported. Nobody interpreted.”

“You were not asked to report, you were asked to rest.”

“Fourteen shifts.”

“I know how many.”

She looked at him. He had said it too quickly, and a different voice had come out under his own, a lower and unofficial one, and she saw the pastry-smear on his waistcoat, and the sag under his eyes. “I looked at your fourteen, Sallik,” said Mihkel Org. “I looked at them last night with a lamp. I looked at them until the lamp went out.” He turned the hat over. “I should like to be wrong. I should like it very much. But I am not the person who ought to say so on the side of a mountain.”

“Who is?”

“The Keeper. Who left the Hollow at the first bell this morning with six fast horses for Palu. By the river road. With a notice sent ahead.” He said it as if reading the minute of a meeting. “She will be there before the week is out. I do not know what she intends. She did not tell me. I will say,” and here his voice dropped, “that it was a long time since she did not tell me.”

“Then let me go to Palu.”

“No.”

“There’s a valley, Master. Nine hundred people.”

“There are nine hundred people in the Hollow’s own third tier, and I should like them all to remain exactly where they are.” He settled the hat upon his skull with a smack. “Rule Forty. I will take you back through the Gullet to the Guild wayhouse at Kesk’s well, where the ground has been pinned for eighty years and a Surveyor can sleep as she likes. We start within the hour. The caravan will turn about. It is a very reasonable arrangement.”

“Rebane,” he added, to the air, as Aino went by below them with an armful of tethering rope. “You are engaged by the Company and not by the girl. I trust we understand each other.”

Aino did not break step. “Do we know each other, Master?” she said over her shoulder.

“By reputation.”

“Mine’s terrible,” said Aino cheerfully, and went on.

Reet filed it. She had not told him the guard’s name. She did not think anyone had. She put it with the basket, and the clatter like shaken cards, and the north-pointing lantern, and she did not take the three out to look at them; it was not yet time. She said “Yes, Master,” in a voice that had no stammer in it, since she was not lying, she was only agreeing to a thing she had no intention of doing, and walked down the slope.

Toomas was sitting on a wagon-step with his bad leg out and a face of settled and total innocence. He had watched the whole conversation from forty yards off. He looked, as she came, at her hands and not at her face.

“He wants to go back through the Gullet,” she said. “To the wayhouse. Tonight.”

“Mm. And what does the Gullet say?”

She had walked it at noon, in the long dry hour after the bridge. She had walked it as she walked everything, counting, and she had it still, in the place where she kept her ground: a cleft three hundred and eighty yards long through the shoulder of a mountain called Hob, with walls of grey limestone leaning in, and in the middle a throat where the cleft pinched to two yards and a foot. In the throat, against the east wall, leaned a slab the size of a cottage door. It had come off the cliff in the night. It stood braced at a slant against the opposite stone by no better means than habit, and the wagons had gone past it with a hand’s breadth to spare on either side, and Taavi had walked through with his eyes shut and his hands in the air, saying that technically it was holding itself up by good manners.

“It’ll move tonight,” she said. “Everything in there will. If we go back in at dusk, with forty wagons—”

“Quite.”

“If it isn’t there at all, if there’s no way back through the Gullet—”

“Mm.”

“I need a quarter of an hour. And a rope.”

“Rule Forty,” said Toomas, gently, “is a fine thing. I wrote the fourth schedule to it myself. It says nothing at all about a pass that is shut.” He did not move his eyes from the sky. “You will want Aino.”

“I don’t know whether I can ask her.”

“No. You cannot. But you may stand where she will see you, and look at the slab.”

She went to the water. That was the excuse, and it did very well; Mihkel’s riders saw a young woman with a tin cup go up the track toward the black pool in the ferns, and one of them sighed in the voice of a man who would rather have been home. She filled a horn cup from the seep, and her hands were quite steady, and she crouched there in the ferns with the cup between her knees and looked up the throat of the Gullet, sixty yards off, where the slab stood in its slice of afternoon light. She did not turn her head. She looked at the slab for a long time.

She heard the boots behind her. They stopped.

Aino was breathing through her nose. She was carrying a coil of the Company’s heavy rope on her shoulder, and she stood very still at Reet’s back with her face turned up toward the cleft, and what was in it Reet could not see. For a long time she did not say anything. Reet thought, with some distinctness: she is deciding. Then Aino said, in a flat voice, “That slab’s been wanting to come down since the cock crowed.”

“I think it has.”

“It’d want a hitch about the top. Four of the heavy oxen. A good man up the wall.” She swallowed. “Treasurer’s pulled worse. Treasurer once pulled a bridge-post out of a bog with a mouthful of nettles.”

“Aino. If it falls, there’s no way back.”

“Then there isn’t,” said Aino. She did not look round. “I don’t know what you’ve done, Sallik. I don’t know what you are. I’ve been told a number of things about you by a number of people and I’ve not liked any of them.” She hitched the rope on her shoulder. “Draw whatever you’re going to draw. I’ll be quick.”

It took eleven minutes. Reet found, afterwards, that she could not account for the order of it, and this was not like her: Taavi up the east wall of the cleft like a squirrel with a loop of rope in his teeth; Aino roaring at the oxen by their names, Treasurer, Auditor, Guildmaster, Registrar, who put down his principles for once and leaned; Mihkel’s voice coming from far down the slope in a rising and indignant series of rule-numbers; and then the slab, which had stood all night by good manners, rocked, tipped forward with a long grinding groan, and went across the throat of the Gullet like a door being slammed in another house.

The noise went on for some time. It was the walls, answering. A cloud of white dust came out of the mouth of the cleft and rolled down the slope, and the horses screamed, and all through the dust the echoes ran up and down the mountain’s throat saying shifting place, shifting place, shifting place, until they ran out.

She was already kneeling. She had her field book across her knee, and the horn cup, and her stub of day-ink, and a brush. The throat, filled now to the roof with fallen limestone, stood sixty yards from her in a settling smoke. She drew it. She drew it quickly and exactly, left-handed, as she had been taught: the east wall, the west wall, the slab where it lay, the shoulder of the mountain above it and the long grey back of the ridge, because a drawing that left out the slope the rubble leaned on would be a lie of omission, and she had never wanted to find out whether the ink agreed. She stirred the day-ink with the stood-water of the seep. It went from grey to black.

“I stood here,” said Reet. “I drew only what I saw.”

Beside her, Toomas, who had made his way up the track on the chain-staff without her noticing, said very quietly, “Mm. A yard or two, for a night, is what the day-ink will hold.”

“Then it’ll hold the plug,” said Reet. “That’s two yards.”

“It will take a great deal more than two yards from you.”

“I know,” she said, and had no idea, and drew the last line.

The stone settled. It was a small sound, a creak and a tick, like a joint going home. And then, as with the Hallik stone, there was a silence in the world around the heap of fallen rock, a stillness that lay on it like a hand. The dust fell straight. A pebble that had been rolling stopped rolling. She felt the Gullet hold, and she felt something else go with it, a long, cold, quiet slipping at the back of her skull, like a coat sliding from a hook.

Mihkel came up at a gallop and pulled the bay round in a spray of grit. His face was the colour of tallow. He looked at the rubble, and at the dust, and at Reet on her knees with a book in her lap, and at Aino with the rope still wound on her fist, and at the four oxen standing about with the benign and blameless air of beasts who have not been consulted.

“That,” he said, “is damage to Guild property under Rule Ninety-one.”

“It’s a mountain, Master.”

“It was a Guild mountain!” He looked wildly at the sky. The light had begun to lengthen. Low in the south the first dark was gathering along the horizon, and the shadows of the riders stretched out long and thin across the heath. He did the sum on his fingers. Reet watched him do it. He was a man who had spent thirty years in the Guild House in the belief that the Rules were a kind of weather, and she watched them close over his head. There was no way back through the Gullet. There was no held ground on this side of it. The sun would set in two hours, and there were twelve Surveyors of the Guild sitting in a shifting place.

“Rule Forty,” said Mihkel, hoarsely.

“Yes, Master.”

“There is a beacon-house at Hob Foot. Held ground. Eleven miles, round the mountain’s east shoulder. If we start now and ride hard—” He stopped. His gaze came round to her, and he was not angry; it was something worse. “You stopped me with the Rule.”

“You stopped me with it first.”

“I shall be back at first light, Sallik.” The bay fidgeted. “At first light, with a warrant. Do not move.”

“I won’t move, Master,” said Reet, and did not stammer, because she was telling the truth. They would not move at all. They would be gone.

He mounted. He turned his men with a roar, and the eleven wheeled and went off at a smart trot to the east, along the foot of the mountain, round the long grey shoulder of Hob, turning back from the plugged pass to find another way. She watched the mustard waistcoat shrink until it was a button, a seed, and was gone.

Nobody spoke to her for a while, which she was grateful for.

She sat on a boulder with her field book shut on her knee. Taavi had come down the wall and was sick behind a rock. Toomas stood beside her with both hands on the chain-staff, not looking at her. The oxen were being led away. The Company’s wagons had begun to form up again, in the last yellow light, for the long southward road, and she could hear Hendrik Loo giving orders in a voice that suggested he had done all this himself.

She put her hands in her lap. They were shaking. She watched them with interest. They were the left hand, ink-black to the knuckle, and the right, ink-black to the wrist, and they shook together like a pair of birds. She had never seen them do that before.

A shadow fell over her. It was Aino, who had come down without a sound, which for a woman of that height was a considerable feat. She looked at the hands. She looked at Reet’s face. Whatever she saw there she kept to herself; she opened her mouth, and shut it, and reached into the pouch at her belt and brought out an egg. It was hard-boiled, still warm, and peeled in a single curl.

“Eat that,” said Aino.

Reet took it. She ate. Aino stood over her and looked south, at the darkening road, with the red scarf stirring at her neck, and nobody said a word of the thing that had been said by the seep.

Reet finished the egg. She sat for a time with the taste of salt in her mouth, and because it was her habit, because it was what she did when she was frightened, she tried to take herself back down the road she had come. She began at the Wharf Gate, where the barges lay under the wall. That was there. She went out along the heath, across the wool-train’s track, to the Three Pines, and—

There was nothing.

She tried again. She tried from the other end, from the bridge, working north: the gorge, the rim, the pony’s flank. And behind the gorge, where the road ought to have run up the long back of the ridge to Kesk’s well and out across the heath, where the milestones were, and the ditch, and the hawthorn on the wrong side of its wall, there was a smooth place, a hush, a pale soft expanse like a sheet of snow. Not a gap, as at the Hallik stone, a tooth’s worth. It was a country. The whole of the north road had been taken out of her, and she had not felt it go, and she did not know what had been there.

She sat very still. She tried the Hollow’s gate, and found the gate, and the stair; but she could not remember how she had come to it. She could not remember how she had come here. She groped, as one gropes in a dark room for the wall, and her hand closed on nothing but the day, the long bright afternoon, the heat of the egg, and a pair of broad brown hands holding a tin mug, and a white moustache, and a milky eye turned on her with mild inquiry. Toomas’s face. It was the only thing in the whole country that she could be sure of.

She took hold of it. She held it as one holds a rope, with both hands.

chapters.title: Haldja Ford
chapters.html:
The river had moved a hundred yards east since last month, and Veikko Pent’s ferry had not.

Toomas saw the whole of it from the saddle of the pony Clerk, in the last copper light of the fifth day, as the Salt Company’s wagons came down off the heath in a long creaking file. There was the landing stage, with its two weathered posts. There was the great cable, thick as a man’s wrist, running out from the near post across a hay-meadow. And there in the long grass, hung upon the cable by its iron wheel, sat the ferry-scow itself, a flat black barge with a pole-rack and a bench, listing a little to one side, waiting for a river. The river was not there. At the lowest part of the meadow the cable sagged into a pewter puddle with a heron standing in it, and beyond the puddle, beyond the alder that had once been a bank, a hundred yards off across the grass, the Haldja ran down in its new bed, quick and brown and perfectly indifferent, with the sound of someone clearing a throat.

“Ah,” said Toomas. “He is going to be insufferable.”

He was, from the first. A small, brown, fierce old man had come out of the reed-thatched hut by the landing stage with a long boat-hook in one hand and a bowl of something in the other. He was seventy, and thin as a rail, and the left side of his head was bare wrinkled skin where an ear should have been. At his knee trotted a large grey nanny goat with a beard like a scholar’s and the flat yellow gaze of a magistrate. Both of them stopped at the sight of the wagons. The old man’s mouth opened. The goat’s did not, but it gave the impression.

“No,” said the old man.

“Veikko,” said Toomas.

“No. You’re dead. Rule, look at him. He’s dead. I sang it at the Midsummer fires. I had a verse.”

“The reports were exaggerated.”

“You were buried. You were buried by the Assembly, in a minute, with a pension.” Veikko Pent came across the grass at a trot and halted at the pony’s shoulder and peered up with his one ear cocked. He smelled of tar and smoke and boiled fish. “God’s teeth, Veskimae, you’ve got old.”

“You were old when we met.”

“I was thirty-one. I had a full head. And what is that on your lip, a dead badger?”

“It is a moustache. You will recall that you once admired it.”

“I admired it as one admires a shipwreck.” And then the old man did a strange thing; he put up his hand, with the boat-hook still in it, and touched Toomas’s boot, once, where it hung from the stirrup. It was a very light touch. It lasted less than a second. Then he brought the hand down and rapped his own chest with the bowl, so that fish-broth leapt over the rim, and shouted at the sky. “Soup! There’s soup! Nobody’s to say I didn’t feed the dead!”

It was a very small hut for five people and a goat. The goat, whose name was Rule, was in the hut because it had always been in the hut, and it took the best corner by the fire with the air of long and legal tenure. Veikko ladled pike soup into wooden bowls, thick with dill and barley and onion, and watched them eat with his single ear tilted forward, like a man listening to music. He had not had company since the thaw. It was in everything he did. It was in the way he refilled Taavi’s bowl before it was empty, and in the way he said, over and over, eat, eat, as if any pause in the eating would be the pause in which they got up to go.

Toomas ate slowly. He watched Reet.

She had been quiet for the whole of the day. It was not her ordinary quiet. In the afternoon she had asked him, twice, in an even voice, how far it was from the gorge to the Gullet, and the second time she had asked it she had looked at him afterwards as though she were waiting for him to say that she had asked it before. He had said, “Four hours by pony.” He had not said anything else. The hands on the spoon were steady now, the ink-black left hand and the ink-black right, but he had seen them tremble yesterday on the boulder at the Gullet’s mouth, and he had seen what had been in her face when she stopped looking at the egg and looked at him.

“Master Pent,” she said. “I’ve a question. May I?”

“Veikko! I’m no master. Ask.”

“The river moved. The ferry didn’t. Why not?”

“Ah,” said Veikko Pent, delighted. “Ah, that.” He put down the ladle. He wiped his hands on his coat. “Well, now. I’ll tell you.” And, to Toomas’s complete lack of surprise, he did not tell her. He opened his mouth and sang.

It was a rough old voice, cracked down the middle like a bell, and it was perfectly in tune. He sang with his eyes shut and his chin raised and one finger beating the time against the bowl, to a tune that went up in the first line and came down in the second, like a boat riding a swell. The goat lifted its head.

The river rose up in the dead of the night / and shook out its hair in the stranger’s light, / and the ferryman rose and pulled on his coat / and cried, Who stood here? Who stood? Who spoke?

The far hand writes, the near hand holds. / Stand and say, and the water stays.

“It is a ferrymen’s song,” said Veikko, opening one eye. “Older than the Guild. My grandmother had it off her grandmother, who had it off a woman who poled the Ford the year the Atlas was drawn, and she had a second verse that’s not in any book.” He closed the eye and sang it.

A clerk in the city drew me a bank / and wrote me a willow where the willow sank, / but I took up a stone from the bed of the stream / and said, I stood here, and it was not a dream.

The far hand writes, the near hand holds. / Stand and say, and the water stays.

Nobody ate. Taavi had gone very still, with a spoon halfway to his mouth, and a drop of broth ran down the handle and fell on his freckled wrist. Toomas had known the song for forty years, as a tune that ferrymen whistled, a thing for children. He had never once heard it as a set of instructions. He thought of the Hearth-Stone, and kept his face as it was.

“What does it mean?” said Taavi, in a small voice. “I’m sorry. Technically I realise that’s an enormous question. But it sounds as if it means something. It sounds like—”

“It means what it says,” said Veikko.

“But what does it—”

“It means,” said the old ferryman, with great patience, “what it says. The far hand writes. A clerk, or a king, a woman in a tower with a good pen, whoever. She writes that the bank is here. The near hand holds. That’s me. I stood in the water, and I said, I stood here. And the water stays.” He leaned back, and the bench creaked. “Water remembers, lad. It remembers whoever stood in it. The whole river’s one long remembering of every fool who ever got his boots wet. It’s not hard. A child could do it. Most do, before they learn to doubt it.”

“Water doesn’t have a memory,” said Taavi, with the sad firmness of the trained.

“Doesn’t it?” said Veikko. “Then why’s it keep coming back to my landing?”

There was a pause. Toomas found that he had set down his spoon.

“Mm,” he said. “And the song has a third verse, I think. About the white.”

“Has it? Has it?” Veikko’s one ear swung round like a compass-needle. “Well, I’ll be sheared. Veskimae, you’ve been listening.” He sang it, then, in a lower voice, very softly, and the fire had burned down so that the words came out of the dark like fish out of a pool.

Where the white begins the wind lies down. / Walk till you hear the quiet. / Hilja set her hearth on the whitest ground, / and nothing moved, and nobody died, and she kept it.

“Walk till you hear the quiet,” said Reet. She had said it aloud, to herself. She did not seem to know that she had.

“That’s what the old women say,” said Veikko, contentedly. “It’s the Blank, girl. Six miles of it, in the middle of everything. No wind. No Shift. No bird. My grandmother walked into it once, for a bet, and came out three days later and said it was the loneliest place in the world and she’d stay there if only it had a decent pie.”

Aino came in from the dark at about the time the bowls were scraped. She came in sideways, with her head lowered under the lintel, wet to the thighs. She had left the table half an hour before, with a scowl, to look at the ferry-rig, because a woman who is afraid of bridges likes to see for herself what else is trying to kill her, and the goat Rule, who had slipped out behind her, followed her in at her heel with a look of vindication.

“It holds,” said Aino.

“I told you it holds,” said Veikko.

“You told me a song.” She stood dripping. “I put my whole weight on the cable. I hung from it. I hung from it by one arm like a ham in a smokehouse, and I want you to know that I’m going to say it was fine, and I’m going to be right. The new anchor on the east bank’s good. Who did it?”

“I did. Last week.”

“By yourself?”

“With Rule.”

Aino looked down at the goat, and the goat looked up at her. “I owe you an apology,” she said to it, in an altogether different tone. “I called one of my oxen after you. Rule Forty. He’s a great lump. He eats his own rope. I shouldn’t have done it, you’re a clean-living animal with a fine moral character, and it was a liberty.” She bent from the waist. “I’m sorry.”

The goat considered this. Then it turned its back and lay down on Toomas’s foot.

“She accepts,” said Veikko.

“It’s not a she,” said Aino. “It’s a Rule.”

“Both.”

Toomas laughed. It surprised him. It came out of him like a cough, a short rusty bark, and Reet looked round at the sound with her lips parted, as though she had not heard it in some time, and then, very slowly, she smiled.

He saw what she did next. She drew her field book from her satchel, the small dark one with the swollen spine, and a stub of pencil, and turned to a clean leaf. She held the book on her knee and the pencil in her left hand, and she said, “Master Pent. Veikko. Would you sing the first one again? Slowly.”

He sang it. She wrote.

She wrote fast, and exactly, bent over the page, and he watched her do it because it was a thing he could look at. The cropped dark head. The notch through the right eyebrow. The left hand, black to the wrist, running steadily from word to word, with the small hooked letters of a surveyor who writes for a reader that will not be present. It was a pleasure to see work done well. It had been a long time since he had seen anybody do that, and it was a girl of nineteen, copying a ferryman’s song in a hut on a dry river, who had in her skull at this moment the whole mapped skin of a country, and a rapidly growing country of silence beside it. He thought: she is writing it down because she’s afraid she will not have it by morning.

He thought: she will find Soo.

It was not a thought he had had before, not in this form. He had known that Soo existed. He had known where; he had always known where, to the half-mile, as one knows where a bad tooth is. Soo-on-the-Slope lay a morning’s ride from the Ford up the Haldja, on the Company’s own road, and he had been telling himself since the Hollow that there was no help for it. But he had been thinking of the road as a thing that passed, and not of the girl on it. A girl who could recite the valley of Soo from a stolen Dawn Sheet, bend by bend, to the crooked sluice of the mill, was a girl who would stand on the slope above it and know to the yard where each house had been. She would count the roofs. She would count the roofs that were not there.

He opened his mouth to tell her. He shut it. It was a very quiet shutting.

“One more,” said Veikko. His voice had altered. He had picked up the boat-hook from beside the fire and was holding it upright between his knees like a staff, and he had put his head back and his eye was a good way off. “There’s a last verse. We don’t sing it at Midsummer. I put it in myself, the winter after the flood, and I’ve sung it every night since, for the company. I pulled three of them out of this ford, Veskimae. Did you know that? Three. They’d come a long way down.”

Toomas did not answer.

“It’s only the names,” said Veikko gently. “That’s all it is. It’s a ferryman’s trade to know the names.”

He sang.

Marten the baker and Ilse his wife / and Mikk who was six, who was six, who was six, / Ode who made barrels, the Pärn twins, the two, / Toivo and Tarmo, who never were—

There was a sound in the room of a bench being pushed back. It was Toomas’s own. He heard it as one hears an event in another person’s house, with a faint, polite surprise, and he found that he had got to his feet, and that the chain-staff was in his hand, and that the hut was too hot and the goat had shifted off his boot. Reet had looked up. Her pencil had stopped on the fourth name. He saw her lips move over Ode, saw her not turn her head, and knew that she had begun to count.

“Excuse me,” said Toomas. “The knee.”

He went out. He closed the door behind him with great care, so as not to make a noise.

The yard was cold and very clear. The first stars had come out above the alder, and below it the new river muttered on in the dark, going to a place that it had settled upon by itself, and nobody had asked it. He stood with his back against the wall of the hut and his eyes shut. Through the planking he could hear the old voice going on, rough and gentle and entirely steady, laying one name after another into the quiet like stones into a wall. Rein the miller. Anni the weaver. Jakob. Helmi. Oskar.

He knew them all. He did not need to hear the rest.

chapters.title: Eleven Stones
chapters.html:
Everything in Soo-on-the-Slope was built to look downhill.

Reet saw it from the top of the track, in the thin grey light before sunrise, with the Company’s wagons grinding up behind her. Forty cottages of grey fieldstone climbed the hillside in three rough terraces, each with a slate roof and a deep-set door and a single window, and every window faced the same way, south, toward the bottom of the slope, where something lay flat and silver under a lid of mist. Nobody had hung a curtain on the downhill side. She counted the windows without meaning to. Forty-one. A woman in a doorway was shaking out a rug, and as the wagons passed she turned her whole body away, so that she did it with her back to the valley.

“Slope market,” said Hendrik Loo, riding up on his cob with the hat pulled down. “Every sixth day, at dawn. Eggs, eel, wool, sedge baskets. We take their salt order and sell them our remainders. An honest little place. Don’t ask them about the pond.”

“What pond?” said Taavi.

“Precisely,” said Loo.

The market ran along the top terrace, under a row of lime trees whose leaves had gone the colour of toast. It was a poor affair of trestles and handcarts. There was a man selling smoked eel off a string, and a girl with sedge baskets stacked up to her chin, and a woman in a brown shawl with two wooden crates of eggs, brown and speckled, laid in straw. At the end of the row, on an upturned bucket, sat a man with a lame dog across his knees and a hat on the ground for pennies. He was selling nothing that Reet could see. But there was a ring of people about him with their heads together, and as she came past, a voice said, “—and that’s why they won’t drink from the well, the well’s the same water—”

Rumour sold itself in Soo at about two coppers the piece. She stopped, and listened, and gathered it up like a surveyor taking soundings, and it was all of it much the same. The pond took a lamb every spring. The pond was warm in the middle, even in January. A man in a grey coat had come last winter with a brass tube and a boy, and taken readings, and been seen off by the dogs. “The Guild calls it a lost leaf,” the man with the lame dog was saying. “That’s what’s written down. A lost leaf. We call it Soo.”

“Eggs,” said Aino, who had followed her up with a sack of salt on her shoulder and the red scarf pulled up to her nose. “You want eggs. You’ve gone the colour of a candle.”

“I’m perfectly well.”

“You’re white as a sheet. Go on. Buy a dozen. It’s the only advice I’ll give you today.”

The egg-woman was somewhere past fifty, with forearms like a baker’s and grey eyes set deep in a face that had had a lot of weather. She counted twelve eggs into Reet’s satchel one at a time, in straw, without being asked, and named the price, and Reet paid it. Then she looked up over Reet’s shoulder and her face did something.

It did not change. That was what Reet noticed. It went on being a face, a plain, tired, middle-aged face, but a certain quality that it had had a moment before simply went out of it, like the colour from a pan taken off the fire.

Toomas had come up behind her. He had been lagging at the bottom of the terrace, on Clerk, and he had got down to walk the last of it. He stood with both hands on the chain-staff, and the white eye turned on the crates, and the brown one on the woman, and he said, in his mildest voice, “I should like a dozen myself, if I may. For the road.”

“Veskimae,” said Aino, helpfully, from the next stall. “Tinta Row. Binder. He’s with us.”

The egg-woman looked at him. She said nothing at all. She turned her head a little to the side, and spat.

She did not spit on him. It would have been easier if she had. She spat on the stones, a hand’s breadth short of his boot, a neat dry little spit, and the grey stone took it and went dark. Then she bent, and took up a dozen eggs, and began to lay them in a straw nest with exactly the same care as she had laid Reet’s. She named the price. Toomas laid the coppers on the trestle. She picked them up with two fingers and put them, without counting, back into his palm. She closed his hand around them, firmly, like a woman closing a book.

“I’ll not take your money,” she said. “Take the eggs.”

“Madam—”

“I said take them.”

He took them. He thanked her. His voice was exactly as it always was. He turned and went away down the terrace with the eggs held in the crook of his arm, leaning on the staff, and as he went the people in the market parted for him, not hurriedly, not with any air of making room, but in the manner of a hedge that has been told a man is coming. Reet stood with her satchel against her chest. She looked at the spit on the stones. It was already drying, from the edges inward, in a shape something like a coin.

“Well,” said Aino quietly, “that’s a thing.”

“He didn’t say anything.”

“Didn’t he?” said Aino. “Funny. I thought he’d said a great deal.” She hitched the sack. “I’ll see to the salt. You go and look at your pond, if you’re going. It’ll be there. It’s not got anywhere else to be.”

It was a quarter of a mile down. The track dropped through a stand of birch and a field of stubble and then came out above the water, and she stopped at the edge and stood with her hands at her sides, and did not at first do anything at all.

It was a shallow, silver, windless pond about three hundred yards long. In the east it was fringed with reed. At the west end a ridge of raw yellow gravel stood out of it like a dam, and that, she knew without being told, was the place where the new water had come through. And in the pond, under two or three feet of water as clear as glass, was a village.

She had not been ready for that. She had read the pre-flood Dawn Sheet of Soo a thousand times, the three bends, the nine-stone ford, the fourteen roofs. She had thought of it as a drawing. She had drawn it from memory on the floor of her loft at sixteen, to the link, in the lamplight, with a ruled pencil. And now it lay beneath her, laid out in the water in the true colours of drowned things, green and brown and dull gold, with the weed streaming over the doorsteps, and she saw that her drawing had been right. Every roof was where she had put it.

She walked the shore. She walked it slowly, with her eyes on the water, and she counted as she went, the way she counted everything. The chimneys came up out of the shallows one after another, squat stone stacks, some of them still wearing their pots, with the thatch long gone from between them and the rafters standing like ribs. The miller’s. The weaver’s, with its wide low door. The one with the green shutter that she had marked on the sheet as a bakery, because of a little drawing of a loaf. In the middle, on a spit of sand, stood an ash tree. It was dead and had lost its bark. It stood up white and bare from the water, and in the shallows at its foot, with only one end showing, there lay a bench.

“Fourteen,” she said aloud.

She had walked the whole shore and counted fourteen stacks, and she knew with a perfect cold clarity, as she knew the number of her own fingers, that she had counted them correctly. It was the same fourteen as on the Dawn Sheet. Nothing had been lost but the people.

She stood a little longer. Then she turned and looked up the slope.

The stones stood on a rise above the east shore, in a half circle, facing the water. They were not tall. They had been rough-dressed out of the grey fieldstone of the hillside by somebody with a hammer and no great skill, set upright in the turf, each a different height, and each cut, deeply, with a name and a mark. It had been done in a hurry, and with love, and afterwards, over a good many years, by many hands. She could see that there were three or four ways of making an R.

She went round them from the left. She read them without touching, as she would have read a sheet.

Marten Kõiv. A loaf, round, with a cross cut across the top. Ilse Kõiv, below it, a ladle. Ode Raidma, and the hoop of a barrel, with the staves splayed. Two stones side by side, the same height, the same grey, Toivo Pärn and Tarmo Pärn, and over each a single oar, one slanting left and one right, so that when you stood between them the oars crossed. Rein Aavik, the eye of a millstone. Anni Kuusk, a shuttle. Jakob Mets, a crook. Helmi Vaher, a milk pail, with the handle drawn too big. Oskar Lepik, a wheel with all its spokes.

She counted ten. She stopped before the eleventh. It was the smallest of them. It stood a little apart at the end of the arc, no higher than her knee, and it was newer than the rest, the cut cleaner, and from the lichen she estimated it had been set a winter later. She did not read it yet. She looked, instead, at the little piles of things that had been left on the grass before each stone: a heel of bread, a sprig of rosemary, a cooper’s nail, a handful of grey feathers. Someone had come this morning. Someone had come every morning. The grass was trodden to a path, round the half circle, and the path was worn into a groove, and the groove was the exact width of an old woman with two sticks.

The mill was a hundred yards farther on, on the high ground at the north end of the pond, where the village had once had the sense to stand. It was the only building that the water had not wholly taken. It stood above the shallows with its feet wet, a tall roofless shell of grey stone, with the three sluices still in the wall beside the wheel-pit, and Reet, who had read of the crooked middle sluice in the Dawn Sheet and had never thought to see it, stood with her head on one side and measured it by eye. Seven degrees off true. Exactly as drawn.

She was not looking for anything. She was only taking the bearing. But the door of the mill had a stone lintel over it, a single long slab, pale and weathered, and as she passed under it her eye fell to the left end, where the lime wash had flaked away, and she stopped.

It was a scratch. A tick, with a short hook on the downstroke, and two small dots beside it. It was cut deep, much deeper than a pencil-knife would go, deep enough to hold a thumbnail, and the edges were clean. It had been recut. Somebody had gone over it with a nail, again and again, a good many times, so that the grooves were as sharp as a new wound.

She knew the tick. Every Surveyor’s tick was lodged with the Roll in the Day-book room, and she had read the Roll for amusement at sixteen. A hook on the down-stroke, two dots. It was a tick that had been entered in Guild Year 271 by a young man from the south country, and she had seen it since in a different place: in the corner of a map, drawn out of memory, in a bookbinder’s workshop, in the pencilled margin of an error he had planted on purpose.

She put out her ink-black hand and set the tip of her finger in the groove.

It was cold. It fitted her finger exactly. She stood a long moment under the lintel and felt the whole ground of her inward map turn quietly over, like a page. He had been a Keeper. He had been dismissed in the year after the flood. He had told her it was a matter of an Assembly minute. The man on the bucket had said, that’s what’s written down. And here was the tick. Here it was, cut on the mill of the drowned village, by the man who had been Keeper when the water came, and kept sharp by somebody, every year since, so that no one in Soo should ever forget whose hand it was.

Lost leaf, she thought. And then, rather slowly: Whose?

She found them on the rise.

She had come back round the shore, unhurried, with the eggs in her satchel and nothing in her head that she was ready to look at, and she saw them from some way off: two figures at the end of the half circle of stones, one sitting on the grass and one standing, and then the one standing sat down. She stopped under the birches. She did not go nearer.

Toomas was on the turf with his bad leg straight out in front of him and the chain-staff laid across his knees. He was sitting by the smallest stone. There was a tin mug beside his hand on the grass. She could see from where she stood that the tea in it had gone cold; there was no steam, and a leaf of birch had blown onto the surface and lay there, turning slowly. He had not drunk it. He was looking at the water with his good eye, and the white one, as ever, at nothing.

Taavi had found him. He must have come down the track at a half-run, because his bandolier was still swinging and clinking, a small agitated sound that went on for some time after he had sat. He sat down on the grass beside Toomas, not near, a good three feet off, with his knees drawn up and his grey-blue fingers laced round them. Reet saw him open his mouth. She saw him shut it. She saw him consider, with the whole of his freckled face, a number of things he might say, and put them all down one after another. He took a twist of paper from a pocket and held it out. Mint.

Toomas looked at it. After a moment he took a leaf, and put it in his mouth, and chewed. The two of them sat side by side and looked at the pond. Neither said anything. The wind came up, and moved the reed, and turned the birch-leaf in the mug.

She did not go to them. She went to the smallest stone.

She had put it off long enough. She crouched in front of it with her satchel in her lap, and the grass was wet through her knees, and she looked at the heap of things that had been left there. A tin whistle. A bit of bread with a bite out of it. Four white pebbles, laid in a row by a hand that did not know how to count to five. The mark on the stone was a top, the kind a child spins with a string, cut with a very careful chisel, and cut again, and cut again.

“Mikk Kõiv,” said Reet, aloud. “Aged six.”

She had spoken quietly, and she did not think anyone had heard. But as the last word left her, something at the back of her head let go.

It was not like the Gullet. It was not a country going; it was something smaller and quicker and more exact, a gentle sweep of cold across a single page. She felt the pond go out. The shore, the fringe of reed, the gravel dam, the ash tree standing white in the shallows with the bench at its foot, the fourteen chimneys she had counted one by one, all of it went dark in her mind in order, like lamps being put out down a long street, and where it had been she felt nothing but a smooth, cool, pleasant blankness, the quiet of a sheet of snow.

She had drawn nothing. She had touched no ink. She had only come, and looked, and read a name.

She sat on her heels in the wet grass and remembered that there had been a pond. She remembered the number. She remembered the names, all eleven, perfectly. And she knew, quite clearly and without any pleasure in the knowing, that the ground had taken a toll for the looking, and had not asked her leave.

chapters.title: What Ene Ots Asked
chapters.html:
The crock was blue, and it stood on the third shelf to the left of the stove, where it had stood in the other kitchen, in the other house, a quarter of a mile downhill and eleven feet under water.

Toomas noticed it first. He noticed it before the old woman, before the table scrubbed white and the two kitchen chairs and the smell that came off everything, a hard clean smell of lye soap and fried onions. It was a salt-glaze crock of the old pattern, a hand high and wide in the belly, with a chip in the rim shaped like a bite. He had seen it thirty years ago. He had come into that other kitchen as a young surveyor with a chain-boy and a head full of Soo’s contours, and a woman had given him cold barley beer from a jug and kept her flour in that crock, and he had written the house on his sheet as the fifth along the lane. He had written down the colour of the door. It had been green.

“Come in or go out,” said Ene Ots. “You’re letting the heat out.”

She sat at the end of the table, in the one chair with arms. She was eighty, and had been small to begin with, and age had folded her up like a carpenter’s rule, so that she seemed to be built entirely from joints. A black shawl lay over her shoulders. Two ash sticks, polished dark at the top by her palms, were propped against the table beside her, and her hands were folded on its edge, and they did not shake. Her eyes were the colour of tin. They had not left his face since he came through the door.

She had not asked him to sit. She had not offered tea. On the stove behind her a kettle sat on the hob, cold, with the lid off.

A boy of nine or ten had fetched them from the rise: an egg-woman’s grandson, with a runny nose, who had come tearing along the track and halted a good ten feet off to deliver his message at the top of his voice. Gran Ots says if the Guild’s man is on the Slope he’s to come to her. She says now. She says bring the girl if he won’t come alone. He had said it in one breath. Then he had run back up the hill without turning round. Toomas had got up off the grass. It had taken longer than he would have liked. Taavi had offered an arm and he had not taken it, and Reet had said nothing and had fallen in a pace behind him as one falls in behind a coffin.

She was in the doorway now. He did not turn round. He knew where she stood, as he knew the knee, by a pressure on the back of his shoulders: a small, level, intelligent attention, taking in the room.

“You came to my door once before,” said Ene Ots.

“I did, madam. Thirty years ago. You gave me beer.”

“I gave a great many people beer. I don’t recall you.” She looked at his boots, and up. “I recall the other time. The third day. You came down the hill alone, in a Guild coat. You went into the water to your knees, in your good boots, and you stood in front of Rein’s mill with a nail. I watched you from the wash-house roof. I’d gone up to see if the cow had floated.” The tin eyes were quite steady. “I thought: there goes a man who knows exactly what he’s done.”

He said, “I came to look at it.”

“We didn’t need looking at.”

“No.”

“Do you know what I’ve wanted for twelve years?” said Ene Ots. “I’ll tell you. Not an apology. I’ve had an apology: a clerk brought it in a folder, with a seal. Not money. I’ve had money. I’ve wanted one thing, and I’ve wanted it so long that I’d stopped believing I’d see the man to ask.” She lifted her hand from the table by an inch. “Name them.”

It was very quiet. Out in the lane a hen complained, and was answered. The kettle ticked.

He had thought a good deal about this moment. He had thought about it in the workshop, with the awl in his hand, at the hour past midnight when the second cup stood mouth-down on its saucer; and in the Hollow, in his old chambers, before they took the keys; and on the road tonight and last night and the night before. He had written speeches. He had been a Keeper of the Atlas, and had a gift for the structure of a sentence. He had composed whole paragraphs, in the long watches, about circumstance and intention and the weight of an office, and he found now that every one of them had gone out of his head like water from a sieve. There was only the ordinary thing. She had asked him a question. He was a man who answered questions.

“Marten Kõiv,” said Toomas. “Thirty-four. Baker.”

He did not look up at the shelf. He looked at the table, at the white scrubbed grain of it.

“Ilse Kõiv, his wife. Twenty-nine. She kept the shop and the books. Mikk Kõiv, their son. Six years.” His voice was a plain voice, slow and low, and it did not alter. “Ode Raidma. Sixty-seven. Cooper’s widow.”

“Cooper.”

“Madam?”

“Cooper,” said Ene Ots. “Thirty years she was the cooper. Her husband never lifted an adze in his life. He was the widow in that house, if you like. She’d have spat in your eye for that.”

He was silent for the space of a breath. “Ode Raidma,” he said. “Sixty-seven. Cooper.” It cost him something to say it. He had said it wrong, every night for twelve years, in the dark. “Toivo Pärn, twenty-three, ferryman. Tarmo Pärn, his brother, twenty-three, ferryman. They were twins, and the elder by a quarter of an hour. Rein Aavik, fifty-three, miller.” He heard behind him the faint small sound of Reet’s breath. “Anni Kuusk, forty-one, weaver. She had a daughter at Kesk, who was sent for. Jakob Mets, seventy, shepherd, whose dog came through. Helmi Vaher, nineteen, dairymaid. She was due to be married at midsummer.” He paused. “Oskar Lepik, fifty-eight. Wheelwright.”

He stopped. He had counted them as he went, with the fingers of his mind, as he did every night: ten, eleven. It was the entire list. It had taken him less than two minutes.

“Is there any more?” said Ene Ots.

“No, madam.”

“There’s one you’ve missed.”

His heart went over, once, like a stone turning in a stream. He ran through them. Marten, Ilse, Mikk. Ode. The twins. Rein, Anni, Jakob, Helmi, Oskar. He had them. He had them as he had his own name.

“Eleven,” he said.

“Eleven,” she agreed. “I only wished to see if you’d count.” She shut her eyes briefly. When she opened them, something in her face had altered, a very small thing, a loosening, as if a string pulled through her for twelve years had been given a quarter-inch of slack. “You’ve said them before.”

“Every night.”

“Have you.”

“I do not sleep before I have said them.”

“Good,” said Ene Ots, without cruelty. “I’d have thought less of you if you hadn’t.”

She talked then. She talked in the same voice, a flat dry level voice, looking not at him but at the stove; and he stood where he was, on the bad leg, and listened.

The flood had come in the dark, in the third week of October. Two of them had been found by morning, and five in the week. The last had been found at the thaw. By the middle of November the ground on the slope was iron, the frost so deep that a spade rang on it like a bell, and the village had gathered on the rise with its dead in the snow, wrapped in sheets, and found that there was nobody to dig. They quarrelled about it. It was a bitter little quarrel and she recalled all of it. The men had said the rise belonged to Hanno Tamm, the farmer above, who wanted a rent. The women had said the dead belonged to nobody but themselves. A clerk had ridden out from the Hollow with a form to say that the new ground was not on any sheet and was therefore, strictly speaking, unsurveyed, and no one had authority to grant it. “Unsurveyed,” said Ene Ots, to the stove. “We stood in it. We were standing in it, in the snow.”

In the end they had lit fires. They had burned stacked birch on the rise for two days, and thawed a strip of earth three feet deep, and dug with the pick and the poker and the flat of a coal-shovel; and Ilse Kõiv had gone into the ground on the second night, with her boy beside her, in a hole that was not deep enough. They had to go back in the spring and dig it over.

“She was mine,” said Ene. “My son’s daughter. I took her at nine, when her mother died, and she learned the loaf from that boy at sixteen. She told me that bread was nothing but patience, and I said that was no way to talk to a man.” Her mouth moved. “Mikk had a whistle. He used to blow it from the bakery door at five in the morning, and nobody ever had the heart to make him stop. It was in the water. It was in the mud. A girl found it in March, in the shallows, on its string.”

“I saw,” said Toomas. “On the stone.”

“Did you?” said Ene Ots. “Then you’ve been up there.”

“Not until this morning.”

“No. You wouldn’t have.” She was quiet. Her fingers moved on the table, a quarter-turn, like a woman turning a coin. “Twelve years. A clerk from the Hollow once a year, with a folder, to ask if there was any further claim, and the word lost on every page. A lost leaf. As if it were a glove.” And then, quite gently, she said, “Where were you?”

“At my bench. In Tinta Row. I was binding.”

“Binding what?”

“Ledgers. Fish merchants’. A psalter once.”

“And in the evenings?”

He said, “I said them.”

He did not defend himself. He had known he would not, and still it was a surprise: there had been a hundred small defences standing by, ready to be called, and not one of them presented itself. He did not say that it was not what he had intended. He did not say that he had been a young man in love with a sister, in the grip of an office he had been taught to consider sacred, or that the water, in his reckoning, had been given somewhere else to go, a place of no account, a pasture. He did not say any of it. He stood with both hands on the chain-staff and the sweat standing on his lip, and the knee beginning, under him, a long slow whining note, and he said nothing, because the woman at the table had not asked him.

He did not weep. He was not a man who did. He knew, with a distant surprise, that he had perhaps hoped to, that it might have been a kind of payment, and that it would have been a theft.

At some point he became aware of the doorway. Reet had not moved. She stood with her back against the jamb and her satchel held to her chest in both arms, and he did not turn his head, but out of the corner of the brown eye he could see the notch in her eyebrow and the cropped dark head, and her face. It was perfectly white, and perfectly attentive. It was the face she turned on a hard piece of ground. It had been a long time since anyone had looked at him with such complete and impartial regard, and he found that he could bear it, and that this was a worse thing than if he could not.

His knee began to buckle. He felt it go, a small treacherous give, and he locked it with his whole will, and the staff creaked under his hands. The old woman’s tin eyes flicked down to the leg and up again, and she said nothing, and she left him there. It was another minute before she lifted one hand.

“Sit,” said Ene Ots.

He sat. He sat on the second chair, rather too suddenly, and the chair complained. He put the staff across his knees. She did not offer tea.

Outside, in the lane, Aino Rebane was being told no.

She had come up from the wagons with a sack of salt over each shoulder, a cut lip from an argument with Hendrik Loo, and a great deal of business in her head. The Company turned west at Soo. It always did: its charter stopped at the Slope market, and Loo was not a man who would carry a pilgrim one yard beyond the printed line. So she had bargained two oxen out of him, the slate-grey Registrar and the dun beast she had named for the Master-Surveyor, in lieu of three months’ wages, and now she needed a cart and a pony to go behind them. She had found a man in the lane with both. He was thin and bald, with an egg-woman’s jaw, and he leaned on his gatepost with his arms crossed and looked at her sacks as a man looks at a fire in someone else’s house.

“I’ve heard whose party you are,” he said.

“I’m the guard. I don’t have a party.”

“You came up the road with Veskimae.”

“I came up the road with a hundred and four of the Company’s customers, and one of them has a bad leg.” She put down the sacks. “You’ve a cart. I’d call it a good cart. It’s got all its spokes. I want it for a month, and I want the pony.”

“Not for him.”

“I didn’t say for him.”

“Not for his sake. Not a cart, not a pony, not a drink of water. I’ll not do a kindness to that man. I’ll not give him a crust.” The thin man’s voice shook, unexpectedly, with something that had been shut in a long time. “My wife’s sister is on that hill.”

“Ah,” said Aino. She stood for a moment with her hands hanging. She was a woman who always had a joke, and she looked for one, and it did not come. “I’m sorry for it. Truly. I am.”

“Aye. Well.”

“I’ll not ask you for his sake,” said Aino. She bent and took up one of the sacks, and set it, with a small clean thump, on the top of the gatepost between his arms. It was Flats salt, grey-white and fine, from the pans at Orav, the best in three provinces. “I’ll ask you for the salt. There’s two of those. Two sacks for a month’s lend, and I’ll bring the cart back with all its spokes. If you’d rather shut your gate on it you may, and I’ll think no worse of you.”

The thin man looked at the sack. He looked, for rather a long time, up the hill toward the rise and the lime trees.

“It’s good salt?” he said.

“It’s the best you’ll get this side of the Flats.”

“My wife’s been out for a month.” He cleared his throat. “I’m not selling for his sake. You understand.”

“Nobody asked you to.”

“It’s for the salt.”

“It’s for the salt,” said Aino. “I’ll write it in the book.”

The old woman was looking at her hands.

“I won’t forgive you,” said Ene Ots.

“No, madam.”

“I want that understood. I’ve no intention of it. If I were to forgive you, I’d be forgiving something that happened to those eleven, and it’s not mine to give.” She raised her eyes. “But you’ve something in your mouth. I can see it. You’ve had it there since you came through that door, like a man with a stone under his tongue, and you’ve not said it, and I don’t think you’ve ever said it. Have you?”

He opened his mouth. He found, to his great disgust, that his voice had gone.

“Not aloud,” said Toomas.

“Then I’ll hear the rest.” She looked beyond him, at the doorway, at the white-faced girl with the black hands, and her voice dropped, a little, to something very nearly human. “But not from me. I’ve had enough of you for one day. Go and say it to the girl.”

He rose. It took both hands on the staff. He stood for a moment in the clean-smelling kitchen with the blue crock on its shelf and the cold kettle on the stove, and he bowed to the old woman, as he had bowed to the Assembly, from the neck, and she did not return it. He went past Reet. She stood aside to let him through. He did not look at her, and she did not speak.

The yard behind the cottage was small and cold, with a wash-house, and a well, and a washing-line strung between two posts with a single grey sheet on it. A hard wind had come up off the water. He crossed to the middle and stopped, and stood with his back to the house and the staff planted, and heard her come out behind him and halt at a distance of about six feet. He did not turn. It was easier, speaking to the pond.

The words were there, as they had been for twelve years, at the back of his tongue. He had never spoken them. He took a breath that went all the way down.

“Twelve years ago,” said Toomas, “I redrew a river.”

chapters.title: The Night Outside the Rope
chapters.html:
He told it to the sheet on the washing-line, and Reet counted the pegs.

There were eleven. She counted them twice, because it was easier to count than to listen, and the second time she noticed that the third peg was a different wood from the rest, a paler wood, ash against the others’ beech. She noticed a chip on the well-lid, and a drain with a green lip, and the black knot in the wash-house door that looked, if you were fond of such things, like the Gullet from the south. She went on noticing. It was what she did instead of weeping, and it had never before failed to work.

“It was the autumn of the year two ninety-nine,” said Toomas. “It rained eleven days. You will not remember it; you were seven. The Haldja came down out of the gorge above Palu the colour of a cattle-trough and began to eat the east bank, a yard a night, and the surveyors at Palu said it would be in the streets before the month was out. Palu is built on forty bridges, Reet. It is a town that stands on rope. A river that changes its mind in that gorge takes the whole of it, and the houses, and the women in the houses. My sister lived there. Helju. She wrote to me every Midwinter and twice in a bad year, and that October she wrote three times.”

“And the Assembly?”

“Voted against evacuation on the ground of cost. They said the bridges would hold. They said the Atlas merely records.” He was silent for a breath. “I was Keeper. I held the Atlas in my two hands every day of my life, and I had known for nine years what it did.”

She did not move. A gust took the grey sheet and filled it and let it fall.

“By accident,” said Toomas. “I want you to know that, though it is no defence. It was a small thing. A drain at the Hollow’s own foot, which I had redrawn on the leaf for the sake of tidiness, and found changed, nine nights later, to match. I thought it a coincidence. I made six more tests. They were all of them very small. And then I understood what I held, and I told nobody. I wrote it in a notebook. I thought I was a man who would never use it.” The chain-staff turned a quarter-turn in his hands. “On the ninth day of the rain I went down into the vault with the last jar of Founding base in the Guild’s keeping, and a vial of Palu’s water from the assay shelf, and I took the leaf, and I drew the river away.”

“Away where?”

“Down a side-valley to the south. It was a pasture, I thought. I had it from the contours.
