A long dry fold with a few barns in it, running out on the far side of Leaf Hundred-and-sixty-three and down the Haldja’s old course to the Ford.” The brown eye was on the sheet; the white one on nothing. “I drew one stroke. It took four minutes. I did not think about where the water would go. I looked at the contours of my sister’s town and I drew the river out of them, and the edge of the leaf was there, and the channel ran off it. I did not turn the page.”

She said nothing.

“On the ninth night the river left Palu. The bridges stood. The barns were not barns. The valley was Soo, and it was on the next leaf, and it had fourteen roofs, and one night’s water in the dark.” He said it quite flatly. “The Assembly dismissed me the following spring on the ground of negligence. I did not speak. The leaf was struck from the Atlas as lost. It was neater, and nobody asked what had been lost from it.”

“What did it cost you?”

It was the surveyor in her that asked. It came up out of her like a reflex. He turned his head and looked at her for the first time since the doorway.

“Mm,” said Toomas. “I drew six miles of river. I have not been able to see the gorge above Palu since that night. I know that it is there. I am told that it is. I could walk it with my eyes shut and I would not know a single bend.” He lifted a hand a little, and put it down. “You have, I think, begun to learn what I mean.”

She had. She could have told him the exact size of it, and the colour, and the hush of snow. She said nothing about the pond.

“Where is the notebook?”

“In the false drawer of the Keeper’s desk. I did not go back for it.” And then he said, in the same flat voice, “My assistant had the desk after me. She was a very exact young woman, who kept the vault inventory and held the lamp the night I drew the river. She was not told what I did. She was told that she would one day be Keeper, and she was.”

“Kaie.”

“Yes.”

“The dividers.” Her voice had gone quite thin. “The bent leg. The four millimetres. You looked at my tracing in your workshop, Toomas, and your eyes went to the pinhole and stayed there, and I watched them. You knew.”

“I suspected.”

“You told me a far hand is beaten by a near one. You told me someone had to stand in Palu. You sat in your kitchen and made me tea and let me say ‘fourteen Shifts, nine nights apart’ as if it were something I’d found out on my own, and the whole time you knew exactly whose hand—” She stopped. She was shaking. She could not afford to be shaking; the ink would not take it. “You told me a true thing. And you left out the one that mattered.”

“Yes.”

“Do you know what Rule Eleven says?”

“That a rider reports and the Keeper interprets.”

“It says that. And Mihkel said it to me, and you said it was cruel. And then you did it too.” The wind took the sheet again, and it bellied toward her, and fell back. “I don’t know who you are. I’ve been walking beside you for four days.”

“No,” said Toomas. “You have not known me at all. That is rather what I had hoped for.”

She looked at him then. He stood in the cold yard with his moustache stirring and his bad leg in a tilt, a stooped old man in a Guild coat that had gone green at the seams, and she felt at that moment no pity whatever and found she could not name what she did feel. She thought of the eggs. She thought of a spit drying in the shape of a coin.

“I’m going to see to the oxen,” said Reet, and went round the wash-house, and did not look back.

They rode out of Soo-on-the-Slope at noon, behind two oxen and a borrowed pony, in a cart that smelled of eels. Nobody mentioned the yard. Taavi, who had been told nothing, understood everything, and spent the afternoon making himself small in the corner of the cart-bed with his bandolier pressed against his chest. Aino drove. Toomas sat beside her on the board with his staff across his knees, looking at the road.

The country turned empty and open. The slope fell away behind them into a long rolling grassland, mile after mile of it, yellow as a lion, with here and there the pale smear of a salt-lick, and no road at all except the track the oxen made. Reet sat in the tail of the cart with her back to the direction of travel and her feet dangling. She watched the Slope go down behind the hills until even the lime trees were gone. She counted the miles by the oxen’s paces. The number was exact. It rested in the place she kept all numbers, and she was aware of the pond, somewhere near it, in the hush, and of how little the hush weighed.

They made camp at dusk in the middle of nothing.

Aino walked the ring. She drove four iron stakes at the corners of the wagon-ground, and ran a rope from one to another, waist-high, hand over hand, and knotted it, so that the cart and the oxen and the cookfire stood in a square of tight hemp with a lantern hung on every side. “That’s the rope,” she said. “In the dark you hold the rope, and you go along the rope, and it takes you back to your fire. I don’t care who you are. Outside the rope after the sun goes, you’re on your own.”

“I know what a rope is,” said Reet.

“I’m sure you do.”

She ate. She ate everything on her plate and did not taste it. Toomas, across the fire, made a small attempt at a remark, a question about the quality of Aino’s fried eel, and was answered by Taavi, because Reet did not look up. It was early dark. The stars were out, thick and cold. The ground steamed a little as it gave back the day’s heat. Somewhere in the north-east a wolf, or a dog, was saying something to no one.

She stood. She took the chain from the cart, sixty-six feet of it, coiled and weighted, and the plumb-bob on its cord, and the field book. From the box under the seat she took a vial, an empty one, and tucked it into her glove.

“Reet,” said Toomas, very quietly.

“I’m going to measure.”

“Mm. Measure what?”

“You said that unheld ground moves at night, and that a drawing lands. I have taken both of those on your word for four days.” She did not stammer. She was telling the truth. “I have seen where the ground was. I’ve never seen it go. I should like to see something I can write down before I believe any more of what you say.”

“Aino has a rule about the rope.”

“Aino’s not my Master,” said Reet. “And neither are you.”

Aino, on the far side of the fire, said, “Oi.” But Reet had stepped over the hemp and was walking out into the dark, with the chain over her shoulder and her own shadow going long behind her in the lantern-light, and nobody came after her.

She walked two hundred paces due east. She counted them. At the top of a low rise, where the grass was short and a few flat stones stuck out of it like teeth, she stopped, and put down the chain, and drove the iron pin.

Then she did what she had been taught to do. She took three bearings on the three fixed marks she could see by starlight, the notch in the western hills, a lone thorn, and the faint glimmer of the cart-lantern. She ran the chain out a hundred links to the east, and pinned it, and ran it back, and wrote the figures in her book by the light of a shuttered lamp, and when she had finished she found that she was no longer angry. The anger had gone somewhere. It had been replaced by a clean, bright, steady stillness, the feeling of work.

It was very cold. The stars wheeled slowly. She sat on the flat stone with her back to the pin, and the field book on her knee, and waited, and thought, with a great calm, that she would be quite able to tell him the truth in the morning, whichever it was.

She did not know how long she waited. Time did not hold, in the Seam, in the small hours; it came in jerks. A little before midnight the wind dropped. Every sound she made began to come back to her half a breath late, as if the dome of the sky had been drawn tight over a mast. And then, from the south, from a long way off, there came a very low sound.

It was not like the night at the camp, which had been a roll, a ship turning. She was not inside the ring. She was on a rise in the open, with nothing round her, and the sound came toward her at the pace of a man walking, a vast steady grinding, and the whole dark country to the south rose up against the stars.

She watched it come. She would remember that. Something in her, in the cold white clarity of the surveyor, went on standing apart from the rest and taking notes. The hill to the south, a long low whaleback she had marked at dusk, stirred and lifted; the grass on its flank rippled outward in a wave, like a sheet being shaken out of a window; and the whole hill came forward with the grace of a tablecloth drawn across a table, sliding down upon her with its turf folding over in a long slow curl. The ground under her feet tilted. It tilted by degrees, the way a floor does on a ship, and her pin went over on its side, and the chain slithered away down the slope with a clatter, and the lamp rolled out of her hand and went out.

And at her feet, where there had been dry grass, there was a lake.

It came up out of the earth as she watched. A lake of white. Salt, not water; a crust of it first, blue-white in the starlight, pushing up through the turf like frost on a pane, and then the brine welling under, black and bright, in a sheet, spilling over the stones that had stuck out like teeth. It ran over her boots. It was so cold that for a moment she did not feel it. It smelled of the Flats, of the sea, of a thousand dead summers.

She ran.

She did not decide to. The body decided. She ran north-west, toward where the camp had been, with the brine slopping at her heels and the ground rolling like the back of an animal, falling twice, and rising, and running again with her book crushed in her fist. Behind her the whaleback hill came over the rise with a long soft roar and the lake rose to meet it, and she could not see the lantern. She could not see the lantern. She had lost the rope, and the camp, and every bearing she had taken, and there was nothing in the whole dark world but the sound of the ground moving.

Something seized her by the scarf.

It was her own. She had worn it round her neck since Soo, a strip of grey wool. It was hauled backward so hard that she choked and her heels went out from under her, and a huge hand closed on the back of her skull and wound itself in her cropped hair and pulled. She was dragged. She was dragged through salt and grass for a space she could not measure, and flung down on her face, and a voice in her ear roared, “Hold it! Hold the damned thing!”

It was a stake. She had her arms round it. It was iron, as thick as her wrist, driven into the earth to the last hand’s breadth, and Aino Rebane, all six feet two of her, lay across her back with one arm locked round the stake and the other round Reet, and the red scarf had come unwound and was flapping across both their faces.

“Don’t let go!” bawled Aino. “I don’t care what it does! It’ll do things! Don’t let go!”

“I’m holding!”

“Hold harder!”

The world roared. It tilted forward and back, and the stake sang in her arms like a plucked string, and something huge went past in the dark with a noise like a sea, and she shut her eyes, and held.

It took a long time to end. She never afterwards knew how long. The ground stopped moving, and then moved a little more, and stopped again, and in between the quiet came back by degrees, so slowly that she could not have said when she first heard it. They did not let go. Aino’s arm had stiffened round her like a bar of iron, and the stake was cold, and the salt had dried to a crust on her face and hands.

Neither of them spoke for the first hour. Then Aino began to name the oxen, in a low steady voice, like a woman telling beads. “Registrar. Auditor. Guildmaster. Treasurer. Rule Forty. Mihkel. The Second Clerk of Works. The Deputy Under-Keeper of the Weights...” She had a great many more than thirty-six. She was inventing them. She went on for some while. At the Deputy Assistant Surveyor of Sluices her voice cracked in the middle, quite suddenly, and she said in a different voice, “You stupid girl. You stupid, stupid girl.”

“I know,” said Reet.

“I heard you go. I counted ten and then I came.”

“I know.”

“If you ever—”

“I know, Aino.”

They lay in the cold, holding the iron. And through the long hours, with her face against the salt-crusted grass and the great black bowl of stars turning overhead, Reet thought.

She had been wrong. She had come out to measure a lie, and she had measured the truth. The ground moved. A hill had come down upon her like a cloth, and a lake had stood up out of a dry field, and every yard of it had been done in the dark by something that could be told what to do; and somewhere in the Hollow, in a vault, in a Keeper’s gloved hands, a pen had been lifted. She thought of the Gullet, stopped like a mouth. She thought of Kuld Mere, set down on a heath as carefully as a hand sets a cup. She thought of a river, led off the edge of a leaf in four minutes.

It had drowned Soo. That was the first thing, and it was true, and it would be true when she was old. But the other half of it lay against it like a coin’s other face. A hill could be asked to stand. A river could be led away from nine hundred people on forty bridges. If it could be done to kill, it could be done to save, and the only person on the whole continent besides Kaie Tammaru who knew how it was done lay, at that moment, in a cart two hundred yards off, with a bad knee, and a milky eye, and a stain on his heart that she could not forgive.

She did not need him to be good. She needed him to know.

At first light the sky went grey and then rose, and she saw what had happened. The camp lay two hundred yards to the west, on its square of rope, whole, with its oxen standing and its lantern still burning. Between her and it was a lake. It was about a mile long, flat and pale as a plate of milk, with salt heaped white on the shores and a few dead reeds standing in the shallows, and the whaleback hill lay beyond it, in a new place, with its turf peeled back like a lid. It was perfectly still. A single wading bird stood in the middle of it.

She let go of the stake, finger by finger. Her hands would not at first open. She sat up, and Aino sat up beside her, and the two of them looked at the lake. In her fist was her field book, soaked, and in her glove, she found, still corked and intact, the vial. Without thinking, as every rider does, as she had done since she was fifteen, she knelt at the edge and filled it with the new water, and sealed it, and wrote the label with a wet pencil. Unnamed lake. First light.

Toomas was waiting at the shore. He had walked round the long way, on the bad leg, with the staff, in the cold, and he stood there with a tin mug of tea in his hand that he had carried the whole distance and had not spilled. He did not say a word. He held it out.

She took it. She drank. It was sweet, and too strong, and she supposed Taavi had made it.

“Teach me how it’s done,” said Reet.

She said it without a stammer, in a level voice, to the lake. She had not looked at him.

Toomas was silent for some time. The bird lifted off the water, and wheeled, and went away to the south. “Not yet,” he said.

chapters.title: The Blank
chapters.html:
The wind gave out at a line you could have ruled.

Toomas felt it go from his moustache first. All morning it had come at the cart out of the west, thin and cold and persistent, picking at the tarpaulin and combing the grass into long yellow stripes, and he had borne it as he bore the knee, by pretending it belonged to somebody else. Then the grass thinned to grey stubble, and the stubble to bare grit, and a pace beyond the last scrape of lichen the air simply left off. It was like a door being shut in a house of many rooms.

Aino hauled on the reins. Nobody had told her to. Registrar and the ox called Mihkel stood in the yoke with their heads low and their flanks going like bellows, and the cart rocked forward on its axle, and settled, and was still.

Ahead of them the plain began.

He had been told it was white. He had been told so by a ferryman’s song, and had made the usual allowance for song, and still he was not ready. It was white as the inside of a mussel shell. It lay flat as a plate and so bright that the horizon had no edge, only a place where the white thinned to a paler white and was called sky. Salt crust over chalk, he judged, and nothing on it: not a stalk, not a stone, not a bird. Six miles across, if Veikko’s grandmother had paced it honestly, and she had walked in on a bet, which is not a condition that favours honest pacing.

“Walk till you hear the quiet,” said Reet.

She sat in the tail of the cart with her heels hanging, as she had sat since the lake. It was the first thing she had said that morning that was not a number, and she did not say it to him.

“I don’t hear anything,” said Taavi, from among the sacks. “Technically that’s the point of the— no, wait. I do. I can hear it. It’s the absence of the— oh, that’s horrible. Can everyone hear that?”

“There’s nothing to hear,” said Aino.

“That is what I’m saying.”

Aino clicked her tongue, and the oxen went forward onto the white.

The wheels bit the crust with a short dry sound like a thumb on a drumskin, and the sound did not go anywhere. It was struck and it was over. Toomas tried his voice. “Taavi,” he said, at the ordinary pitch, “would you be so good as to see to the tea?” The words left his mouth and dropped on the board at his feet. They did not carry. They rang off nothing. A voice on the Blank, he discovered, was a thing you set down like a parcel, and it stayed where you set it. Behind him Taavi said, “Of course,” and it came out flat and close, as though the boy had spoken from inside a cupboard.

By the first mile the light had become a difficulty. It came up off the crust as well as down from the sky, so that the eye was struck twice, and Aino, who drove with her scarf pulled to her nose, had begun to weep from the glare, steadily and without drama, like a tap left running. Taavi produced a stoppered horn from his bandolier and said that technically it was an almanac remedy for snow-blindness, that he saw no reason salt should be any different, and that nobody was obliged. He put a thumb of lamp-black under each of his own eyes. Then, because he could not bear a job left unfinished, he did Aino’s, and Reet’s, with the grave tenderness of a man blacking a stove.

“I look like a widow’s cat,” said Aino.

“You look like a person who will not go blind. Technically.”

“Do the old man.”

“Mm,” said Toomas. “I have one eye that cannot be dazzled. It is the first employment I have found for it in six years, and I shall not waste it.”

Reet had got down to walk. She went beside the near ox with her chin up, counting, and after the first mile she stopped doing it aloud, because her voice fell out of her and lay on the crust behind like something dropped by a child. He watched her small straight back. He did not speak to it.

He had thought of little else since the lake. Leaf Two-oh-six lay in the very middle of the Atlas, as near as four hundred and twelve leaves can be said to have a middle, and it was the only leaf in the vault that a Keeper was forbidden to touch. The man of the sparrows had told him so on the day he handed over the keys. It has never needed correcting, the old man had said, and so it shall never be corrected, and if you find yourself reaching for it, Veskimae, go and lie down. It was bare vellum, creamy and a little foxed. In its centre was a small square with a dot in it, and under the square no name. For years of mornings he had looked at it and taken it for a courtesy to a legend. It had needed twelve years in Tinta Row, and a girl asking to be taught, before it occurred to him that the one place in Orrin that never moved was the one place on which the Atlas said nothing at all, and that this was not a coincidence either.

He had said Not yet at the lake because he wished to see the thing before he opened his mouth. A man who has learned everything by breaking something has no business teaching by the same method. He wanted a witness better than himself. The difficulty was that the witness might not be there. He had a verse, and a blank leaf, and an old man’s habit of listening to ferrymen, and on those he had staked the only trust anyone had offered him in twelve years.

At the third mile Registrar faltered. It was a small thing, a hitch in the great slate-coloured shoulder, but Aino saw it, and her hands went tight on the reins.

“Rest them,” said Toomas.

“At the stone.”

“What stone?”

“The one in the song.” She did not turn her head. “There’s always a stone at the end of a song. That’s what they’re for.” Her voice cracked on the last word, and she cleared it with a noise like a boot in gravel, and drove on.

It was Reet who saw it. She stopped dead in the middle of the white and he watched her shoulders come up, and then she said, quite clearly, in a voice with no echo in it anywhere, “Six thousand two hundred paces from the lichen. And it’s a stone.”

It was black. That was the first wrong thing about it, in a country of white: there was no dark rock within sixty miles of this spot, and so somebody had brought it, on something, across the crust, and had not thought the labour worth a remark.

“How?” said Taavi. “It must weigh a ton.”

“A ton and a half, I should say. On an ox, I imagine.” Toomas lowered himself from the cart, which took a while. “Which she then named.”

“Something rude,” said Aino, with feeling, and for the first time since the lake she looked a little like herself.

It lay on the white like a loaf on a cloth: long and low, knee-high, the top dressed flat by someone with better tools than patience. At its centre sat a brass stud, green with three hundred years, of the pattern every Guild datum had worn since. From the stud a groove ran straight to the south edge, a hand wide and a finger deep, dry as bone, its floor furred with salt. And along the north edge, facing the way they had come, were the letters.

They were cut deep in square capitals, each as long as a thumb, without a flourish. The A’s had no crossbar and stood like tents. The R’s closed with a tail that flicked out at the foot like a cat’s. He knew the hand. He had signed his name beneath it on the Founding Charter every year of his Keepership, because Keepers did, as a courtesy to a woman three hundred years dead, and he had never once looked at an R and thought a living person made this.

“That is her,” said Toomas. “Hilja Orm’s own hand. I have been copying that R since I was twenty-six.”

He read it aloud. The voice dropped dead at his feet, as every voice did here. “’I stood here. I drew only what I saw.’”

Beneath the line, smaller, two hands were carved in low relief. The upper one held a pen above a plain rectangle, which might have been a leaf. The lower was pressed flat against a wavering line, fingers spread, which might have been ground or water. Between them stood a few words more. “’The far hand writes,’” he read. “’The near hand holds.’” And last, at the foot, a name, H. ORM, and a single upright stroke that could only be the numeral one.

“Year one,” said Reet. “She dated it before there was a Guild to date by.”

“Mm. The Guild dated itself by it, I think. Afterwards.”

“That’s Veikko’s song.”

“Or Veikko’s song is that. I should like to think his grandmother’s grandmother, poling the Ford that year, was listening to somebody.”

She had not looked at him since the cart stopped. She stood with her field book shut in her hand, reading the capitals the way she read everything, as though they might yet be wrong. Then, without turning, she said, “You said not yet.”

“I did.”

“Why?”

“Because I was frightened, certainly. But also because everything I know I learned by breaking something.” He leaned his weight on the chain-staff and set its iron shoe against the black stone, lightly, as a man touches a sleeping animal. “I did not wish to teach you by the same method. I wanted a better witness than myself. You have had a great deal of my word, Reet. This is not my word.”

She turned her head at last. The lamp-black under her eyes made her look like a very serious owl. “Then ask me something,” she said. “You always do.”

“What is a benchmark?”

“A fixed point. A mark of known height that everything else is measured from.”

“And what makes it fixed?”

“Someone sets it and swears to it.”

“Swears. Mm. And when the next man’s level disagrees?”

“Then the next man checks his level. The mark is the mark.”

“Why?”

She opened her mouth to say because it is, and he watched her not say it. He watched the surveyor in her go and look, as she had been trained, for the thing underneath. “Because she stood there,” said Reet slowly. “And he didn’t.”

“Because she stood there. Now. At the Hallik stone, where the Atlas had drawn a lake and the boundary was creeping toward it. You drew it as you saw it, and said you stood. Who won?”

“I did.”

“Because?”

“Because I was nearer.”

“Because you were there.” He tapped the staff once on the stone. It made no ring. “I spent thirty years under the impression that the Atlas ruled the ground as a king rules a county. That is how a Keeper is taught to think of it, and the Guild’s own teaching is the cover over that: that the Atlas merely records, as a clerk records. I learned the lie and then the secret, by accident, with a drain at the Hollow’s foot, and I thought the secret was the whole of it. The Atlas does not merely record. It decides. A king decides, you see. I thought I had found the king. And here is an old woman’s hand, saying that she drew only what she saw.” He looked at the lower carving, the palm flat against the wave. “A king does not stand anywhere. A clerk does not stand anywhere. Neither is believed by a hill.”

“Say that shorter,” said Reet.

He had said it to her a dozen times. He found it was a different thing to have it said back.

“The ground believes whoever stood on it,” said Toomas.

For a while nobody spoke, which on the Blank was no different from speaking, since the words did not go far in either case.

“That’s,” said Taavi, in a very small voice, “technically a remarkable thing to build a continent on.”

“It’s a remarkable continent,” said Aino.

“But the vials,” said Reet. She had gone quite still. “The assay shelf. Every rider fills one on the spot and writes the place on the label. We think it’s for chemistry. The Guild says it’s for assay.”

“Thousands upon thousands of small witnesses in glass. A far hand cannot write on a place unless it holds that place’s water, because it is the water that remembers who stood. The vial is a rider’s I stood here, kept on a shelf.” He heard his own voice go flat. “I used a vial of Palu’s, twelve years ago. I never asked whose it was.”

“And Kaie’s using them up.”

“Yes.”

She nodded, once, as one notes a bearing. He did not say the rest of it, which was that three hundred years of Keepers had taken a woman’s I stood here and turned it into I, the Keeper, and that somewhere in the saying the witness had become the throne, and that he had sat on it. She would arrive at that by herself. She arrived at most things by herself, a little before he did.

Taavi spent the next hour on his knees. He scraped the crust into a twist of paper and tasted it, which he said he had been warned never to do, and announced that it was chalk and salt and a thread of iron and nothing living, not a spore, the cleanest ground in Orrin, and that it was a dreadful thing to say about ground. He cleaned the groove with a feather. He examined it with a glass. And at last he sat back on his heels and said, “A gutter cut this carefully has to carry something. I’m sorry. That’s a very obvious sentence. But it has.”

“It’s a noon-line,” said Reet.

She was lying on her stomach with one eye on the brass stud and a pencil laid along the groove. “Due north and south. It’s true to the minute; I’ll have it to the second when the sun’s up. It’s a meridian. She cut it so the sun would stand over the length of it at noon.” She looked up. “How long?”

“An hour,” said Toomas, who had been watching the sky since they arrived. “A little more.”

“Then it fills at noon.”

“There is no water within six miles.”

“That’s what a stood-water vial is for,” said Reet, “isn’t it? The place’s own. She can’t have thought it would be kept anywhere else.”

They waited. Taavi laid out his glass vials in a row on the crust, and in one of them he put a thimble of water from the cart’s barrel, good water, drawn at the well in Soo and drunk by all of them for two days. He touched a speck of Salme’s base to it on the point of a pin. It went the colour of old rust and sat there, a scum on the top, a stain going nowhere. “That’s a failure,” he said. “Technically it’s a perfectly good failure. It needs to be theirs. The ink does. I thought it was only that it wanted to be clean.”

The oxen were unyoked and hobbled. Registrar stood a moment with his great slate head hanging, and then he knelt, front legs first, and then the back, and lay down on the crust with a groan so long and low that even the Blank could not quite lose it. Aino went to him at a run. She put her hand flat on his ribs and counted something under her breath. When she was sure of it she took her hand away and walked, rather quickly, to the black stone, and sat down against its north side in the last narrow strip of shade, with her knees drawn up and the salt-hook laid across them.

Toomas, from where he sat with the knee stretched out, saw it begin. She had her face in her scarf. Her shoulders went up once, and a sound came out of her that was not a sob, because a sob goes on; it was a single enormous noise, torn off the top of her like a lid. The Blank took it without a mark. It lay on the crust at her feet, small and private, and was not repeated. When it was over she wiped her face on the red wool and looked at the back of her hand as though it had said something rude.

He did not go to her. He looked at the ox.

“He is breathing,” he observed, to nobody. “Eight miles without a halt is a day and a quarter for an ox. He will forgive you by supper. Oxen are not subtle.”

“Nine,” said Aino, from the stone.

“Nine.”

“I wanted to be somewhere that wasn’t—” She stopped. “I know what they’re like.”

“Mm.”

“It’s not the ox.”

“No.”

“Don’t ask.”

“I did not,” said Toomas. He had been wondering for four days about the hens, which ate grain and never laid, and he put the thought away carefully, as one puts a letter in a drawer to be answered later. After a time he took the tea Taavi had made and set it on the crust beside her, within reach, and went back to his place by the groove.

At noon Reet said, “Now,” half a second before he saw it.

The head of the groove darkened. It was exactly the way blotting paper takes up ink: a dark that began under the stud and crept south along the channel, then thickened, then was not dark but wet, and then it was water. It rose from nowhere. It came up out of a hairline crack under the brass, clear as air, so cold that the dry light above it seemed to smoke, and it filled the groove from end to end and stood level with the lip, trembling very slightly, with the whole white sky laid in it like a coin in a palm.

Taavi was already moving. He drew a thimbleful with a pipette and dropped it into an empty vial beside the first. A speck of the base, on the point of the pin. This time there was no rust and no scum. The water went black at once and all the way through, the way the pupil of an eye opens in a dark room, and sat there perfectly clear, perfectly black, ink and nothing else, thin enough to run and dark enough to read.

“It’s the same base,” said Taavi unsteadily. “It’s the same pin.”

“It is the same everything,” said Toomas, “except who stood.”

Nobody said anything else. They looked at the little vial in Taavi’s fingers, a thimble of ink that a clerk could not have made, from a place nobody lived, on the word of a woman three hundred years in her grave.

Reet had got to her knees at the south end of the stone. She took off her left glove with her teeth. The hand underneath was small and square and stained grey-blue to the wrist, and he saw it shake once, quite slightly, and then not. She laid it in the groove.

It fitted. He saw that before she did. It was a hand’s width exactly, no more, a hand’s width and a finger deep. Not a Keeper’s width, not a width for a glove. A hand, such as a ferryman has, or a child, or a girl who counts. The water covered her to the knuckles. She looked at the carved palm on the stone above, flat on its wavering line, and at her own flat on the water, and her face did what it did over a hard piece of ground when the figures at last agreed.

“It’s a hand,” said Reet. “That’s all it says. There’s no Keeper anywhere on it. There’s no vault, there’s no seal.” She lifted her eyes. “Toomas. It’s just a hand.”

“Mm.”

“Anyone could do this.”

The plain took it and set it down at her feet, flat and unechoed, where all of them could see it.

chapters.title: What the Pigeon Carried
chapters.html:
Taavi had been gone eleven minutes after kindling, and Reet, who could not help timing things, had begun to wonder what a boy could find to do for eleven minutes on a plain with nothing on it.

She sat with her back to the black stone and her field book on her knee, drawing the carved hands for the fourth time. Each drawing she held at arm’s length against the original, and each time the lines agreed, and she did not trust the agreement. The sun was low and red on her right. The groove had emptied at one o’clock, with a small sound like a cup being set down in the next room, and the afternoon since had gone the way afternoons go after a revelation, slowly, with everyone busy at a distance. Toomas slept upright at the stone’s far end with the chain-staff across his knees and his moustache lifting on each breath. Aino had been with the oxen since noon. The cart stood tilted on its pole against a wind that did not exist, out of habit, and the shadows lay long and blue and perfectly still, because on the Blank there was nothing to move them.

Then Taavi came across the crust with the basket in both arms.

He walked the way a man carries a bowl filled to the brim. His freckles stood out on a face the colour of tallow, and his bandolier made no sound at all, because he was pinning it against his ribs with his elbows. He stopped six feet from her and stood there. In the dead air his voice came out flat as a slate.

“I wasn’t looking in Aino’s things.”

“No.”

“Technically I was looking in the kindling box, under the seat, which is where kindling is, and it has a false back, and I put my hand through, and I’m so sorry, Reet, I’m so sorry, they were warm.”

She closed the book.

It was a narrow travelling cage of peeled willow with a leather hood, and it had six stalls. Five of them held a grey bird apiece, pressed onto its perch like a clerk into a pew. Their eyes were open. They made no sound. The sixth stall was empty and had a ring of red sealing wax on its floor. Tucked into the lid-strap was a roll of tissue slips no thicker than a cigar, and a stiff card of waxed linen ruled in a grid of letters, and across the foot of the card, in a looping hand that put long tails on every g and y, were the words Keep dry. Burn if taken.

She knew the hand. She had been reading it in red pencil for six years.

She had filed this in the ferns at the Gullet, with the clatter like shaken cards and the lantern carried north, and she had told herself that she was waiting for the right time to take it out and look at it. She saw now that she had been in no hurry at all. She liked Aino. It was an inconvenient thing to find out about a person you were about to be right about.

Inside the tissue roll was a slip that had been written and not sent, creased flat, the copy a careful agent keeps until the receipt comes back. It was cipher: a square of paired letters, the row giving the first of each pair and the column the second. She worked it in her head. It took her under a minute.

SALLIK, VESKIMAE, ILVES BOY. PILGRIMS TO PALU BRIDGE. V LAME RIGHT KNEE. S DOES NOT SLEEP. EATS WHAT SHE IS GIVEN. SHE COUNTS. R.

She read the last three words twice. They were true. They were the kind of true that you are when you have been watched by someone who was not unkind about it.

“Put it down on the stone, Taavi. Gently. They’re alive.”

“I know they’re alive, that’s what’s—”

“Gently.”

Aino was at the picket line with a bucket, watering Registrar, who had risen at last and stood with his great head down, drinking like a bellows. She had her back to them. Reet came up on her left side and set the basket on the crust between them, and stood.

“They’re quiet,” said Reet. “For hens.”

Aino looked at the basket. She did not look at Reet. She put the bucket down with care, as though it were still full. “You train them to it. You can’t have a pigeon cooing on a salt road. People ask.”

“Master Org asked. At the Gullet. He said your name.”

“I wondered if you’d caught that.”

“I caught it. I filed it, with the clatter on the first night and the way you carried it north at dusk.” She heard her own voice, flat and level, the voice she used for reading chain-figures aloud. “I’ve known since the Gullet, Aino. I didn’t say. I’d like you to know that I knew and didn’t say.”

“Why not?”

“You gave me an egg. I didn’t want to find out what it had cost.”

Aino laughed. It was not a good sound. Behind Reet, at a careful distance, Taavi had begun to hiccup.

“Three hundred and forty,” said Aino, to the ox. “Silver marks. My brother Rasmus. He plays cards, and he’s clever, and the two of them together are the worst thing that ever happened to a family. There’s a house on Lamp Street that deals them. They hold his note, and his person, and they know where he sleeps.” One enormous shoulder lifted and dropped. “A grey coat from the Surveyor’s office came to the Company yard the afternoon you booked your passage. He paid a hundred down, to keep Rasmus’s hands in one piece, and said the other two hundred and forty would follow the day I did a small service for the Master. It was nothing, he said. A girl called Sallik, and where she went.”

“And Rasmus is in the Hollow.”

“In a room over a baker’s, with two gentlemen who are extremely nice about it.”

“I see.”

“Do you?” It came up out of Aino all at once, as the cry had come at noon. “Do you? With your head full of every road in Orrin, and a Keeper who sends for you and pours you tea? I sent one. One bird, the first night. What you ate. What you said. How many times you looked at the sky. It’s a girl’s breakfast, it’s nothing, and it’s the whole of my brother’s neck. And I haven’t sent another. Three dusks I’ve carried that basket out into the dark and stood there with it, and three times I’ve carried it back. You want to know what that’s like? You want to know what it is to stand in the dark holding the thing that will—”

She had taken the salt-hook off her back. Reet had not seen her do it. She flung it down, not at Reet but near her, and it struck the crust a yard from Reet’s boot with a flat dead clank, like a spoon dropped on a rug.

There was no echo. That was the strangeness of it. A quarrel on the Blank had no audience, and so no way of becoming a performance; it had to be exactly as loud as it was, and no louder, and the words did not go anywhere after they were said. They lay on the ground between the two of them, where they could be seen.

Reet did not step back. She was five feet tall and Aino was six feet two and the hook lay glinting between them, and she tilted her head up and looked, as she would have looked at a cliff, without opinion. “Pick it up or leave it there,” she said. “I’m not going to move, so you may as well decide.”

Aino’s chest was going like Registrar’s. The tears had started again and she did nothing to stop them. “I’ve never said it,” she said, much more quietly. “Do you know that? Not to a soul. That I can’t afford to be honest. I tell jokes. I name the oxen. Do you know why I name them for officials? Every one of them is a man with a say over somebody like me, and I can stand in front of a Treasurer who’s an ox and shout at him till I’m hoarse.” She dragged her wrist over her face. “And then you walked into the yard with a satchel and a way of looking at the ground, and I thought, that one will find me out. And you did. You’ve known for days, and you said nothing.”

“I lied to the Keeper,” said Reet.

Aino’s mouth stopped.

“She asked if I’d spoken to Toomas. I said no. I stammered, three syllables, and she heard it, and so did Toomas, from the next street.” Her hands had closed. She opened them. “I can’t do it, Aino. I never could. So when I say I know something of what it costs, it isn’t kindness. It’s information. I know what it is to be caught by your own mouth. You’ve been caught by your pocket. You’ve a better mouth than I have, that’s all the difference.”

For a while the only sound was Registrar, drinking.

“Who’ve you got, then?” said Aino at last, roughly. “Back home?”

“Ants. He’s eleven. He lights the lamps.”

“That’s the list?”

“My mother. In Sora. She writes about drains.”

“That’s the list?”

Reet considered. “Master Org,” she said, “used to leave me the crusts of his pastries.”

Aino sat down. She did it all at once, on the crust, like a tent coming down, and put her face in her hands, and Reet could not tell whether the noise she made was laughter or the other thing, and thought on the whole that Aino could not either. “Poor girl,” said Aino, into her palms.

“I’m not.”

“You are a bit.”

“I am a bit,” Reet agreed. She crouched, and picked up the salt-hook, which was heavier than it looked, and held it out by the haft. After some time Aino took it.

“Mm.”

He had come across the crust without a sound, which on the Blank any man could, and he had plainly been standing there for some while, leaning on the staff with his bad leg out. His moustache was crumpled on one side where he had slept against the stone. He looked at the basket, and at the card of waxed linen in Taavi’s fingers, and at Aino, and at the hook, in that order, and made no remark about any of them.

“I wondered about the hens,” said Toomas. “They ate grain and they never laid. Aino. How does the Guild pay you for this?”

“By the bird. A bird at dusk, a day’s wage. Where we are, what we do.”

“Where we are and what we do.” He seemed to taste it. “I observe that it does not specify a standard of accuracy.”

“It’s a Guild paper. There’s a clause for everything.”

“Is there a clause about truth?”

Aino’s head came up. She thought. Reet watched her think, and watched a number of long habits of fear rearrange themselves in her face. “No,” she said slowly. “No, I don’t think there is.”

“Then I will say to you what I would have said to any journeyman of mine. You are paid by the day, Aino, not by the sentence.”

There was a pause.

“Technically,” said Taavi, hiccuping, “that’s—”

“Taavi.”

“—brilliant. Sorry.”

“I can’t,” said Reet. “Not aloud. And the Master knows Aino’s hand.”

“Mm. Reet cannot lie. Aino can. It is the better part of her trade. She sold three people passage as pilgrims to a bridge shrine, and kept a perfectly straight face, and I watched her do it.” Toomas turned to the tall woman on the ground. “You need only write a bird that Mihkel Org will believe, and you are not asked to believe it yourself.”

They did it by lantern at the foot of the black stone, as the last of the day went out of the plain. The white crust turned the colour of the inside of a pearl, then of ash, and the stars came on all at once, with nothing between them and the ground. Aino sat on the cart-tail with a slip across her knee and the pencil stub in her fist. She wrote the plain draft first, on the back of the card, in block capitals, and her tongue came out of the corner of her mouth, and twice she stopped and looked at the sky for help.

“Read it back,” she said at last. “I want to hear how it sounds. I can’t tell by looking.”

Reet took the card. She held it to the lantern.

“’Caravan lost in the Seam, night of the sixth,’” she read. “’Hill came down on camp. Salt lake rose from the ground. All drowned. Veskimae last seen holding moustache above water. Sallik went down counting.’” She paused. “’Ilves boy went down apologising.’”

“I thought that was a nice touch,” said Aino.

“’Registrar drowned first, with dignity.’”

A sound came from Taavi, a small high squeak.

“’Auditor sank shouting. Guildmaster tried to bargain with the water. Treasurer kept the receipts above the waterline to the last.’” She went on in the same level voice, since it was only reading. There was no stammer in it anywhere, and she noticed that with a small cold interest, as one notices that a pin does not hurt when it is held against the skin and not pushed. A lie she was reading aloud was not a lie she was telling. “’The ox called Mihkel fought the water to the end and was heard to quote. Writer escaped on a barrel. Bird only survivor. Will not report further. Debt to be closed.’”

Taavi had gone over onto his side. He lay on the crust with both hands on his stomach, laughing, in great soundless heaves that the Blank swallowed, and each one ended in a hiccup that was louder than the laugh. “Registrar,” he gasped. “Is lying there. He’s chewing.”

At the sound of his name Registrar lifted his head, regarded them with enormous contempt, and went on chewing.

“Strike the last line,” said Toomas.

“The debt?”

“A dead woman who writes to ask after her wages is not credible. Let them come to you with it. They will be most gracious about it, I think, and it will be more convincing.”

Aino struck the line. She enciphered the rest herself, with her lips moving, pair by pair, off the linen square, and Reet checked it letter by letter and did not find a mistake. It took half an hour, and in that half hour nobody said anything of importance, and Reet found that she had stopped being afraid of the thing in the cage and had begun to be afraid of the lightness she felt, which was surely not warranted by any facts.

Aino chose the grey one with the white fleck at its throat. She slid the quill capsule on its leg and sealed it with a smear of wax from the stub of the candle, and she stood in the last grey light on the north side of the Hearth-Stone with the bird on her open palm and did not throw it. It stood there. It turned its small round head, one way and then the other. It looked at the plain, and there was nothing in it: no tower, no hill, no hedge, no line of smoke, no river, not a thing for its small stubborn mind to take a bearing from.

“Veikko said there’s no bird on the Blank,” said Reet.

“There’s one,” said Taavi, “for about a minute.”

Aino lifted her hand. The pigeon went up in a clatter of wings that was the loudest thing the Blank had heard in three hundred years, and the sound came back to them as nothing. It rose. It circled the stone twice with its head cocked, looking for something to be told, and found nothing, and hung there in the green light over their faces; and then, as though it had decided to take the world on trust, it turned and flew south.

“It’s going the wrong way,” said Taavi.

“He’ll know when he’s out of the quiet,” said Aino. “He’s got a head like Treasurer’s. It takes a while.”

Reet counted the wingbeats until she lost it, at ninety-one.

Aino had picked up the empty basket and was holding it against her chest, as though there might be some part of it left to keep. “I’ll tell you something,” she said. “Mihkel. The ox. I put in that he fought to the end. I thought: it’s the nicest thing I’ve ever said of him.” Her mouth did something complicated. “I’m not naming another one for anyone I respect. Not ever. It’s a liberty. You can’t put a person on an animal like that.”

“Who do you respect?” said Taavi.

“That’s the trouble,” said Aino. “I’ve started.”

Overhead the sky was perfectly empty, and a long way south, over ground that moved, a bird was finding its way home by a road no one had drawn. Reet stood very still and let the number sit in the place she kept numbers. Two hundred and forty. It did not get any smaller.

chapters.title: Palu Under Its Bridges
chapters.html:
They heard the drums a mile before they saw the bridges, which Toomas took for a kindness, since it gave a man time to arrange his face.

They had left the Blank at first light and found the Seam waiting on its southern side with every hill in a new place, as if it had been rearranged for their arrival and then thought better of the effort. It had been a long day of detours. Aino had driven it with her jaw set, and the two oxen had gone through the hours in a state of injured silence, and toward dusk the track had climbed a long scoured shoulder of limestone, and the drums had begun, very small, like a heartbeat in a wall. Then the cart came over the top, and the ground stopped, and there it was.

The gorge opened in the plateau like a wound that had been left to heal itself. It was perhaps two hundred feet deep and three hundred across, and the town clung to both walls of it, on ledges, on stilts, on shelves of timber driven into the rock, house above house in a stair of steep slate roofs lit from within. Between the walls, from every level, ran the bridges. He had known there were forty. He had not remembered what forty looked like. They spanned the gap at every height and angle, rope and plank, some no more than a cable and a handrail, some broad enough for a cart; and from every cable hung ribbons, red and yellow and green and a blue like the sky over water, so many that the whole town seemed to be draped in a web of coloured breath. Lanterns swung from the spans. Under them the evening was a deep violet, and far below, thin and pale, ran a river.

It was a bootlace. He thought of the river at the foot of the road that ended, and then he put the thought away. This river ran in a bed far too wide for it, with a bar of dry stones on either side, and he knew why. Painted on the east wall of the gorge, twenty feet above the water and bright as a fresh cut, was a red line, and it was dated. 299. It was where the Haldja had stood on the ninth day of the rain. It had never come near it since.

He looked upstream.

He had told Reet of this himself, in the yard at Soo. Still it was a strange thing to do: to turn the head toward a place you know to be there, and to feel the eye slide off it like rain off a waxed coat. There was a gorge. There was surely a gorge. Men had told him there was. But where it bent, and where it fell, and the colour of the rock where the river came white out of the dark, there was nothing in him, not a darkness even, only a smooth cool absence like the place a tooth has been. He stood with his hand on the cart-board and looked at it until Reet came up beside him.

She did not touch his sleeve. She looked where he was looking. “It turns east-north-east at three hundred yards,” said Reet, in her counting voice. “There’s a fall at four hundred and fifty. White. About thirty feet. The rock’s rose-coloured on the left bank and grey on the right, and there’s a birch growing out of the cliff just above the lip, sideways. It’s been there a long time.”

He listened to her. He did not say anything. After a time he heard the fall, a very far, thin hiss that had been under the drums all along, and what he felt was not the return of anything. It was something like being lent a coat.

“Mm,” said Toomas. “Say that shorter.”

“A fall. White. It’s loud.”

“Thank you.”

“Don’t,” said Reet, and went to see to the ox.

The child was sitting on the top rail of the carters’ gate with her legs wound round the post, as though the post might be taken from her. She was eleven or so, in a grey smock with ribbons pinned all down the front of it, and she had a gap in her front teeth and a thumbnail the colour of a ripe plum. Across her knees lay a roll of coarse brown paper.

“You’re from the Guild,” she said.

“I’m a Surveyor,” said Reet. “I’m not here for the Guild.”

“That’s the same.”

“It isn’t. Not now.”

The girl considered that. She looked at Reet’s ink-stained hands, and at the plumb-bob on its cord, and unrolled the paper over the top of the gatepost with a flick, so that it hung down the far side like a flag. “This is Palu,” she said. “Every well. Every goat. Nobody asked me.”

Toomas, who had been prepared for a good many things, had not been prepared for the map. It was drawn in pencil and walnut ink, with a bad pen, by a hand that had never been shown how and had worked it out regardless. It was crowded and crooked and wholly accurate. There were forty bridges, each with a number in its middle, and under each number a tiny drawing of whatever was most important about it: a bakery, a washing-line, a goat in a hat. The bell-tower stood at the square, with the little cross-hatched window turned south. The east ridge was a bare brown hump with a scribble of birches on its flank. The contour ticks, he saw, all pointed uphill.

Reet was reading it with her whole face. She read it as she read everything, rapidly and exactly, and he watched her come to the well in the lower square and put her finger on it.

“Here,” she said. “East of the fish-stairs. That’s where the Dawn Sheet—”

“That’s wrong. The well is by the mulberry.”

“The Dawn Sheet has—”

“The Dawn Sheet’s old. They moved the well when the Lauris’ cow fell in. The mulberry’s seven years old. It’s here.” The plum-coloured thumbnail came down on a small lopsided tree in the corner of the square. “The Lauris’ cow was called Marta. She was all right.”

Reet was silent. Then she said, in a voice Toomas had never heard from her, and which cost her visibly something to produce, “Thank you.”

“For what?”

“The correction.”

The child looked at her with deep suspicion. “It’s just where the well is,” she said. “Are you Uncle Toomas?”

He had not expected it. He saw that he had been standing very straight, with both hands on the staff, like a man waiting to be sentenced, and that he had been looking at the map for some time without seeing it. “I suppose I may be,” he said.

“Gran said you’d be taller.”

“Your Gran,” said Toomas, “was generous. And where is she?”

“Behind the bell-tower. Under the white stone.” She said it as one says in the kitchen. She was already rolling up the map. “I’m Liisu. Dad’s ringing. You’d better come, he doesn’t like it when people are late for the toast.”

The cart-yard was very quiet for a moment. Reet had turned her head and was looking at him with the exact attention she gave a hard piece of ground. Aino was looking at the sky. Toomas stood where he was, on the bad leg, and found that his hands had stopped doing anything at all, and he looked at the gap-toothed child on the gate, who had her grandmother’s way of lifting one eyebrow, and thought: she is eleven. I did not know that she existed.

“Come along,” said Liisu, in the voice of one who has said it once already. “He’s not going to wait.”

The bell-tower stood at the south end of the great central bridge, at the edge of a small square of beaten earth hung with lanterns. The bridge was the longest in Palu, two hundred and ten feet of rope and oak, broad enough for two carts, and from every handrail and every cable trailed ribbons by the thousand, stirring in the draught of the gorge. The square was full. Somebody had set trestles end to end, and on the trestles were plum dumplings, smoked trout, bread hung with ribbons, a roast goat, bowls of the dark blue plums the valley was famous for, and everywhere there were jugs of the brandy that came from them. Three drummers sat on a barrel and beat out a rhythm that made the planks of the bridge shiver. Children ran along the rails of the bridges above, shrieking, at a height from which a fall would have taken eleven seconds.

Aino stopped at the edge of the square and made a small, well-bred sound in her throat.

“They’ve never fallen,” said Liisu, passing her. “Hardly ever.”

The man at the bell-rope was built like a door. He had shoulders on which one might have stood a table, grey at the temples, and a heavy jaw; and when he let go of the rope and flexed his hand, the palm of it was hard and yellow as a horn spoon. He had just rung the toast. The echo of it was still going in the gorge. Nine hundred voices were answering it: And we on it! He looked at the newcomers one at a time, without any hospitality, and finally at the old man with the staff.

“Veskimae,” said Jaan Pold.

“Jaan.” Toomas looked at the jaw. “You have your mother’s chin.”

“She said you’d come.”

“When did she say so?”

“Every winter. Last time, the week before Midwinter. She’d been three days in bed.” The reeve’s voice did not rise. It was a voice used to the bell, and it did not need to. “She said you’d come when you’d got up your courage and not before, and I wasn’t to write, because writing would only make you late. So I didn’t write.”

“I did not know.”

“No.”

“When—”

“The eleventh night of the dark month. The ground was iron that week. We burned a pit for her.” He took up the rope again, and looked at it, and put it down. “She’s behind the tower. You’ll see the stone. There’s a feast, so it’ll wait until morning.”

It was said without cruelty, as a man gives the time. Toomas stood in the lantern-light with a roast goat steaming at his elbow and thought that of all the sentences he had composed in twelve years of the second cup, not one had been I am too late, because it had never occurred to him that a thing might simply be over without a hearing. He bowed to his nephew from the neck, as he had bowed to the Assembly. Jaan Pold did not return it.

Reet spoke. “Reeve Pold. You had a notice from the Guild.”

“On the fifth.”

“A precautionary gathering on the upland. Tomorrow at noon.”

“I had one last autumn.” Jaan did not look at her. “A survey drill. I sent nine hundred people up the Birch Hanger with blankets, and it rained, and the Guild never came, and we lost two goats and a child’s tooth. The year before it was a landslip at the south stair. It wasn’t. Guild notices cry wolf, Surveyor. I’ve a feast to run.”

“The ground in this valley is going to be moved,” said Reet. “On the night of the day after tomorrow. By a drawing in the vault, a week old. The valley is going to be a lake.”

She did not stammer. She said it flatly, as a fact, and it was a fact, and he saw the reeve hear that it was one. He saw something go across the broad face and settle, hardening, as a man will settle his weight when a floor begins to give.

“Then you’ll tell me which clerk,” said Jaan, “and I’ll go and have a word.”

“It’s not a clerk.”

“I’m reeve of Palu.” He said it gently. It was worse than shouting. “I’ll not cancel the Name-Day on a Guild paper. I’ll not send nine hundred people up a hill because a girl in a Surveyor’s coat says the ground has been talked to. If it comes, it comes to me, in the road, with the bell in my hand.” His eyes went to Toomas, once, and away. “I’m not the reeve who ran. You can tell her that. Whoever she is.”

He went off through the crowd toward the plums, with his big shoulders going before him like a plough.

“He’s like that with the bell too,” said Liisu. She had appeared at Reet’s elbow with a flour sack slung on her back, and she looked up with the air of someone who has seen the grown-ups through a difficult scene and can now get on. “Come behind the tower. I borrowed something.”

Behind the tower, in the shadow of the stone, a lantern hung on a nail. Beneath the lantern, with his boots in a bucket of plum stones, a man in a grey Guild coat lay snoring under a trestle. His mouth was open. A brandy-cup rose and fell on his chest like a small boat.

“He came on the fifth with the notice,” said Liisu, “and he hasn’t been sober since. He says it’s the only way to bear the Name-Day.” She took from the flour sack an oblong board of pale lime-wood, the size of a tea-tray, with a sheet of onion-skin pinned to it by four brass pins. “I’m going to put it back before he wakes up.”

Reet took the board in both hands and held it to the lantern.

Toomas looked over her shoulder. It was a clerk’s tracing of a leaf: he knew the hand, the clean impersonal copperplate of the Hollow’s copy-room, and the cross-ruled margins, and the fine pinned register-marks at each corner. It was a leaf of the Atlas, in the new colours. In the middle of it, over the place where he knew the town stood, a wash of clerk’s blue lay across the valley from the gorge to the ridge. A lake basin, with a neat ruled legend. No bridges. No tower. No fields. No street. The east ridge had been shaded to a cliff-line, hatched and clean, and the upland above it left bare.

“Where’s us?” said Liisu. “Where’s the Bell Bridge? I looked all over. It’s not on it.”

“No,” said Reet.

“Is that what the Guild thinks? That we’re not there?”

“I think the Guild has drawn it that way. Yes.”

“That’s wrong,” said Liisu. It was her flat voice, the voice she had used for the mulberry, and it carried exactly the same degree of outrage, and no more. “We’re here.”

Reet had not answered. She had tilted the board a little, and Toomas saw what she was looking at. At the left margin of the tracing, where the vellum folds into the gutter of the book, a clerk had pricked a tiny hole through the onion-skin to register the original’s pinhole: a pin-point of light in the paper. It was very close to the fold. Closer, he thought, than he would have set it. She put the nail of her little finger against it and did not measure.

“I’ll look at it by day,” she said. Her face was perfectly still. “I have to see it in daylight.”

They crossed the Bell Bridge in the dark, toward the reeve’s house, behind Liisu and her lantern. The span was a hundred and sixty feet above the river and it moved a little at each step, with the long slow give of a thing that is used to being walked on, and the drums beat below, and the ribbons whipped at their sleeves. Midway Aino stopped. She put one hand on the cable. She had been walking with her eyes shut and her lips moving, and Toomas had assumed that she was counting.

“Reet,” she said. It was a whisper, and for Aino a whisper was a feat. “They’re the worst thing I’ve ever seen.”

“I know.”

“Forty. I counted them from the gate. And I’m going to cross every one.” She opened her eyes. “I’ve decided. Don’t tell the oxen.”

“I won’t.”

“I’ll do it on my hands and knees if I have to.”

“I’ll count them for you.”

“Would you?” said Aino, with real gratitude. She moved on.

Toomas had stopped at the centre. He did not mean to. His knee had made a remark, and he leaned on the cable to answer it, and the bridge lifted and fell gently beneath him like the chest of an animal asleep. From here he could see the whole of the town in its web of lights. He could see the lanterns on the other spans, and the ribbons streaming out of the dark toward him, red and yellow and blue, and on the cable beside his hand, among a hundred coloured knots, one white ribbon tied with a child’s bad knot.

And next to it, pinned by a loop of string to the rope, a sheet of brown paper. It had been left to swing in the wind of the gorge, with a pebble sewn into each corner for ballast. It was a map. He saw the bell-tower, with its window turned south. He saw the forty bridges, numbered, each with its small drawing, and the mulberry in its corner, and in the margin in a clumsy careful hand: PALU. Liisu Pold. Her map. A smaller one, an earlier one, had hung here last year, no doubt, and the year before. She tied them to the bridge so that the bridge would know where it was.

He stood and looked at it for a long time. It was the town he had saved with one stroke of a pen, and the town his saving had very nearly put at the bottom of a lake, drawn on a sack-paper by his great-niece, whom he had met an hour ago, and hung out over the dark on a string. The white ribbon stirred. The map swung out on its string and back, and he saw that the Bell Bridge, which had been drawn with such pains, was drawn exactly right.

chapters.html:
Taavi had tied the bucket to forty yards of washing-line, which Reet thought optimistic, since the river was a hundred and ninety feet down.

“Three hundred and four steps,” said Liisu, leading the way. “It’s called the Wet Stair. The rope-walk uses it to take the hemp down to soak.” She said it with her back to them, in the flat voice. Reet counted the steps as she descended, because the steps were there and she had never in her life been able to leave a stair uncounted, and she made them three hundred and four, and was displeased to find that she had been checked by a child and had come out equal.

It was dawn, a cold clear one, and the gorge held the blue of the night in its throat. On the bridges above them lamps were going out, one after another, and a few late dancers lay among the ribbons where the plum brandy had put them. Toomas had gone before it was light. She had heard the chain-staff on the boards of the reeve’s loft, and then the stair, and had lain awake in the dark with her eyes open, hearing him go out toward the bell-tower with a sprig of rosemary from the kitchen in his fist. He had not come back. She had not gone after him. She had told herself she was letting him be.

Down on the third bridge from the bottom something moved on all fours, slowly, between the handrails. “Twenty-two!” bawled Aino, in a voice cracked with effort. “Twenty-three next! Count them, Sallik!” Reet lifted a hand and counted them.

At the foot of the stair the river was smaller than she had been led to expect. It was a brown, quick, self-contained thing, thirty feet across, rolling stones along its bed with a sound like a man cracking nuts. The cliff on the east side went up above it in rose-coloured tiers, and high on the face, twenty feet over her head, was the red line with its date.

“That’s the Line,” said Liisu. “Dad says it’s the day the Guild saved us. Gran said it was the day somebody did.” She picked up a flat stone, weighed it, and skimmed it. It went four times. “She never said who.”

Reet looked at the stone going across the water and said nothing. She was not obliged to. She had never in her life been so glad of a thing that was not a lie.

Taavi knelt at the edge with a brass-bound case open on a flat rock. He drew the bucket up hand over hand, and poured a thimbleful into a clean vial, and held the vial up to the light and looked at it as a man looks at a child’s face when the doctor is about to speak. Then he took the pin from his bandolier and touched the point of it to the flask. Reet watched the speck go in. It was grey, a mere grain of dull metal-coloured stuff, and it fell through the water and spread.

The water went black. It was fast, and total, and clean, the whole thimbleful going dark from the top to the bottom like a lamp being turned down. There was no scum, no rust, no settling. It sat there in his fingers, as black as the stuff in the groove at the Hearth-Stone, as black as the sliver he had tested on the afternoon of the green vat in Tinta Row.

“It’s the same,” said Taavi. He was whispering, though no one could have heard him over the river. “Technically, it’s the same black as Sora’s. It’s the same black as the Blank’s. Reet, it doesn’t matter which water. It has to be the place’s, but it doesn’t have to be a vial. It’s the river. It’s the river, and it’s been the river all along.”

“Row a hundred and sixty-three on the shelf,” said Reet slowly. “A hundred and twelve vials. Bare.”

“She has them.”

“She has Palu’s water in glass in the vault. That’s how she draws it from there.” She looked at the thin brown river, at the stones, at the red line high on the cliff. “She doesn’t need the river. We don’t need her vials. Anyone who stood here can dip a bucket.”

“Anyone with the base,” said Taavi.

“Anyone with the base.”

“Which is, technically,” said Taavi, “me.”

He had gone quite white under the freckles. She saw that he had understood, in that moment, that he was no longer a boy who had come along to see a thing for himself. She did not tell him that she had known it since the green vat. It was not the kind of thing you said to someone before breakfast.

She did it that morning. She did not ask Toomas, who was at the grave. She told herself this was because he was at the grave. She knew it was because he would have said not yet, and she had had her fill of not yet; she had a clock in her, and it said that the Keeper was on the road with twelve horses, and that the ninth night was the night of the following day, and that the ground did not mind who was kind to it.

She laid it out for Taavi on the Wet Stair, step by step, in the voice of someone reading figures. A drawing made on the spot beats a drawing made far away. Therefore she would stand on East Rise, where the whole valley lay below her like a leaf, and draw it as it was, with the town in it, in true ink, and swear. Then the vault’s lake would find the ground already spoken for, and could not land.

“That’s brilliant,” said Taavi, miserably. “Technically it’s exactly right. It’s the most correct thing I’ve ever heard. And it’ll cost you the whole valley.”

“Then it costs the valley.”

“Reet, it’s nine hundred people and a—a hill, and some fields, and a river—”

“Yes.”

He gave her the pot. He stood with it in both hands a moment longer than he need have, like a man handing a child to a surgeon. It held a spoon of base and a pint of river water, and enough of the first to make the second black as the inside of a boot.

The east ridge was bare and brown and cold. She went up it alone, with the field book in her satchel and the brush behind her ear, past the Birch Hanger on the north flank, whose leaves had gone the colour of old brass, and at the top she turned and looked down, and there it was. The whole valley. The gorge, the green and yellow patchwork of the fields on the plateau beyond, the thin road, the smoke from nine hundred chimneys, and the forty bridges hung across the cleft like threads. She stood and let it come into her, and there was a moment, one clear bright moment, in which she thought: I could do it. I have the memory for it. I am the person who can.

She began with the field at the foot of the ridge. It was a plot of barley stubble, a long strip with a thorn hedge on the downhill side, a ditch, a gatepost of split oak with an iron ring through it, and a stile made of two flat stones. Ruus’s barley, Liisu had called it. She knelt on the cold turf and said, “I stood here. I drew only what I saw,” and the first line went onto the page black and cold and sure, and she felt it take.

She drew the hedge. She drew the ditch, the gatepost, the ring, the stile. And as she drew, the field began to leave her.

It was not like the Gullet, which had gone like a coat sliding off a hook. This was slower, and she could watch it. It was as though someone were carrying the furniture out of a room she stood in, one piece at a time, while she described it. The hedge went out of her head as the nib left the hedge. The ditch, the stile, the shapes of the stones. She went on drawing from the page, and from what was left of her eye. When she looked up for the next field she did not know where it began. There was a flat brown stretch of land, and a line in it that might have been a wall, and she could not have told you what it was for, or how many paces long, or what the soil was, and her hand, going on without her, made a line.

The line went grey. It spread on the page like a drop of tea on a cloth. It was a lie, because she could not see, and a lie would not take the ink, and the whole valley went sideways, and the sky tilted up toward her like a tray.

“You can’t stand in all of it,” said a flat voice, from a long way off.

She felt the cold grass against her cheek.

“We can,” said Liisu.

She woke in a sheepfold.

It was a low round building of piled stone with a roof of turf, and there was straw under her and a sheepskin over her and a sheep, a large and contemplative sheep, standing in the corner looking at her with an air of waiting for her to explain. The light came in a slanting bar through the door, and in it was Liisu, sitting on an upturned pail with the stolen board across her knees, drawing on its margin with a stub of pencil. Her tongue was between her teeth.

“You were out two hours,” said Liisu, not looking up. “Taavi wanted to fetch the bell. I said it would only frighten the sheep. I put the coat on you. It’s Dad’s.”

Reet lay still. She tried the field. She went to the place where Ruus’s barley had been, and found a smooth cool hush the exact shape of it, a long thin strip, with a hedge-shaped edge. She tried the valley around it, and the valley was there, whole, and it was nothing to her. It was a thing she had been told. She sat up slowly, with her head full of brass, and the sheepskin slid, and she looked past the girl through the low door.

The whole of Palu lay below her in the noon light.

She saw it as she had not seen it from the ridge. A woman was hanging washing on a line strung between two bridges, shaking out a sheet, pegging it, shaking out another. A boy ran along a span with a bucket and a very long pole. Smoke rose from a hundred chimneys and leaned over the same way. Two men at a gate argued, on a field she did not know the name of, with their hands. A dog crossed a bridge. A girl sat on a roof. Nine hundred people were standing in this valley. They had stood in it all their lives, on every yard, in their own doors, at their own wells, in every field and ditch and under every gatepost. They knew it as she knew a leaf. They knew where the cow had fallen in.

She is not the one who stood, she thought. They are.

It was so simple that it was embarrassing. She sat in the straw with the lost barley field in her head like a missing tooth, and looked at the valley, and thought of all the afternoons she had spent in the Day-book room, alone, with her lamp, believing that the truth was a thing a perfect record could keep safe, and that she was the one to keep it. She had never once asked anyone. She had never needed to. She had had no one to ask.

“They were here first,” said Reet aloud. “I’m only the one who can draw.”

“Yes,” said Liisu, as if it were a thing that had been settled some time ago. “That’s what I said.”

Taavi came at one o’clock with a loaf.

It was a round dark rye the size of a dinner plate, and he carried it as he had carried the basket, in both arms, against his chest. He sat down on the straw without a word and put it between them. Behind him in the doorway was Aino, filthy to the elbows, with a long raw graze across her chin, saying nothing, and swaying faintly; she had done twenty-nine bridges before breakfast and been asked to stop.

“I did the sums in the night,” said Taavi. “I do that sometimes. Think. It’s inconvenient.”

He did them aloud, because it was the only way he could do them, and they came out in recipes. “Take one gill of base. Add sixty gills of stood-water. Steep an hour in copper, strain through a cloth. That’s a pint and a half of ink, near enough, and it’ll write a lot more than you’d think; the ink’s mostly for being believed. A household is a gill of that. Take three hundred and twelve households. That’s, I’m sorry, that’s, technically that’s under three pints of base. For the whole town.” He swallowed. “My mother gave me, roughly, two quarts. Roughly is her word for a thing she doesn’t want to measure, so I measured. It’s two quarts and a gill.”

“It’s more than we need.”

“It’s four times what we need. Which means we can afford to lose a lot of it. And I hate having that sentence in my head. It’s the kind of sentence you could do a lot of harm with.”

“Why would we lose it?”

“Because she’ll look for it,” said Taavi. “Your Keeper. She’s had eight years of my mother’s casks. She knows my mother. She knows my mother would send a flask. Technically she’ll have the whole inventory in her head.” He took the loaf and turned it over, and she saw that someone had cut a neat round lid from the heel and replaced it, and glued it with a flour paste so exactly that the seam was a thread. Inside the loaf, packed in straw, was a small stoppered crock of grey stoneware. “Half of it goes here. This is Liisu’s. She’s agreed. Nobody’s ever looked in Liisu’s bread.”

“Nobody has ever found it,” said Liisu, “where I take it. I know a place under the grain store that nobody goes.”

“And the other half?”

He had taken the flask from the back of his bandolier. It was the stoneware one, tied about the neck with a red thread, warm still from his body. He held it a moment in both hands. She saw him look at it as one looks at a thing one is going to do to somebody. Then he uncorked the larger of the Ilves Black vials from his belt, and with a hand that trembled very slightly, he poured it into the flask until it was brimming.

“It’s going to look like it,” he said. “And smell like it. There’s enough base left in there for the clove. It’s half the real thing and half my family’s honest ink.” His freckles stood out on a face the colour of paper. “That’s a lie. I’ve never told one on purpose. I’ve omitted things, but I’ve never put it in a bottle. I don’t know how people do it.”

“They get used to it.”

“Please don’t say that,” said Taavi.

He pushed the stopper home. The flask’s red thread hung down. Reet looked at it, at his stained fingers, at the honest and wretched face, and found that she could not say any of the things she might have said, and so said the one she meant.

“That’s the first brave thing I’ve seen anyone do in this valley.”

“It’s a bottle,” said Taavi.

“It’s a bottle that cost you something.”

He looked at his hands, and nodded, and for a minute the sheepfold was entirely quiet except for the sheep.

When they had all gone, she took the board.

The light had shifted. It lay now across her knees in a clean white bar, and she held the tracing in it and did what she had said she would do. She took the ivory rule from her satchel, two inches long, marked to the half-millimetre, and laid it along the gutter fold. She pressed the end against the pin-point of light, and read the figure, and read it again.

Four.

It was four. It was not five. She had seen five on Leaf 88 two years ago, and four on Leaf 88 last week, and a five-millimetre pinhole was a thing the Guild did, to the hair, as it did its dividers and its lamp-wicks. And she had a theory, and she was sorry for it.

She had it whole, as she had everything that was not ground. She went to the library of her memory and took down the afternoon in the Keeper’s rooms, a small neat table, a tray of tea, and a woman’s gloved hands setting a pair of brass dividers to Reet’s fourteen-column draught. She watched them step along the columns, one leg planted, the other swinging. Every interval landed. The right leg stood straight. The left stood off the true like a dancer’s foot, bent in the long shank, so that it leaned as the Tower at Orav leans. She had noticed it at the time, because she noticed such things. She had not known what to do with it.

She took two pencils and a length of thread from the satchel. She laid one pencil along the gutter, and the other at the lean she remembered: three up, four across. She measured the thread against it, and the thread was five. A true leg, shouldered against the gutter fold, puts its point five millimetres in. A leg that leans three-four-five puts its point at the end of the slant, and the slant is five along, and four across.
