She did it twice. She did it a third time, because she did not want it to be so.

Four.

The sheep shifted in the corner and breathed out. In her lap the board lay quite still, and the pin-point of light in the margin looked at her through the onion-skin, small and exact and bright as a star.

It was not a theory. A clerk had pricked it; a Keeper had made it. Every Shift for eight years, every lake and drain and boundary, had gone through the same bent leg. The Keeper’s hand was in the Atlas, and she was sitting in a sheepfold with the proof of it in her lap, and she had suspected for a week, and had not been able to put a ruler to it.

She had begun to fold the tracing when the bell rang.

It was not the bridge-bell. It was the small cracked lookout bell at the head of the gorge road, and it rang once, and then again, and then in a quick hard run, as a bell does when the man at the rope has seen a thing that will not wait for him to finish his sentence. She went to the door of the fold, with the board in her hand.

The road came in from the north across the plateau, white in the afternoon light, and along it, small as seeds, trotted a file of horses. She counted them. She did not mean to. Twelve horses, in a file, at a smart even pace, without any hurry in them, as though the road were a corridor. At the head of them, on a pale grey no bigger than a cat at that distance, rode a figure so small that it would have been taken for a child; and down its back, catching the sun like a wire of silver drawn through the air, hung a braid.

chapters.title: The Keeper Comes to Dinner
chapters.html:
She had not aged. That was the first thing, and it was a stupid thing to think, and Toomas thought it anyway, at the reeve’s window, with his hand flat on the cold glass.

The twelve riders had left their horses at the carters’ stables on the south lip, where the rope bridges began, and Kaie Tammaru came across the Bell Bridge on foot. She walked it as she walked the corridors of the Guild House, at a small unhurried pace with her head up, and the bridge bore her weight as though she were an idea. She was under five feet. The braid hung to her waist, and it had been the colour of a wet fox when she held the lamp for him twelve years ago and was silver now, a rope of it, catching the lantern-light at every step. Her gloves were white. They had pearl buttons at the wrist. A rider walked on either side of her, and a pace behind, mopping his scalp with a handkerchief and carrying his tall black hat as a man carries a sick bird, came Mihkel Org.

Palu had stopped. The drummers on the barrel had run out of rhythm in the middle of a bar. Children who had been racing along the rails of the upper bridges had come down off them and stood in a row with their ribbons trailing, and at the end of the span the bell-rope hung in Jaan Pold’s two hands without moving, as though he had forgotten what it was for.

“Mm,” said Toomas, to the glass. “She has brought her own weather.”

“Is that the Keeper?” said Liisu, at his elbow. She had come to stand beside him on the box she used for looking out of high windows. “She’s small.”

“She is.”

“I thought she’d be bigger. For all the notices.”

“So did I,” said Toomas, “for a good many years.”

They met on the step. The reeve’s house stood at the north end of the bridge on a platform of black timbers over the gorge, a long low house of seven rooms with a floor that hummed when the bridges swayed, and its door opened onto a landing that was also the end of the span. Jaan had set down the bell-rope and come to it. Toomas, in the doorway behind him, with Reet at his shoulder, heard the Keeper’s voice before he saw her face. It was exactly as he remembered it: quiet, complete, with every consonant set down as carefully as a dish.

“Reeve Pold. I am Kaie Tammaru, Keeper of the Atlas. I have ridden eleven hours, and my escort with me. I ask the hospitality of your house.” There was the smallest pause, a pause he knew, in which she looked at a thing and chose whether to say it. “And supper, naturally, if there is any to be had.”

Palu had a custom about guests. It was older than the Guild, and older than the bridges; it was the sort of law that does not need a book, because it lives in the body, in the hand that offers bread. Toomas saw it take hold of his nephew. He saw the heavy shoulders try to lift in refusal and be held down by something heavier. A man cannot turn from his door a stranger who has asked for salt. Not on the Name-Day. Not with the whole of his town looking on.

“Sit,” said Jaan Pold. “Eat.”

“You are very kind.”

“It’s stew.”

“Naturally,” said Kaie.

She came in. She passed Toomas without turning her head; her eyes went over him as over a doorpost, and came to rest, with the faintest flicker, on Reet. “Surveyor Sallik. You have been missed at the Day-book.” Then, to Mihkel, who had halted on the threshold with his hat against his chest and the expression of a man who would give a year’s pay to be in the wrong building: “Master Org. You will see to the horses and to the men, and then you will join us.”

“Keeper,” said Mihkel. He looked at Toomas. “Veskimae.”

“Org. I understand you have mislaid a mountain.”

“I have a letter from the Guild’s insurers,” said Mihkel, with bitterness, “on the subject of one mountain.” He went out.

The reeve’s table was a long one of scrubbed pine, with a bench down either side, and there were seven at it: Jaan at the head, the Keeper at his right hand, then Toomas, then Reet; across from them Liisu and two of the riders, who sat very straight and ate as if they were being timed. The stew was grayling, with dill and cream and small yellow potatoes, and it came in wooden bowls. Beyond the window the gorge went blue with evening. Under the floor the bridges moved, a long slow breath, in and out.

Kaie ate in her gloves.

Toomas watched it with a feeling of unreality. She broke bread with white kidskin fingers, and a pearl button at her wrist dipped once in the cream, and she wiped it, unhurried, with the corner of her napkin. At the far end of the table Liisu had stopped eating altogether.

“Why are you wearing gloves at supper?” said Liisu.

“Liisu,” said Jaan.

“It is a reasonable question, Reeve.” The Keeper turned her pale brown eyes on the child with perfect courtesy. “It is a habit of the vault, Miss Pold. Rule Nineteen requires two gloves on vellum, and in twenty years I have found that I forget to take them off.”

“There isn’t any vellum.”

“Naturally not.”

“Then you can take them off.”

“I could,” agreed Kaie, “and I shall, when I have finished.” She smiled at her. It was a good smile; it was the thing that had made the Assembly vote for her. “That is a very fine map of yours, I think, upon the bridge. I saw it as I crossed. The mulberry is exactly where it should be.”

Liisu looked at her, and then at her bowl. It was the first time Toomas had ever seen her unable to say a thing.

“Reeve,” said Kaie, when the bowls were empty. “May I put some figures before you?”

“Say them.”

She drew a folded sheet from the breast of her coat and opened it on the table among the crumbs. It was ruled in columns, in a clerk’s neat hand, and as she laid it flat he saw Reet’s whole body go still beside him, the stillness of a hound that has seen the hare.

“The Seam widens one mile in the year. I say it as one says that the river runs downhill, because it is the same kind of fact.” The gloved finger moved down the paper. “The Hollow’s rim lies thirty-one miles from the Seam’s northern edge on the line of the Cold Stream. That is thirty-one years. In the year three hundred and three, when I was given the keys, it was eleven. If I had done nothing, the edge would be at the Guild stair in three.” She did not raise her voice. “Forty thousand people live in the Hollow, Reeve. They cannot be moved in a season, or in ten. They can be moved in forty years, with the Assembly’s help, if the Assembly can be made to believe in the necessity. The Assembly voted against moving your own town, twelve years ago, on a question of cost. You may remember.”

“I remember,” said Jaan.

“I do not intend to ask them again until I have gained the time to be refused.” She turned the sheet a little. “I have gained twenty-eight years, in eight places, on land that was thinly peopled. I moved every household first. I paid for it from the Keeper’s own purse, as grain-relief. Not one soul has been harmed. Palu is the ninth place I have had to ask.”

The word ask sat on the table among the bowls. Toomas saw his nephew look at it.

“On the night of the tenth,” said Kaie, “this valley will be a lake. I will not discuss the means. I ask you to believe the date. It is tomorrow night, Reeve. The weight of the Seam settles here, on the throat of the Haldja, where it is thickest, and the water will stand to the lip of the upland, and Palu will be forty feet under it. I do not want your people under it. I have brought riders and forty ropes and a plan of march. I have Orav, with its empty pans and three hundred roofs, which the Hollow has held since the sickness. You would have timber for your bridges. You would take your goats.”

“And the dead?”

It was said very quietly. For the first time something moved in the Keeper’s face. “That,” said Kaie, “I am sorry for. I have not found a way.”

“My mother’s behind the tower.”

“Yes.”

“Thirty-one of my family are behind the tower.” Jaan’s two hands lay flat on the table on either side of his bowl, heavy and still, the bell-rope callus gleaming yellow. “I rang a bell over every one.”

“Surveyor Sallik,” said Kaie gently, as though he had not spoken. “You have the best head for figures in the Guild. Tell the reeve whether I am wrong.”

Reet had not spoken since the door. She had her hands under the table, and her chin up, and Toomas, who sat beside her, felt her draw in a breath and thought: she cannot lie to this woman. She will have to answer it. “The figures are right,” said Reet.

“Thank you.”

“The sum is wrong.”

“Which line?”

“I don’t know yet,” said Reet.

It was true, and she said it without a hitch, and he saw the Keeper hear that it was true. Something went across the small, pointed, lovely face and was put away.

“No,” said Jaan Pold.

“Reeve—”

“No. Not tomorrow. Not Orav. Not forty ropes, not a plan of march, not any of it. Nine hundred of us have stood here since before there was a Guild. You’ll not walk us out of it on a paper.” He stood. The bench scraped. “Eat what you want. There’s a bed. You’ll be gone in the morning.”

“Naturally you may refuse,” said Kaie. She had not moved. She folded the sheet along its creases and put it in her breast. “I will ask again.”

She asked him, later, in the yard.

It was Toomas she asked. She said, “Master Veskimae, will you walk with me?” as if inviting him to cross a courtyard, and he got up, and the reeve looked at the two of them, and said nothing.

The yard was a ledge of bare rock behind the house with a rail along its edge, and below the rail the gorge went down in the dusk to the bootlace of the river. There was a woodpile, and a rain barrel, and half a dozen buckets turned upside down to dry, and from the other side of the chasm the sound of a drum, picking up again, rather uncertainly, as though someone had gone to find it and brought it back. The lantern on its nail made a small gold room in the dark.

“You have grown a moustache,” said Kaie.

“I had one when you last saw me.”

“It was smaller.” She stood at the rail with her gloved hands folded, looking not down but across at the far wall of the gorge. “I did not expect you to come. I expected Sallik, in time. I believed I had given her enough to think about.”

“You gave her tea.”

“Naturally.”

“How many, Kaie?”

She did not pretend. It was one of the things he had admired, once, in the thin brown clerk who kept the inventory and held the lamp: she did not pretend. “Eight places, on fourteen leaves. Palu is the ninth. The first was Tallow Moor, in the autumn of three-oh-three, a heath with a farm on it, four souls, who are in Orav now, with a cow. Two hundred and eleven in all. Nobody has died.”

“Nobody has died,” said Toomas, tasting it. “Mm. And I?”

“Eleven.” She said it at once. “I know the claim file by heart. I have read it more often than the Rules.”

“Where did you find the notebook?”

“In the false drawer, behind the lamp-oil receipts. Two years after you were dismissed. I was thirty-eight.” She spoke to the far wall of the gorge. “I read it on the vault stair, with a candle, in one night. In the morning I went down with a vial and a leaf and proved you right on a heath near Tallow Moor. I held the lamp, you will remember, the night you drew the river. I watched your hand. It did not shake. I thought: that is a man who knows precisely what he is doing.” She turned her head. “I did not learn until I read the notebook that you had no idea.”

“No.”

“The notebook began it. I would not take that from you.”

“You did not ask me.”

“No.”

“Why?”

“Because you would have said no,” said Kaie.

“Yes,” said Toomas. “I would.”

“And the Hollow would have gone on dying politely, in the interests of consultation.” She said it without heat, as she said everything. “I am forty-eight, Master Veskimae. I have been careful. I move the people first. I draw nothing on a leaf that I have not read twice, and I turn the page.” She let that rest. “You did not. That is the difference between us.”

“Is it?” He looked down at the river. “It costs you, I suppose. The drawing.”

“Less than it cost you. I draw from the leaf and not the ground. But it is not nothing.” The pale eyes did not leave the cliff. “I could not tell you tonight where Sora Crossing lies, though I have its population to the head. Tallow Moor I know as one knows the moon.”

“Then you cannot see them.”

“I do not need to see them. I need to count them.”

He was silent for some time. The drum across the gorge had found its pattern again. “And the water?” said Toomas at last. “It is borrowed. I used a vial of Palu’s, myself, and never asked whose. Every vial on the shelf was filled by a rider who stood in the place and said so. They did not know they were lending.”

“Naturally they would have objected.”

“Mm. As would I.”

There was the small sound of a footstep on rock. Toomas turned his head.

Mihkel Org stood at the corner of the house with a lantern in one hand and his hat in the other. He had come, plainly, to report on the horses; he had, in the tradition of his office, a sheet of paper in his coat and a Rule on his tongue. He had been standing there for some time. In the lamplight his face had gone the colour of tallow, and the walnut fringe stood up at the back like a cock’s comb. “Keeper,” he said. “The riders—”

He stopped.

“Master Org,” said Kaie. “You were not meant to hear it like this.”

“The ninth,” said Mihkel.

“Mihkel.”

“I audited the Correction Book. I audited it every quarter for nineteen years. Re-inking, I said. It is a matter of maintenance.” His voice had gone up, like that of a man trying to speak while walking on a plank. “The notebook. Veskimae’s notebook. You said, a moment ago, the notebook began it. And Soo. You said eleven.”

“How was it you wished to hear it?” said Kaie.

“I should have wished to hear it in some other way. I should have wished to be told.”

“Gently,” said Kaie. “In the Hollow. In due course.”

Mihkel Org opened his mouth. Toomas saw it, and was to remember it for the rest of his life: the round pink face, the lantern shaking, the whole pillar of the man drawing itself up for the one resource he had never lacked. He opened his mouth for a Rule. And for the first time in thirty years there was not one.

He sat down. He sat on an upturned bucket, in the exact middle of the yard, with the lantern on his knee, and the bucket gave a small, damp, fishy sound, as of old herring-heads settling. He did not seem to notice.

“It was very tidy,” said Mihkel, to nobody. “The Book. It was a very tidy Book.”

They went in. Kaie asked the reeve for pen and paper, and a candle, and was given them; she sat down at the head of the pine table and drew the sheet toward her, and wrote at the top of it in a hand as small and clean as a row of seeds. Toomas stood by the window. Reet stood at the foot of the table with her back straight and her hands at her sides. The reeve had not sat down again. Liisu was in the corner on the box, perfectly motionless, with her thumbnail between her teeth.

“Master Org,” said Kaie, without lifting her head. “You will take Surveyor Sallik and Master Veskimae into custody. The Ilves boy also, and the guard Rebane. They will be held in the grain store, and watched, and treated with every courtesy, until the night of the tenth is over.”

Mihkel stood in the doorway. He had put on his hat, as a man puts on a coat in a house where he has not been asked to stay. “Under what Rule, Keeper?”

“Rule Forty.”

“Rule Forty,” said Mihkel. His voice was very flat. “No Surveyor sleeps unwatched in a shifting place.”

“For their protection. Naturally.”

“Naturally,” said Mihkel. A long breath went out of him. “Rule Sixty-two requires that an order of custody be signed in the hand of the issuing officer. Bare.”

It was the habit of thirty years. It rose in him without his leave, like a hiccup. He heard himself say it, and his round face did something terrible, and Toomas, who knew what it was to be caught by one’s own reflexes at an hour of disaster, felt for him something so close to love that he had to look away.

“Bare,” said Kaie.

“I beg your pardon. It is in the Rules.”

“I know that it is.” She laid the pen down. For a moment she did nothing. She looked at her own hands on the paper, the white gloves folded over each other, and Toomas saw her decide. She took hold of the pearl button at the wrist of the left glove, and undid it. She drew the glove off, finger by finger, slowly, as one draws a sheet off a body. She did the same with the right.

Nobody in the room breathed.

The hands beneath were small and fine-boned and stained to the wrist. It was not the pale grey-blue of Ilves Black, which comes off in a week’s soap. It was the dark one, the true one, blue-black with a gloss on it like a beetle’s wing, soaked into the skin to the depth of the pores and stopped at the wrist-bone in a line as sharp as a cuff. It had been laid down in layers over years. It was a colour Toomas knew from the inside. His own hands had been that colour once, before twelve years of Tinta Row and a great deal of lye.

In nineteen years Mihkel Org had never seen the Keeper’s hands. Rule Nineteen. He had thought it was modesty.

Kaie took up the pen and wrote her name.

From the yard, as she signed, came a crash, a bellow, the unmistakable clang of a salt-hook meeting a Guild shield, a stream of oaths in a woman’s voice, and the heavy rattle of ox-chain being run through a wheel. Nobody looked round. Reet’s eyes had not left the Keeper’s hands. Toomas saw her take it in, all of it, in the way she took in a hillside, and set it where she kept such things.

“You’ve been drawing for years,” said Reet.

Kaie Tammaru blew gently on the wet ink, and set down the pen.

“Naturally,” she said.

chapters.title: The Grain Store
chapters.html:
There were forty-one sacks of barley in the store, and Reet had counted them twice by touch, because there was no light to count them by.

The building stood on staddle stones against the mice, a long timber barn with a plank floor a yard above the ground, and its single window was a slit under the eaves too high to reach and too narrow for anything but the night. A thread of lantern light lay under the door. By it she had found the sacks, and the stacked flails, and the scoop, and a coil of old rope, and the place against the north wall where the barley dust lay thickest and Toomas had settled himself with the chain-staff taken from him and his bad leg out in front like a plank. He had been coughing for an hour. It was a dry small cough, polite, the cough of a man who does not wish to be a bother in a house that has locked him up.

She took off her scarf and put it round his mouth. It was the grey wool strip she had worn since Soo.

“Mm,” said Toomas, through the wool. “It is not necessary.”

“Hold it there.”

“I am sixty-two. A man of sixty-two has the right to cough in a granary.”

“You have the right to cough with a scarf,” said Reet, and he said nothing more, and held it there.

From the yard came a whisper. It was a very loud whisper, and by now Reet knew its rhythm as she knew the sound of her own chain. Aino had been chained to the near wheel of the reeve’s grain-cart with a length of ox-chain through the hub, and had decided, evidently, that if she could not break the chain she could at least dispose of the men who held it. “And the one at the gate,” breathed the voice, “is the Under-Keeper of the Weights, and he’s a cousin of Treasurer’s, and I can tell because he stands like a man waiting for a pardon. And the fat one with the cough is Auditor. And that one, with the hair—” It paused. “That one’s the Assistant Registrar of Sluices, and if he doesn’t take his boot off my salt-hook he will find out what a Registrar’s mother is made of.”

“Eleven so far,” said Reet.

“Technically she’s inventing some of them,” said Taavi.

He had not said anything since the door was barred. He sat against it, in the thread of light, with his knees up and his arms round them. His bandolier was still on his chest; Reet had noticed that, and noticed that the riders who had brought him in, a boy found under the sacking in the cart with a perfectly serene expression, saying that technically he had only been counting, had been told by someone not to touch his things. She had wondered who. She knew now. It was an odd thing, to be afraid of a knowledge you have not yet been given, and to have it arrive on the other side of a door.

The bolt went back a little past the second hour of the night.

She had been lying on her back across two sacks with her eyes open, doing what she did instead of sleeping. It was an exercise she had never needed before, because she had never before had so much of a country gone out of her: she went to the Hollow’s gate, and found the gate and not the road to it; she went to the Wharf Gate, and the barges, and the ducks; she went to the pond at Soo, and there was a smooth cool silence the exact shape of a pond. She had begun to keep a ledger of what remained. It was not a long ledger. The door opened, and the lantern came in, and she sat up.

Kaie Tammaru had brought it herself.

She came in alone and shut the door behind her. She wore a plain grey wrapper over her riding things, as though she had been about to go to bed and had thought better of it, and she carried in her left hand the lantern, and under her arm a folded blanket, and in her right a stone bottle with a cork. Her hands were bare. In the yellow light the stain on them looked almost purple. She set the lantern on a sack, laid the blanket across Toomas’s knees without a word, and put the bottle in his hands.

“Salted tea,” she said. “Hot. The cook at the house was most obliging.”

“Keeper,” said Toomas. It was all he said. He drank.

She sat down on a sack opposite Reet. She was so small that her feet did not quite meet the floor, and she crossed her ankles to hide the fact. She said, “Surveyor Sallik. I have read your fourteen columns eleven times.”

“I made them so that you would.”

“They are the finest piece of work done in the Day-book room since I came to the Hollow. Naturally I mean that as the Keeper and not as a woman who has been caught.” She spoke very quietly, in the voice of the Guild House, every consonant set down. “I have been looking for a long time for a Surveyor like you, and I will not insult either of us by pretending that it is chance that I found you at nineteen. I am forty-eight. Each lake costs me a little of the ground I draw. By the end of the thirty-one years I will have very little left of myself, and there is no one in the Hollow I would trust with the keys.”

Reet said nothing.

“I should like you to take them,” said Kaie.

It was so plain that for an instant it did not seem to be a sentence. Reet heard Toomas’s bottle stop.

“You cannot forget,” said Kaie. “That is the first thing. In the vault, with the leaves open before you, you would hold every one of the four hundred and twelve at once, and see how they lie against each other, as I cannot. You can do in a week what takes me a season. And you cannot lie.” She said it with a kind of tenderness. “You stammered at me over the tea. I have thought of it every night. Do you understand what that is worth in a Keeper? An Atlas written by someone who is unable to deceive it, or herself, or the ground. I have wanted that all my life.”

“I’ve lost a road,” said Reet. It came out before she had decided. “And a pond. And a field.”

“I know you have. Org told me of the pass, and I have eyes. You keep looking at the place where a door was.” The pale brown eyes did not move from her face. “Out there, with the ink on your hand and your heart in it, you will pay for every yard, and you will pay all of it in the end. You have seen what it did to him. Six miles, from one stroke. In the vault you would lose almost nothing, because you would be drawing from the leaf and not the ground. I am not offering you a throne, Sallik. I am offering you a way to do this without being emptied.”

She had thought she would be angry. She waited for the anger and it did not come. What came instead was a slow clear cold, such as she felt over a piece of ground that did not close. She sat with her hands on her knees, in the thread of light, and made herself look at what was there.

“Your numbers are right,” said Reet.

“Thank you. Few have said so.”

“I did them in my head while you ate. The Seam, the rim, the Assembly. Forty thousand is a real thing. I’m not going to tell you that it isn’t, because it is, and I can’t tell you what I don’t believe.” Her voice was level. “But you didn’t ask Palu.”

“Palu would have said no.”

It was said gently. That was what Reet remembered afterward: not the words but the kindness in them, the sorrowful patience, the tone in which one explains to a child why the fire is hot. “Palu would have said no, Sallik. I have asked the Assembly, and it said no. I asked the reeve tonight and he said no. No one in the history of the world has said yes to being moved. Naturally I stopped asking.”

“Then that’s what’s there.”

Kaie’s head tilted.

“A no is information,” said Reet. She heard herself say it with a great, odd, growing wonder, as though she had heard it said by someone else. “It’s a fact about the ground. They like their bridges. They’ve got thirty-one of the reeve’s family in the yard. That’s there. You can’t draw a lake around it and call the place empty. You’ve done the sums of the Hollow and left off the other column.”

“And the other column is to be given a vote? Forty thousand against nine hundred?”

“I don’t know. I don’t know the sum.” Her own hands were cold. “But my mother lives in Sora.”

Something moved in the Keeper’s face.

“Leaf Eighty-eight. The drain behind Kalda’s mill. It moved last spring, and my mother wrote to say her cellar had been dry for the first time in twenty years, and she wondered if the Guild had done something about it. She was pleased.”

“Then she is the happier for it.”

“She’s pleased because she doesn’t know.” Reet’s voice cracked at last, a hair’s breadth. “She’d have said yes, perhaps, if you’d asked. Or no. I don’t know. I’ll never know. I only know that I don’t know what she’d say, and neither do you. Nobody does, because nobody asked.”

For a time the Keeper looked at her. She sat quite straight on the sack, small, silver-braided, with her stained hands lying in her lap like two things that belonged to another woman. “The seventh place,” said Kaie, at last, quietly. “Your mother’s marsh. I moved the drain a quarter-mile into the basin. The cellar was a consequence, not a purpose. I am sorry for it. I did not know whose leaf it was until after.”

It was the nearest thing to an apology Reet would ever hear her give, and she was almost sure it was meant.

“You may think about it,” said Kaie, and rose. “I shall not ask you before dawn.”

At the door, with her hand on the latch, the Keeper stopped.

“There is one other matter. Master Ilves.”

Taavi had not moved. He sat against the planks, a foot from her skirts, with his knees drawn up. Reet saw the freckles stand out on his face like dropped seed. “Technically,” he said, “I’m not sure I’m—”

“Your mother gave you something. A stoneware flask with a red thread. I imagine you have it on you.” She did not make it a question. “Stand up, please.”

He stood up. He stood, and she came across the floor to him in three small steps, and put out one bare hand and turned him a little by the shoulder, as one turns a coat on a peg. She found the flask at the back of the bandolier, in the angle where the little vials did not hang. She slid the red thread off its hook. It came away easily.

“She has never told me,” said Kaie, weighing it in her palm, “that she kept back a measure. But she does, naturally. She has been honest with me in every particular except that one, and I have honoured her by not enquiring.” She drew the stopper and held the neck beneath her nose. “She still puts in the clove.”

The smell reached Reet across the room, warm and sweet and wrong. Kaie looked down at the flask for some seconds. Then, quite calmly, she tipped it.

It came out black. It ran out of the neck in a thick glossy cord and struck the boards, and spread. It went into the cracks between the planks and along the grain, and where it touched the barley dust it drank it in and darkened, and the dark crept outward in a long spreading lobe like a coastline. The smell of cloves came up out of it, strong enough to taste. Reet watched it as she had watched Kuld Mere, and Soo, and the black stone on the white. She found that the stain had a shape. It was the exact shape of the Pale Flats on the Guild’s great map in the Day-book room, and she did not know why her mind should have done that.

She did not look at Taavi. She looked at the ink.

Kaie shook the last drops from the neck. She stoppered the empty flask and set it carefully on the sack beside the lantern. The satisfaction in her face was small and private, like a woman’s at a letter written.

“Is that the whole of it, Master Ilves?”

“It’s the only flask I carry,” said Taavi, in a very small voice.

The pale eyes turned. “Surveyor?”

Reet felt her heart go over once, like a stone. She had been a girl who could not lie for nineteen years, and she had been taught by a bird, a basket and an old man’s remark about sentences that there was a space between a lie and the truth where a person might stand and be neither. “That was all that was in the flask,” she said.

It went out of her mouth level, and clean, and unstammering.

Kaie Tammaru studied her for a count of three. Nothing in the small face altered. “Naturally,” she said. She went to the door. “Good night, Master Veskimae. I did not mean it to be so cold.”

The bolt dropped behind her.

Nobody spoke until the sound of her steps had gone down the yard.

Then Taavi sat. He slid down the planks until he was on the floor against the door with his legs out, and he laid his hands palm-up on his knees, and they were empty, and he looked at them. His shoulders were shaking. He did not make a sound.

“Taavi,” said Toomas.

“I’m sorry.”

“No.”

“I lost it. It’s all gone, it was the last of it, and my mother said not to lose it, she said don’t lose it, and I—”

“Taavi.” Toomas had put down the bottle. He put his two hands on the chain-staff that was not there, found nothing, and laid them on his knees. He had never looked so old. “I should like to say something to you, and I should like you to let me say it to the end.”

Taavi’s head came up. Reet saw his eyes find hers, once, across the dark, and saw what was in them. It was the look of someone who has been given a gift that he cannot spend, and who has to sit in the room with the person who is sorry.

“I should have stopped it,” said Toomas. “Twelve years ago, and every year since. I should have taken the notebook to the Assembly, and my neck with it. I should have burned the key. I did neither. I went to Tinta Row and bound fish ledgers, and while I bound them your mother sold a woman a thing I had made possible, and she had a customer, and you had a flask. It is the sort of arithmetic I am good at.” His voice was dry, even, entirely without self-pity. “I am sorry, Taavi. I do not often say it. I am told I am out of practice.”

“It’s not— technically—” Taavi had gone grey. “It wasn’t you, it was my mother, it was—”

“It was a good many of us. I begin with myself.” He leaned his head back against the sacks. “That is all.”

Reet looked at the floor. She would have told him. She would have said it out loud, there and then, with her whole heart: it’s in the loaf, Toomas, it’s safe, he’s not lost it, he’s cleverer than any of us. But the barn had ears; it had a man outside it with a lantern; and she had learned in the past hour exactly how narrow a ledge she stood on. So she sat with her hands on her knees, and her face still, and let an old man apologise to a boy who had not done anything, for a loss that had not happened, and she was ashamed.

She heard Taavi weep after that. It went on for some time.

Out in the yard Aino’s whisper had faltered. It went on, now and then, in bursts: Deputy Assistant Surveyor of Culverts, you great lump, and then not.

The town had gone quiet.

She had not noticed it happen. The drums across the gorge had stopped, and the singing, and the sound of feet on the planks; the lanterns on the bridges had been put out one by one, and the dark had come up out of the river. Through the slit in the eaves she could see a single star. The floor beneath her had its slow breath in it, the bridges settling, and somewhere a long way off a dog barked once and thought better of it.

She lay down again. She put her hands behind her head and looked at where the ceiling would have been.

She had never forgotten a thing in her life. It was her one gift, and her one comfort. And now the ground went out of her whenever it pleased, a road, a pond, a field of barley, and in the places where it had been there was nothing, a clean cool snow, and she had thought that was the worst that could be done to a person. She saw now that it was not. The ground left. What people did to you stayed. A white kidskin glove coming off a finger at a time. A small bare hand tilting a flask. A boy’s face. An old man’s voice saying he was sorry, in the dark, to the wrong person.

She wanted, very badly, to forget this. She lay there and tried. She went to the place where she kept things and she took out the whole of the evening and set it on the snow and looked at it, and it did not go.

It would be there in the morning. It would be there when she was old.

She had nearly slept when it came.

It came from below. It was very small, and it came up through the planks beneath her back with the faint dust of the barley: three notes, rising, rising, falling, the sort of whistle a child makes to call a dog that is hiding. It came again.

chapters.title: Under the Floorboards
chapters.html:
In sixty-two years Toomas Veskimae had been whistled at by dogs, by watch-sergeants, by the wind in a hundred chimneys and once, memorably, by a heron. He had never before been whistled at by a floor.

He lay where he was on four barley sacks, with Reet’s grey scarf still wound across his mouth against the dust, and considered the sound. Three notes, rising, rising, falling. It was not a rider’s signal, which was two short, and it was not a lamp-boy’s, which went up at the end like a question. Somebody small had made a tune of her own and was using it with the confidence of a person who has never been told that an idea was bad.

Across the barn Reet had sat up. He heard it rather than saw it, the crisp small rustle of a girl turning over in barley. She had laid her bare left hand flat on the planks and was listening with it.

“Third board from the wall,” said a voice, very near, muffled by earth. It was flat and clear. “The one with the knot like an eye. I’ll push. Don’t pull, it sticks.”

Out in the yard the rider on the door had been singing to himself for an hour, a mournful ballad about a mule who loved a widow, with more verses than the widow had earned. It covered a good deal.

The board lifted an inch, then three, with the dry complaint of a nail not asked to move in forty years, and rose clear and was drawn down out of sight. In the oblong of dark where it had been there came a faint yellow gleam, and above the gleam a smudge of face. It was a child’s face, filthy to the eyebrows, with a gap in the front teeth. Her hair had been tied back with what Toomas realised, after a moment, was a length of feast-ribbon.

“Somebody was crying,” said Liisu Pold. “I waited till they stopped. It seemed rude.”

“That was—” said Taavi thickly, from the dark by the door. “Technically I was only—”

“It was fine. Come on.”

Reet was already on her knees at the hole. “How wide is it?”

“Two feet and a bit. I measured with Peep Laan’s bread-board.”

“The roof?”

“Barrel staves. They hold.”

“How do you know they hold?”

“I’m still alive.” The gleam moved: a tin lantern, shuttered to a slit, with a stub of tallow inside. “It goes eleven yards to Peep’s woodshed. Peep’s got a hip and can’t do the stair, and Papa’s clerk weighs the tithe loaves, so Peep’s was always a loaf short. So I made a back.” She looked past Reet into the barn, at the long shape of Toomas on the sacks, and her face did what it had done on the bridge on the night of the feast. It took a measurement. “The big one might stick.”

“The big one,” said Toomas through the scarf, “has been called a number of things in his time.”

“You’ll stick under the wall. Breathe out.”

He went last. He lowered himself through the floor feet first, like a man entering a very cold bath, and the knee spoke to him at length on the subject. Under the planks was a space the height of a hearth, floored with powdered barley and mouse droppings, where the staddle stones stood about in the gloom like a congregation of toadstools. At the far end a round black mouth had been cut into the footing and ringed with the staves of a cooper’s reject. Out of it came a smell of wet clay, tallow and, quite unmistakably, yeast.

“Eleven yards,” said Reet’s voice ahead of him, small and flat in the earth. “And a foot. She’s right.”

“I’m always right about yards,” said Liisu, further on. “Mind the root.”

He minded the root. His hands found, one after another, the cold ribs of the staves, each worked smooth by the hands that had set it there, and he thought with some distinctness that in thirty years of Keeping the Atlas he had gone everywhere by stair, upright, in a good coat. Now, at sixty-two, he was leaving a prison on his belly, behind an ink-maker’s boot-soles, down a hole that a girl of eleven had dug with a spoon. A man should not be rescued in the same posture as a dog.

But it was Helju’s way. He knew it as the clay crept past his ears. She had always gone into a thing head first and without discussion: into the Hollow’s cold schoolroom at nine, with her plaits like two ropes; into a marriage with a bridge-wright she had known a week; into last winter, forbidding anyone to write. Whatever her granddaughter had dug had been dug in exactly that spirit. There was no use his saying it was not safe. He had said a good deal about safety once, on a certain night, with a lamp held for him, and they had been excellent arguments.

Under the wall he stuck. The clay closed on his shoulders and the footing stones leaned on his back, an enormous patient pressure, as if the whole of Palu had decided to sit down on him, and for some moments he lay with his cheek in the cold and thought of nothing, which for him was rare.

“Out,” said Liisu, from somewhere ahead, quite calmly. “All of it. Then push with your feet.”

He breathed out until there was nothing left. Hands closed on his collar from the front, a small pair and a larger, Taavi’s grey-blue at the fingertips, and the wall let him go with a sound like a cork.

His head came up through a trap in a floor of wood-chips into a smell of split birch, and a glow, and the first thing he saw was a pair of black buckled shoes, polished until they shone like wet slate. His eye travelled up from them. It passed over a pair of stout calves, a mustard waistcoat done up one button out, a round pale face above the waistcoat with a walnut-coloured fringe standing on end, and, held out at arm’s length like a man offering a dead bird to a cat, a lantern.

“Veskimae,” said Mihkel Org.

“Org.” Toomas was on his hands and knees with clay in his moustache. It did not seem a position from which to say much else. “Good evening.”

“Rule Forty.”

“Yes?”

“Rule Forty,” said Mihkel again, with a great effort at steadiness, and the light ran up and down the log wall. Reet and Taavi had got themselves upright behind Toomas, shapeless with clay, and stood against the stacked birch looking at him as one looks at a man who has put a pistol on the table. In a corner Liisu sat on an upturned bucket, eating something. “’No Surveyor sleeps unwatched in a shifting place.’ It was framed in the year fourteen, after Heron Weir, and has never been amended. I have been through the Rules. Twice. By this lantern. I wish it understood that I am here under Rule Forty and under no other authority whatsoever.”

“I should like to understand it,” said Toomas. “Slowly. I am sixty-two.”

“The Keeper has placed four persons in a barn, under Rule Forty. The barn stands in a valley which the Keeper, by her own account at supper, has entered in the Atlas as a lake. A valley so entered is a shifting place. The persons were, by my reading, sleeping, and were not watched. The rider on the door faces the yard, which I observed, and the yard is not the persons.” He swallowed. “That is a breach of Rule Forty, and I am compelled to remedy it. I intend to watch you. I intend to watch you very closely. I shall be at your elbow, at a distance of no more than thirty feet, from now until the lake. That is Rule Forty.”

“Technically,” said Taavi, “I’m an ink-maker, not a Surveyor, so I don’t think—”

“Rule Forty is to be construed generously, Master Ilves.”

“You’re letting us out,” said Reet.

“I am watching you. Under Rule Forty.”

“By way of a hole.”

“Rule Forty is silent on holes.”

“Org,” said Toomas, gently.

“Rule Forty,” said Mihkel. It came out quite quietly. He tried again, to the lantern, in a voice gone small. “Rule Forty.”

“That,” said Reet, “is the eleventh time.”

He looked up. “I beg your pardon?”

“You’ve said Rule Forty eleven times since we came out. I counted.”

Mihkel Org looked at her. In the shaking light the round face seemed to come a little loose at the corners, like a loaf left in the rain. “Have I,” he said. “Well. It is a good Rule.” And then, quite simply: “I did not know what else to say.”

“He was sitting on Papa’s herring heads,” said Liisu, with her mouth full. “In the yard, after supper. He looked like he needed a job. I asked if he had the keys and the rota and he said what was it to me, and I said it was my yard.”

“She remarked,” said Mihkel, “that Rule Forty did not sound like a barn.”

Toomas got himself up by the log-pile, one joint at a time. The lantern would not keep still in the Master-Surveyor’s hand. Beneath one arm he held a small book bound in black oilcloth, the Rules of the Guild, one hundred and twelve, clasped as a drowning man clasps a spar. Toomas knew the look. It was the look of someone who has kept a very large clock all his life and has just been told it was telling the time to someone else.

“Did you find it, Org?” he said. “The Rule for when the Keeper is wrong.”

“I looked under Keeper.” Mihkel’s mouth worked. “There is a Rule about her gloves. She has kept every one, Veskimae. I checked. The custody order was signed bare-handed, as Sixty-two requires. She has broken nothing. She has not broken one single Rule, and that is what I cannot—” He stopped. “I do not know what to do. I am a Master-Surveyor. I know what the Rules say. I find I do not know what they are for.”

“Mm. Then do the one you have in your hand,” said Toomas gently, “and see.”

“Here,” said Liisu.

She slid off the bucket. From between two logs she drew a long object wrapped in a flannel petticoat and held it out to Taavi in both hands, the way one offers a baby to a stranger. “It’s gone hard. I wanted to eat it and I didn’t.”

Taavi turned back the flannel. It was a rye loaf of the heavy dark kind, split along the top and lidded with its own crust, and when he lifted the lid there was a hollow, and in the hollow a crock of grey stoneware no taller than a man’s hand, stoppered and sealed with red wax. He did not take it out. He held the open loaf against his chest and shut his eyes, and said, in a voice from which every hedge had been removed, “It’s all here.”

“What is?” said Toomas.

“The base.” Taavi opened his eyes. “Half of it. The half I kept back. I couldn’t tell you in the barn, there was a man at the door with a lantern, and the flask was a decoy. Technically a half-decoy. It was half the real thing and half my family’s honest black, with the clove put in so it would smell right, and then you said all those things to me, and I let you.”

Toomas regarded him. He regarded the loaf, and the child with the ribbon in her hair, and Reet, who had found something of great interest in the toe of her boot. “Let me be sure I have this,” he said. “In the dark, with great feeling, I made an apology.”

“Yes.”

“A good one.”

“It was very good,” said Taavi miserably.

“And the finest ink in three hundred years was at that moment in the arms of a child, in a hole, in a loaf.”

“And the only one in the barn who did not know was myself.”

“And Aino,” said Taavi. “Aino didn’t know either.”

“I should like it noted,” said Toomas, “that it was an excellent apology.”

“It was the best I’ve ever had,” said Taavi. “I’d like to keep it, if it’s all the same.”

Toomas laughed. It came out of him without warning, a dry creak like a gate not opened since spring, and Reet looked round at him as though a dog had spoken. He leaned on the log-pile and laughed until the knee hurt, and went on a little after. “Keep it,” he said. “Keep it, you terrible boy.”

They went round by the lane, in single file, along the foot of the yard wall, Mihkel in front with his lantern held high as men carry them at funerals. The wind had got up in the gorge. Palu was never silent at night. Its forty bridges worked at their cables like ships at anchor, and the whole town ticked and groaned and sighed in the dark, taking every sound that was made in it and giving it back as a piece of the creaking. Toomas had loved that, at twenty.

At the yard gate a rider sat on a stool with a cloak over his knees. He was on his feet before the lantern reached him.

“Rider Joosep. Rule Sixty-six: horses are counted at the third bell. It is past the fourth.” Mihkel let that sit. “You will take Rider Anu from the barn door. It is a two-man count. The south lip, twice, and write the number down.”

“They’re all there, sir. I saw them tied.”

“Then it will be a short count, and you will have the pleasure of being right. Go.”

They went, arguing amiably down the lane over whether a mule counted. Toomas could not remember a Rule Sixty-six about horses, but he could not remember most of them, and Mihkel had never in his life forgotten one. The singing at the barn door stopped, and the quiet that came after was larger than the singing had been.

The gate opened before Mihkel could touch it. Jaan Pold stood behind it with a lantern hooded under his coat and, in his other hand, a hammer with a head the size of a loaf. A cold chisel was thrust through his belt.

“In,” he said. “Quiet.”

The yard had gone to charcoal and silver under a sky with no moon: the rail over the gorge, the upturned buckets, the grain store squatting on its stones with nobody at its door. At the far corner stood the reeve’s grain cart. Against its near wheel, with her long legs out before her and a chain round her ankle, sat Aino Rebane, and she was whispering. She was giving a speech about the Deputy Assistant Surveyor of Latrines, in a low and level and devoted voice, and she did not stop when they reached her. She said, in the same breath, without turning her head, “You took your time.”

“Hold the wheel,” said Jaan.

Reet held the wheel. Jaan knelt, laid a folded grain sack over a link of the chain and set the chisel on it, and then did a thing Toomas had not seen a man do since he was a boy in Palu himself. He waited. He tilted his head toward the gorge. A moment later a gust came up out of the dark and every bridge in the town groaned together, forty ropes taking the strain at once, and Jaan said, “Wind,” and struck.

The blow went into the groan and was gone.

“She came to me at the second bell,” he said, in the gap, so low that Toomas had to lean to hear it. “With the map. Hers.” He listened. “Wind.” He struck again. “And the clerk’s. The lake. Laid one on the other with a rule.”

“And?”

“My porch step’s forty feet down.” The third gust came, and the hammer, and the link parted with a sound like a dropped coin. Jaan sat back on his heels. He was not looking at Toomas. He was looking at the chain. “I can argue with a Keeper. I can’t argue with my own front step.”

“Jaan—”

“Not now, Veskimae.”

“No,” said Toomas. “Of course.”

Jaan only got to his feet and held out one big yellow-palmed hand, and when Aino took it he hauled her up as if she were a sack of meal.

“Right,” said Aino. She stamped each foot in turn. She rubbed the wrist, which was raw. “I’d like it noted that I wasn’t frightened for a moment, and that I’ve named every man in that yard after somebody at the Guild, and that I need my hook, and an egg, and the privy, in that order.”

“Item,” said Mihkel.

From beneath his cloak he produced a canvas bag, and from the bag, one by one, with the air of a man reading out a will: a long salt-hook, its steel dark with oil; a chain-staff; a leather satchel; a surveyor’s chain wound tight in its brass cuffs. “Held in my tack-room under Rule Fifty-one, which provides that impounded implements shall be kept dry and sharp. They have been kept dry and sharp.”

Aino took the hook. She ran her thumb down the edge. “You oiled it.”

“Rule Fifty-one.”

“You great round—” She stopped. Toomas watched her search for the officer, and not find him, and give it up. “Thank you, Mihkel,” she said. She had said the name of the man, not the ox, and it sounded strange in her mouth, and she let it.

The chain-staff was warm from the bag. He took it in both hands. The knee felt, at once, that it had been given a friend.

“Then what?” said Jaan.

They had drawn together at the end of the yard, under the eaves of the reeve’s house, where the platform of black timbers jutted over the gorge and the floor hummed beneath their boots. Mihkel told them what he knew, standing very upright, as he might have reported to a board. The Keeper slept in the east room, at the reeve’s own invitation, over the gorge.

“The best room in the house,” said Jaan, to no one. “It hums.”

She rose by habit at the fourth bell. She would ask the reeve for her answer at first light, as she had said, and thereafter ride up to the upland camp to see to her carts, with eight of the twelve, and she would not be back before noon. She had told Mihkel so herself, and had left the disposition of the prisoners to him.

“Then I’ll say noon,” said Jaan. “I’ll say the town answers at noon. She’ll like that. It’s tidy.” He glanced at Mihkel, who did not flinch. “I ring after she’s gone. Second hour of day.”

“And then the town,” said Reet. She was looking at the east, where nothing yet showed, only a deeper black along the top of a ridge. “All of it, on East Rise, by the afternoon. With Taavi’s ink, and every household standing where its house will be. They’ll want to know why. I’ll tell them.” She stopped. “I’ve never told nine hundred people anything.”

“No,” said Toomas.

They all looked at him.

“Before you tell them a word of ink or Atlases, I shall tell them what I did. In the square. Standing up.” He had his two hands on the chain-staff and his weight on them. “I should rather they heard it from me than from a clever girl who has been kind enough to leave it out. If they are to stand on a hill and trust her with their houses, they must first know what sort of man is standing beside her. Mm?”

Reet did not argue. She had spent a good part of the last week arguing with him about the order in which true things ought to be said. She looked at him, a small exact girl with clay to the elbows, and she nodded once.

“They’ll spit,” said Jaan.

“I should think less of them if they did not.”

They crossed the Bell Bridge to the tower, because the bell was there and because the reeve wished to be with his rope. It was two hundred and ten feet of oak and cable over a drop of two hundred, and the planks answered every step like the keys of an instrument. At the north end Aino stopped.

“That one’s the thirtieth,” she said.

“Thirty-first,” said Reet. “You did the Cutler’s span at dusk.”

“I did not.”

“You did. I counted.”

“Count loud, then.” Aino took a handful of Reet’s sleeve in one fist and the salt-hook in the other. She was grey about the mouth. “Count out loud and don’t stop and don’t be clever.”

“Yard one,” said Reet. “Yard two.”

She counted them across. She counted in a plain, even, small voice, a yard at a time, and Aino went over behind her step by step with her eyes open, which Toomas thought a braver thing than any hammer. Taavi followed with the loaf. Mihkel, a pace behind, said “Rule Forty” once under his breath and appeared startled to have done it.

At yard thirty-five, which was the middle, Toomas stopped.

Nobody asked why. He put his hand on the cable. The little map was still there, pinned by its loop of string with a pebble sewn into each corner, swinging in the draught: the bell-tower with its window turned south, the forty bridges each with its small drawing, the mulberry in its corner, and in the margin, in a clumsy careful hand, PALU. Liisu Pold. Her map. He had stood here on the night of the feast and seen it hang there, and thought, with great clarity: and I nearly. He thought of his sister under her white stone. He thought of the porch step.

Below him the gorge was filling with grey. The black ridge in the east had a rim to it now, a thread of something paler than itself, and above the ridge the stars were going out one at a time, like lamps put out by a patient hand.

“I have never been so frightened,” said Toomas, “or so glad.”

chapters.title: The Assembly of Bridges
chapters.html:
The bell of Palu had a voice like a cracked pot, and Jaan Pold rang it the way other men split wood. Reet counted the strokes. She had counted bells since she was four, and by the ninth she knew that this was the wrong number for a fire and the wrong number for a funeral, and by the thirtieth she had stopped, because Liisu, beside her in the tower doorway, said flatly, “It doesn’t finish till he’s tired.”

“Why not?”

“So they know it’s not a drill.”

The square lay below them like a dish of people being filled. They came in feast clothes still, the red sashes and the embroidered waistcoats, stained with plum down the front and creased from sleeping in them; they came with their hair unbrushed and their eyes small, carrying children on their hips and quarrelling in undertones, down the stairs from the upper bridges and along the rope walks from the north bank, until the beaten earth at the tower’s foot was full and the overflow had climbed on to the Bell Bridge itself and stood along it rail to rail. Thirteen of them had gone up on the roof of the carters’ stables. Reet counted them as well. She could not have stopped herself if she had been paid.

She had been in the tower since the fourth bell. At first light she had stood at the little south window with her cheek against the stone and watched a rider go up the east road to the upland, a small rider on a pale grey horse with a rope of silver down her back, followed by eight in grey coats. The rider did not look at the tower. She sat very straight, as one sits who has been told she is being watched, and then the road turned behind a shoulder of rock and there was only the road.

“Gone,” Jaan had said, at her back. “Asked me at the door. I said noon. She said naturally.”

Now Reet came out of the doorway and down the steps with her satchel, and a murmur went over the square and died. She had washed her face in the bell-tower cistern. It did not help. She was five feet tall, and had a notch through her right eyebrow, and had been awake for thirty hours, and in the whole of that great quiet crowd she could see exactly one face that she was sure was friendly, and it was eleven years old and had no front teeth. Beyond the last row, against the wall of the stables, stood Mihkel Org in his mustard waistcoat, tall hat in one hand, eating a sugar pastry in the manner of a man at his own execution. He was watching them. She had never in her life been so glad of a person who was watching her.

“Quiet,” said Jaan. He did not raise his voice; the bell had done that. “Sit if you can’t stand. Veskimae first.”

The drummers’ barrel from the feast stood on the earth in front of the tower, with its skin split. Toomas climbed on to it. It took him some time. He stood on it at last with his two hands on the chain-staff and his white moustache combed, which Reet had not expected, and his milky left eye turned a little away from the crowd, as it always was, so that he seemed to be addressing the people on one side of him with some severity and the people on the other with some doubt.

“Good morning,” said Toomas. “I am Toomas Veskimae. Some of you know the name. Those over twenty will know the other thing I am called, and have not said it to my face. Is there anyone here who remembers the flood of the year two hundred and ninety-nine?”

Hands went up, a great many, slowly, like reeds.

“Do you remember what stopped it?”

“Somebody did,” said a voice, from somewhere in the middle. It was an old woman’s, dry and flat. “My gran said. Somebody did, the day it came. We put the line on the east wall.”

“She was right,” said Toomas. “I did.”

Reet had thought she knew how quiet nine hundred people could be. She had not. It was not an absence of noise. It was a held thing, like the stillness of the Blank, but with a pulse in it.

He told it plainly. He told it as he had told it in the cold yard at Soo, slowly, in the questions that were his only way of saying a hard thing: Did they know why their river lay in a bed as wide as a street, and ran as thin as a bootlace? He had drawn it. Did they know that he had been Keeper then, and that his sister had lived in this town? He had loved her. He had stood in the vault with a vial of Palu’s own water, and he had redrawn the river off the face of this valley with one stroke of a pen, and it had worked. He had not asked where the water would go. “I didn’t ask. Do you understand that? It was not a mistake of arithmetic. It was a question that I did not put. It went to Soo.”

And then he said the names. All eleven, with their trades, in order, from Marten the baker to Oskar the wheelwright. It took less than a minute. It was the longest minute Reet had ever stood through, and she counted every second of it, because it was the only thing she could do with her hands.

Somebody on the Bell Bridge spat.

It was not the spit of a person making a point. It was the spit of someone who has held a mouthful for a long time. “Twelve years,” said a woman’s voice, high and unsteady. “Twelve years I’ve put a candle in the window on the flood-day. For whoever it was. For whoever.”

“Yes,” said Toomas. “I am sorry that it was me.”

Elsewhere an old man was crying, quite openly, with his hat over his face. A child asked loudly who had died, and was hushed. Reet looked for Jaan, who stood at the bell-rope with his arms folded and a face like a shut door. He did not look at his great-uncle. He did not look away from him either.

Toomas climbed down off the barrel. It took even longer than getting up. He stood beside Reet with his hands shaking on the staff, and said without turning his head, in a voice meant for her alone, “Your turn. Mm? Say it shorter than I did.”

She had prepared three sentences in the tower. She forgot them. She went up on the barrel, which wobbled, and said the first thing in her head.

“I make it eight hundred and ninety of you, and thirteen on the stable roof.”

Somebody laughed. It was a startled laugh, and it ran along a row and died, but she felt the square give an inch.

“My name is Reet Sallik. I’m a Dawn-Surveyor of the Guild, or I was. I count things, so I’ll count this. Tonight, between midnight and first light, the valley you are standing in goes under forty feet of water. It is not a flood. Nobody is going to open a sluice. The Keeper of the Atlas has drawn it that way on a leaf in the vault, in a good ink, and the land will do what the leaf says. It does that. It has done it eight times, in eight other places, and you’ve been told the Atlas only records. It doesn’t. It decides.” She heard her own voice go quiet and level and clear, the voice she used for a bearing. “You’ll want proof, and I haven’t any I can carry up here. I can only tell you that I walked a lake to the yard nine days ago, and it was where the Book said, and I—”

“That’s the skipping song,” said a small voice from the front.

Reet stopped. A girl of about seven, with a rope-burn on one elbow, was looking up at her with extreme patience. “The far hand writes,” said the girl, “the near hand holds. It’s the skipping song. You jump on stays.”

“Stand and say,” said somebody behind her, slowly, “and the water stays.” And a woman in the second row put a hand over her mouth.

She did not know who began it. It went through the square in a rush, like wind through barley, a line here and a line there: not sung, but muttered, rattled, the way one repeats a thing one has never once examined. The far hand writes, the near hand holds. Children had it. Their mothers had it. An old man at the back who must have been ninety was saying it under his breath with his eyes shut, his lips moving on the stays. It had been jumped on every bridge in Palu for three hundred years. It had been a set of instructions all that time, and they had used it to keep the rope turning.

Reet found that she had to wait for her voice.

“It means what it says,” she said. “A drawing made far away is beaten by a drawing made on the spot, by the people who stood there. The Keeper’s lake is far. We can be near. I can draw the ground, on East Rise, as you mean it to be, and the ground will believe whoever stood on it. That’s you. It isn’t me. I’m only the one who can draw to the yard.” She made herself look along the faces. “There’s a cost. The one who draws forgets the ground drawn, in proportion. A boundary stone is a yard of memory. A town is all of it. I’ll lose every road I’ve ever walked. I’ll know your faces. I don’t know what else I’ll know.” Her left hand had found the cord at her neck and the brass plumb-bob on it, and she held on. “I’m not asking you to like it. I’m asking each household to say where it wants its house, standing in the place, aloud. That’s all the drawing is. And you may say no. If you say no I won’t draw. The Keeper has carts on the upland, and a place called Orav with three hundred roofs standing empty, and she’ll take you there, and you’ll live. I’m telling you that because it’s true.”

“Can you promise it’ll take?” said a man, from the Bell Bridge.

She opened her mouth to say yes. She heard, a long way inside her, the little hitch that comes before a stammer.

“No,” said Reet. “I’ve never drawn a town. Nobody has since Hilja Orm.”

It took two hours. Afterwards she thought it had been like trying to carry water in a sieve, and the sieve had been the happiest she had ever been in.

“Orav!” That was Epp Mänd the cooper, a woman built along the lines of her own barrels, who spoke as she hooped, with a bang. “Three hundred roofs, standing empty, and paid for. I say take the roofs. I’d like a house I didn’t have to fix.”

“And be what, in them?” said someone. “Guests of the Guild? Charity cases?”

“It’s grain-relief,” said the cooper.

“It’s charity with a better coat.”

“My barley,” said Old Ruus, who farmed the long field below the east terrace and had not been heard to speak above a murmur in the whole of Reet’s acquaintance with him, which was one night. “Can’t carry a field. Can’t carry a ditch. I’ve a split-oak gatepost with an iron ring in it that my father hung. What do I do with a gatepost in Orav?”

“The notice said precautionary,” said a woman with a baby. “Precautionary. Every autumn it’s precautionary. The year before it was a landslip, and the year before that it was the survey drill, and I stood in the road in my nightdress.”

“It wasn’t a wolf this time,” said Jaan, from the rope. They were the first words he had said since the bell stopped.

“A wolf’s a wolf. I never knew a sheep to ask its name.”

“And if it doesn’t take?” said another. “If this girl’s ink doesn’t take? Then we’re on a hill in the cold, and the lake has my kettle.”

“Then you’re on a hill,” said Reet, “and the lake is where it would have been.”

There was a pause, and then an appreciative groan. It was the groan of people who have heard a hard thing said plainly, and are not quite displeased.

It went on. Ivo Tamm and the widow Saar, whose goat shed had stood across their common line for nine years, fell upon each other with a joy that only long enemies feel, over whose goat was in whose shed. The goat in question had come to the Assembly as an interested party and was eating a ribbon. The Lauris and the Mänds, both of whom had a claim on the mulberry in the lower square, and neither of whom would say what it was, argued over who might pick its fruit; the mulberry stained the Lauris’ roof and the Mänds’ washing, and had done so for seven years, to the equal satisfaction of both. A boy of twelve wanted to know if it was true that there would be a school. A man who had never in his life crossed the Bell Bridge without touching the rail three times for luck wanted to know about the bridges.

“Palu without bridges isn’t Palu,” said Jaan.

“It’s a name.”

“It’s a name because of the bridges.”

“There’ll be bridges,” said Toomas, from the foot of the barrel, in the voice of someone laying a stone on a wall. “There is a seep in the birch hanger on the north flank of the Rise that wants a channel. If you mean to cut one, you may mean to cross it. That is the sort of thing the ink will take.”

“And the dead?” said an old woman.

It was a small voice, and it went through the square like a needle. She was sitting on a stool at the edge, with a stick across her knees and her hands over it, very upright.

“Thirty-one behind the tower,” she said. “And Helju Pold under the white stone, and my mother, and my man. I’ll not leave them to the fish. I’ll not go up a hill and leave them.”

Nobody answered. Reet looked at Toomas, who had gone quite white, and then at Jaan, who had let go of the rope. He walked across the beaten earth to the old woman and stood in front of her. He was a very big man. He crouched, so that his face was level with hers.

“Where I go, they go,” said Jaan.

“It can’t be done, Reeve.”

“The ground believes whoever stood on it,” said Toomas, slowly. “Your mother stood, Mistress. Every one of them stood, and there is no one in the whole of Orrin who stood longer. I do not know if it will. I think the stones will. Reet?”

“Draw them,” said Reet. She heard herself say it, and knew, with the part of her that went on taking notes, that she had just promised to put thirty-one graves on a hill. “Tell me where each stone goes. I’ll draw the stones.”

“Wrong,” said Liisu.

She had climbed on the barrel, which seemed to be where the day was being done. She stood in her grey smock with its ribbons and her hands at her sides and her chin up. Reet saw several hundred people turn their faces to her with the helpless attention of the audience for a child’s recitation.

“You’ve left out the school,” she said. “The Guild says children can’t draw maps. We’re going to have a school where they have to. It’s got a room with a table big enough to put the whole town on, and it’s got a window that looks at the Rise, so we can tell what’s changed. And a well by the mulberry. And I don’t care if the Lauris and the Mänds don’t like it. It was a good well. It’s the best place to meet.” She considered. “And the goats can’t see into the kitchens. That’s all.”

There was a very long pause. Somebody at the back said, “Well, that’s fair.”

“Hands,” said Jaan.

He had gone back to the rope. He stood with his big shoulders squared against the tower wall, and his face did not tell her anything. “One to a house. For the Rise and the girl, a hand up. For Orav and the Keeper’s carts, a hand. Aino Rebane counts. Because someone must.”

Aino climbed on the lowest step of the tower, with her hook slung across her back and the red scarf unwound, six feet two of salt-caravan guard, and surveyed the nine hundred of them with the look of a woman at the start of a long drive. “I count the way I count oxen,” she announced. “In tens. And I name every tenth, so I don’t lose my place. Hands up for the Rise. Keep them up.”

She counted. She walked the length of the square counting, with the hook swinging, pointing a long finger at each raised hand, and her voice filled the gorge like a second bell. “Eight. Nine. Ten, Registrar! Twenty, Auditor! Thirty, Guildmaster!” It was a great deal more efficient than it sounded. People began laughing at the second ten and could not stop. “Fifty, Rule Forty! Sixty—”

She turned round, a little pink, and found the right word. “Sixty, Mihkel!”

“Present,” said Mihkel Org, from the stables, and then clapped his hand over his mouth.

At a hundred and eighty she ran out of oxen and began on cabinet-makers. At two hundred she had Reet’s whole attention, and Reet was holding the barrel steady with both hands and did not know that she was.

“One hundred and ninety-three for the Rise,” said Aino at last. She was out of breath. “Nine for Orav. The Lauris abstain, on the grounds that Marta hasn’t been consulted.” And, to the crowd, in a different voice, quietly: “That’s it. That’s all of them.”

Jaan Pold took hold of the bell-rope with both hands. He pulled it down once, steadily, with all his shoulder in it, and let it fly, and the bell of Palu spoke a single stroke over the town and the gorge: yes.

It would have been the end. That was what the stroke was for. But as the note rolled out and began to die, a small hand closed on the rope above his own, the girl with the burnt elbow, and pulled, and the bell rang again. Then her mother put a hand on it, and a man behind her, and a woman with a baby on her hip, and the old man who had said the skipping song with his eyes shut. A line of hands went up the rope like beads on a string. The bell rang and rang. It rang until the tower hummed, and the planks of the Bell Bridge, and the cables of the thirty-nine bridges after it, and the red sashes shook on the people’s shoulders. Jaan could have let go. He did not. He had hold of the rope with the rest, and he was laughing, in short hard breaths, as a man laughs who has not done so in a year.

Nobody would let go of it.

Reet did not count them.

chapters.title: Everyone Stands
chapters.html:
The goats reached East Rise an hour before anyone could account for them.

They came up the cart-road in a brown stream, nanny and billy and kid, with their bells clanking, and spread over the bare turf at the top as if they had been told to, nosing at the thistles; and behind them, in no order at all, came Palu. It came with stools. It came with cradles on its heads and grandmothers on door-planks, carried four to a plank like kings, and bread under its arms and kettles in its fists and a bridge-wright’s whole family in a hay cart pulled by a donkey who regretted it. A man had brought his bed. He carried it up on his back without comment and set it down at the edge of the ridge and sat on it. Someone had brought the feast drum. By noon the ridge had a town on it, nine hundred strong, crowded and loud and disputatious, breathing hard in the thin air, with a cold wind going through it from the east.

Reet stood in the middle of the bare ground with her chain in her hand and looked at it.

“It’s very big,” said Taavi, beside her.

“It’s six hundred and forty yards by two hundred and ten,” said Reet. “At the widest. It’s not big. It’s a small, steep, windy ridge with a birch wood on one end, and nine hundred people are going to live on it.” She heard her voice come out brisk and exact and was grateful for it. “Is the ink ready?”

“Technically it’s the best ink in Orrin.” He had a copper wash-boiler set on three stones over a fire of birch twigs, borrowed from Mistress Saar with her washing still in it, which had been removed with ceremony and was hanging from a goat. “I mean, in three hundred years. It’s the best ink in three hundred years. I’m sorry, that’s a ridiculous thing to say, but I made it, and I stood on the Rise at six this morning and dipped a cup in the seep in the birch hanger, and it’s the place’s own water, and it went in as if it had been waiting.”

He held up his thumb. The nail was black. It was not the dull black of Ilves Black, which looks like soot, but the black of wet slate and deep wells and the inside of a closed eye, and as she looked it dried, in the length of one breath, into a hard even gloss like glass. Taavi scraped it with the nail of the other thumb. It did not so much as dull.

“It’s going to take,” he said. He looked at his thumb as at a child that has said its first word. “It’s going to take, Reet.”

“Everybody brings a cup,” said Liisu.

She had appeared at Reet’s elbow, which she did. She had a tin cup in her hand, and in the other a sheet of yellow vellum as big as a table-top, rolled and tied with a ribbon, which she carried as though it were hot. “Of their own water. From their own well. Taavi says the ink wants the place’s water, and the place is all of us. So everyone brings a cup, and tips it in.”

Reet looked at Taavi, who looked at his boots. “She asked,” he said. “She asked if it would work and I said, technically, it couldn’t hurt.”

So it was Liisu’s idea, the line. Within the hour there was a queue at the wash-boiler that went the length of the ridge, the longest Palu had ever stood in willingly: each household came up with a cup, a jug, a thimble, a wet palm, from the Bell Bridge well or the lower well or the rain-butt or the Wet Stair spring, and tipped it in over Taavi’s steady spoon, and said whose it was. “Lauri, the well by the mulberry.” “Mänd, the cooperage tank.” “Tamm, the goat trough,” which drew a look from the widow Saar. And Taavi, who had been apologising to every customer in advance since he was fourteen, said “Thank you, it’s wonderful, I’m so sorry about the smell,” and went on stirring.

The vellum was the Charter of Palu. Jaan had brought it up from the chest in the reeve’s house and handed it to his daughter without a word. It was a calfskin four feet by three, with the great seal of the Guild hanging off the foot of it in green wax, granting the town of Palu the bridges of the gorge in perpetuity, in the year one hundred and fourteen. On the other side there was nothing. Liisu unrolled it face down on the turf and weighted its corners with four stones, and the clean back of it lay in the sun like a field after snow.

“Right,” said Reet. She took a breath, a plain one, to the bottom of her lungs. “Aino.”

“Ma’am.”

“I need stakes.”

“You need iron,” said Aino. She was already at the cart. She hefted a sheaf of iron tent-pegs on her shoulder and took a mallet in the other hand. “Where do you want the first?”

Reet looked at the ridge. She did not know. She had stood on a thousand yards of ground in her life and known where it was in her sleep; she had walked into the Seam with a map in her skull that no one else on earth could read. And this, which was bare, which had nothing on it but turf and wind, she could not tell. She had no idea where Palu should be.

“Here,” said a voice.

It was Old Ruus. He was standing a few yards off on a patch of grass no different from any other, with his hat in his hands and his boots together, like a man at a graveside.

“Here’s my gate,” he said. “I’d have the field behind me, down that way, falling off to the east. There’s a thorn hedge on the north side of it, and a ditch, and the gatepost is split oak with an iron ring, and there’s a stile of two flat stones. Fourteen steps from the gate to the house. That’s a long way, I know, but I like the walk.” He turned his hat. “You drew it once, I hear. Before you fainted. Seems a pity not to have it.”

She had drawn it. She knew she had, the way one knows one has been in a room; the field was a clean cool blank where it should have been. She did not remember a thorn hedge. She did not remember a stile.

“Say it again,” said Reet. “Slowly. I’m writing it down.”

She wrote it. She wrote what he said, and not what she knew: gate, here; field behind, E; hedge N, thorn; ditch; post, split oak, iron ring; stile, two flat stones. She found it was not the same as remembering. It was better. It was a thing that someone else had given her to hold, and she would be able to give it back.

“The first stake,” said Reet. “Ruus’s gate.”

Aino drove it. Three strokes of the mallet and the pin stood in the turf, a hand-span of black iron in a green field, and she leaned on the mallet and looked at it and said, to nobody, “It’s still just so we know where we woke up. Only tonight we say it first.”

The Keeper came at noon.

Reet heard her before she saw her, hooves on the cart-road and the clip of shod horses on scree, nine of them, and straightened from the vellum with the pen in her hand and a spray of ink down her wrist. She saw the heads turn along the ridge. It spread like a ripple, as the news of a death does in a market, and the voices went out of the crowd, and the line at the wash-boiler stopped with a cup half-tipped.

They came over the lip of the Rise at a walk, eight riders in grey coats, and in front of them on a pale grey horse a small woman with a silver braid. She drew rein at the edge of the people and sat looking.

Mihkel Org stepped in front of her horse.

He did it quite suddenly, from nowhere, with his hat in his hand and a crumb of pastry on his waistcoat. He did not raise his voice. “Keeper,” he said. “Rule Forty.”

“Master Org.” Kaie Tammaru looked down at him. She was wearing the white kidskin gloves; she sat with her hands folded on the pommel, buttoned at the wrist, and she did not look surprised, or angry. She looked as she had looked in the reeve’s dining room, which was attentive. “I understood the prisoners to be in a barn.”

“They are in my sight, Keeper. I am watching them.
