Rule Forty does not require that the watching be done in a barn.” His round face was the colour of cold porridge, and his hat was shaking, and he did not move out of the way. “I have not lost sight of any of them for a moment. I shall not do so. You will find that I am extremely thorough.”

She considered him for some seconds. Then she looked past him, over his shoulder, at the Rise.

Reet watched her do it. She saw the small head turn, slowly, as a heron’s does, and take in the ridge: the copper boiler smoking over its birch fire; the queue of cups; the stakes, in a ragged line like a fence not yet put up; the grandmothers on their planks and the bed on the edge of the world; the goats; the nine hundred people, standing, with their eyes on the ground, as if they had been put there as seed.

“What,” said Kaie, “are they doing?”

“Standing, Keeper,” said Mihkel, with honesty.

“Mm,” said Toomas Veskimae, from the stake line. He was a hundred yards away, leaning on his chain-staff. He had not raised his voice either. It carried on the wind. “It’s the hard part, I’m told.”

For a time nothing happened. Then Liisu Pold put down the corner of the Charter, walked across the turf with her hands at her sides and stopped in front of the pale horse. She was carrying a milking stool. She set it on the ground at the horse’s feet, and looked up.

“That’s for you,” said Liisu. “It’s guest-right. Papa says.”

The Keeper looked down at the child. In the long pause Reet could hear the wind in the birch hanger and, somewhere, a goat. A gloved hand had left the pommel and was pressing the other, hard, as if to hold it still.

“Naturally,” said Kaie.

She got down. She sat on the stool, in her white gloves and her spotless riding habit, with her small back very straight, and somebody, a woman Reet did not know, came and put a mug of milk in her hands. She held it. She did not drink. She lifted two fingers from the mug and the eight riders behind her stood easy.

She sat there the whole afternoon. It was a good deal longer than a moment.

By the third hour Reet had stopped thinking in words.

She worked by household, in the order they came, Ruus’s gate and then the Lauris’, and then the Mänds’, and then whoever came forward out of the crowd. She asked each of them to stand on the ground where their door would be. They did it with their feet, shyly, shuffling a little on the turf like children on a stage. Here’s our door. Here’s the hearth. We’d want the window east, for the light. A boy of seven put his heels together and said, with enormous seriousness, “Here’s where I sleep.” Four chainmen, borrowed from Mihkel’s riders, who had received the order in the form of a Rule, took the measure to the nearest stake. She wrote the number. Jaan walked behind her with the second chain, and Aino drove stakes, and the line of pins ran down the Rise in a curve like the track of a snake, and it was the strangest survey that she had ever worked, because there was nothing there. There was only what they meant.

She drew on the back of the Charter with Liisu on her knees at the other side of it, holding the edge flat with both hands and her chin. The ink flowed off the nib like silk. It was a pleasure, a distinct one, of the kind she had not felt since she was fifteen: a line laid down the first time right. House by house the plan grew on the vellum in black, the long street of the Rise and the cross-lane and the square; and at her elbow Toomas squatted on his bad knee and fed her the contour grammar, murmuring, as he had once murmured it to a boy at the Guild school. “Short tick for a gentle fall. Mm. Longer here. The ticks go down.”

“Mine go up,” said Liisu.

“In the Guild’s grammar, they go down.”

“That’s wrong.” She considered the page. “It doesn’t matter. The ground can read.”

Reet drew the ticks Liisu’s way, uphill, in the margin, and in the field below the stile of two flat stones, and the ink took them. It took everything. It lay down on the calf and was gone into it, glossy and set. She had never worked with ink so honest.

Only once did it refuse. She had set the line of the goat shed on the common boundary of Ivo Tamm and the widow Saar, as both had said, firmly, in a pair of voices that sounded like a quarrel in the next room, and the line beaded. It drew back on the vellum into a row of shining black drops, like water on a greasy plate, and would not lie.

“Oh,” said Taavi, from the pot, aghast. “That’s not— I tested it. It’s not the ink.”

“Mm.” Toomas bent over the page. “It is not the ink. Reet. Do they mean it?”

She looked up. Ivo Tamm was scratching his neck. The widow Saar’s mouth was a hard line. Between them, on a length of rope, the goat watched the two of them with its flat yellow eye.

“A promise you don’t mean,” said Toomas, very low, “is a lie told forward. The ink knows.”

There was a pause which seemed long. Then Ivo Tamm cleared his throat. “She can have the shed,” he said. “I’ll have the goat. And I’ll build her a new one, out of my own larch, on her side, with the door the right way up.” He did not look at the widow. “I’m tired of it, Marit. Nine years.”

“I don’t want the shed,” said the widow Saar. She was crying, and furious about it. “I want it to stop eating my washing.”

Reet drew the line again. It lay down like a cat.

At the edge of her sight, all afternoon, she was aware of the stool: the small straight figure on it, with the white hands in her lap, and the mug going cold on the ground at her feet. The Keeper said nothing. Once, towards four o’clock, when the plan was half done, Reet looked up and met her eyes across the whole width of the ridge. Kaie looked, as one looks at a very bad letter in one’s own handwriting, and did not look away.

The sun went down behind the Palu gorge in a smear of red, and the wind dropped, and the ridge was quiet.

The drawing was done. It lay on the grass between four stones, black on yellow, a town that had never been, with its streets and its squares and its schoolhouse, its thirty-one stones behind a bell-tower, and its mulberry, and its well; and at its foot, below a small cut in the north flank where a seep would run, a line of little double strokes that were bridges. Not forty. Twelve. The longest was ninety feet. Around it, in an irregular ring, in the light of the dying sun, stood every living soul in Palu, each on the spot where their door would be.

She had not known that they would all do it. She stood in the middle of them in the cooling grass and her legs began to shake.

“Reet,” said Toomas, gently. “The oath.”

The oath on the Hearth-Stone had been cut for one. I stood here. I drew only what I saw. She had said it over a boundary stone and over a barley field, and she had known, without needing anyone to tell her, that it would not do. There was a thing they had not seen. There was a thing that they meant.

She knelt by the vellum. She dipped the pen. In clear square capitals, at the foot of the plan, in the true ink, she wrote what she had worked out in the tower between the fourth bell and the fifth, with Toomas saying shorter at every draft: We stood here. We drew what we saw. We drew what we mean to make.

“Say it,” said Reet. She stood. Her voice was not loud, but it carried across the quiet like a thrown stone. “All of you. Say it the way you mean it. If you don’t mean a word, don’t say it.”

Liisu said it first, in her flat voice, with her hands at her sides. Then Jaan, and then Aino, in a roar. Then a swell of voices, nine hundred, ragged, cracked, in four keys and a dozen accents, all saying it at once. We stood here. We drew what we saw. There were old women saying it with their hands pressed to their chests and children saying it with their eyes on their feet, and it was not an oath of any Guild, nor any king. It was a ridge full of people telling the truth about what they were going to do.

We drew what we mean to make.

She said it with them. She felt the old hitch in her throat coming for her, the little catch before the stammer, and it did not come. It had never been for this. She said it level and clean and unhurried, and under her feet the whole ridge breathed.

The ink took.

She saw it go. Every line on the vellum, from the great square to the smallest stake-mark, lost its wetness at once, the shine going in and a deeper black coming up like a skin of glass, and Taavi, who was crouching by the Charter with his thumb out, made a small high sound, like a kettle taken off the fire.

“It’s in,” he whispered. “It’s gone in. Oh— it’s in.”

Silence. The wind did not blow. Nobody moved, nine hundred people with their mouths open; only the goats went on with their grazing, in the dusk, with a small tearing noise.

“It will not hold against the Atlas.”

The Keeper had stood up. The milking stool lay on its side. She had not raised her voice. She stood in her riding habit with her hands clasped before her, alone at the edge of the people, small and straight as a pin, and she was not threatening them; she was reporting it. “Naturally it will not, Surveyor. The leaf is drawn. I have done this eight times. I know what lands. At midnight the lake will go where it is written, and whatever stands on its path will be under it.”

“It doesn’t have to hold against the Atlas.” Reet’s own voice sounded like someone else’s, level and tired. “It has to be nearer. The leaf is in a drawer in the Hollow, nine nights old. This is under their feet.” She looked at the small figure. She had meant to say nothing else. “I found the line, you know. The wrong one. In your sum.”

“Which?”

“The first. You wrote that the Seam has to land somewhere. It doesn’t. It lands on what nobody holds. You never asked the Hollow to hold it.”

“The Hollow has forty thousand people,” said Kaie, after a moment.

“Yes.”

“They would have to stand on every step.”

“Naturally,” said Reet.

The Keeper’s mouth moved. Something crossed the small face and was gone. Then she bent, and righted the stool with a gloved hand, and sat on it again, and put her hands in her lap.

Reet turned back to the Charter.

At the foot of the plan, below the oath, a space had been left. She knelt and took the pen. Her hand was black to the wrist; the ink was drying in the creases of her knuckles. She wrote the first letter, the R, and as the pen left it the first of it began to go: not with a blow, but with a sort of unthreading, like a cord drawn through a hundred beads. The long white road to the Blank. The pass. Dry Cairn, its brass stud, the datum. It went from her like warm water from a cup. She could feel it go, and there was nothing to be done.

She stopped, with the pen on the vellum. She looked at the one letter, and the space where more should go. It was her name. She knew that it was her name, and that she had signed it ten thousand times; but she could not have said what it felt like. It was as though it were a word in a language she had spoken as a child and had put away.

Sallik, she thought. Sora Crossing. A marsh, a drain, a cellar, a woman’s voice.

She could not see it.

She wrote the rest. She wrote her whole name, Reet Sallik, with her left hand, to the second knuckle, in letters so small and plain that anyone could read them.

chapters.title: The Ninth Night
chapters.html:
Palu sang the ferry song the way it did everything, which was loudly, in four keys, and with the goats joining in.

It had begun at dusk, when the last stake was driven and the boiler taken off its fire, as something to do with the hands and the mouth, and the children started it, jumping on stays. By full dark it had gone through the whole ridge. Nine hundred people sat on the turf in their coats with their knees drawn up, round a few small fires of birch, and sang what they had only ever skipped over: the river rose up in the dead of the night. They did it badly. They did it with their whole chests. Toomas, who had first heard it sung by a one-eared ferryman in a hut with a goat on his boot, found that he minded the tuneless version less than he would have thought. It had been made for poling and wading, not for choirs. It was a song for people with something to do.

He sat with his back against a stake. It was Ruus’s gate, and he had asked Aino to put him by it. Beside him on the turf, her head on his rolled coat and a heap of sheepskins over her, lay Reet, with her bare left hand outside the fleece, the fingers a little curled and the ink dried black into the creases. She had sat down where she stood at the foot of the Charter, politely, as a child sits when told to, and Taavi had caught her under the arms. She had not woken. He had laid the back of his hand once against her forehead, like a mother, and it had been cold.

On her other side, on an upturned bucket, with a lantern between his shoes, sat Mihkel Org.

“Rule Forty,” said Mihkel, in a low voice, to nobody, as another man might have read the time. “’No Surveyor sleeps unwatched in a shifting place.’” He looked at the sleeper. “She is not unwatched.”

“No,” said Toomas.

“I have not left her for six hours.”

“No.”

“I find,” said Mihkel, “that it is not a bad Rule.”

Far down the ridge, at the edge of the firelight, the Keeper still sat on her milking stool. She had not gone. Toward evening she had said a few words to her riders, and they had ridden off up the road to the upland to tell the carts to stand down, and since then she had been alone, with her hands in her lap and her back as straight as a plumb-line. Someone had put a sheepskin round her shoulders. She had let it stay.

Below them, in the valley, Palu burned. It was Liisu’s doing. Every house had been left with a lamp lit in its window, two hundred of them, and the forty bridges had their lanterns hung as on a feast night, so that the town lay at the bottom of the dark in a great scatter of small yellow lights, like a hearth seen from above, like a handful of coals. “Houses should be able to see where they’re going,” Liisu had said, and nobody had argued. It was a thing that should have been absurd. It was beautiful, and it hurt to look at.

He did not look at it for long. He looked at the child.

She had come to sit at his other side an hour ago, with her knees up, in a sheepskin that reached her feet, and she had not said anything. Now she said, flatly, “I’ve got the last verse.”

“Mm?”

“The names one. Reet had it in her book. She said I could copy it.” She was looking at the lights. “Nobody’s sung it. Do you want me to?”

He found that he could not answer. He had left a hut once because of that verse; he had gone out into a yard and put his back to a wall and heard it through the planking, name by name, and known them all. He looked at his great-niece, who had Helju’s chin and the whole of Helju’s unreasonable courage, and who was eleven. He saw that she was not offering him a kindness. She was asking whether the thing could be done, in the way that she asked whether a bridge would bear.

“It is not a thing you owe them,” said Toomas.

“I know. I want to.” She considered. “They stood too.”

She sang it. It was not a good voice, a thin flat clear one like a reed whistle, and she sang it into the dark without once looking at him, to the same tune as the other, the old rocking tune, up and down like a boat. Marten the baker and Ilse his wife, and Mikk who was six, who was six, who was six. She had the whole of it from Reet’s page. She sang the cooper and the twins who never were; she sang Rein at the mill and Anni at the loom and Jakob and Helmi and Oskar. A few voices near her took it up, those who knew the tune, and then those who did not, humming, and the hum went outward through the dark like a ripple in a pool until the whole ridge had it, without words, nine hundred people holding a note under the stars for eleven strangers.

Toomas stayed where he was. He kept his back to the stake, with his hands on the chain-staff, and he did not leave.

A big shape sat down heavily on the turf at his other side. It did not speak. It smelled of tallow and bell-rope. They listened to the end together, he and Jaan, with a yard of cold air between them and a sleeping girl on his other hand, and when the last note had gone out of the world Jaan said, to the dark, “She’d have hit you with a spoon.”

“She would,” said Toomas.

“After.”

“After,” Toomas agreed. His voice had gone. He cleared it. “Yes. I think after.”

It came a little before midnight, as Reet had said it would, and it began with the quiet.

The wind dropped. The singing, which had run down by then into something more like muttering, stopped in the middle of a line, as a clock stops, and no one started it again. Every sound on the Rise began to come back half a breath late. A goat bleated and was answered by its own bleat out of the air. And from the south, from a long way off, there came a very low noise, such as a loaded wagon makes on a distant bridge, and it came toward them at the pace of a man walking.

He had felt it from inside, in the Seam, on a road, in a camp ring, on the edge of a pass that was not there. He had never in his life watched one from outside. In twelve years he had thought of it in his bed, in the dark, the thing he had done: a river led off the leaf, a wet noise, a flood. He had never once seen it land. He had gone home from the vault and been sick in a basin, and the water had gone to Soo with nobody watching.

The Rise did not stir. The turf under his hands was as still as a table. It was down in the valley that the world began to move.

The lights lifted.

They lifted all together, every lamp in every window of every house, two hundred and some, and the lanterns on the bridges with them, as a chest lifts on a held breath. For the length of that breath Palu hung a hand’s breadth clear of the earth, a whole town of yellow windows with the black gorge underneath, and he heard on the ridge around him nine hundred people not breathing. Then it slid.

It came toward them across the dark like a tray carried by an invisible hand. The sound had swelled to a grinding roar, and under it, small and clear, the bridges’ ribbons rattling in their thousands like rain on slates; and the lights tilted as they came, heeling over, and he thought no, and thought the ridge is held, and saw the first of the houses strike the long slope of the Rise a hundred yards below and ride up on it, and go over.

They arrived in a heap. There was no other word for it. They came up the slope in a long tumbling slide, roofs on chimneys, walls on gates, a hay-loft with its door open sitting on a pump, like crockery in a cart going over a rut, and for a space that he afterward found he could not measure there was only noise, and lamps rolling, and a woman on the ridge screaming a name over and over. He had his hand across Reet’s body. He did not know when he had put it there.

And then, from the bottom of the heap, one by one, the houses began to work themselves loose.

They did it as hens do on a nest. A wall shifted, turned, a shoulder shrugged itself free of the next shoulder. A roof rose up on one side and sat back, true. Gables swung, chimney-stacks settled; two houses rubbed up against each other and, with the tired air of neighbours, parted and moved apart by exactly the width of a lane. Each one went a little way across the slope and stopped. He saw a door come to rest on an iron pin: a hand’s breadth from it, and then, with a faint shuffle, on it. Lamps still burned in the windows. Not one of them had gone out.

“Ruus’s gate,” somebody said, near him, in a small stunned voice. “That’s Ruus’s gate.”

A split-oak post with an iron ring in it stood in the lamplight beside the stake at his elbow. It had come up the slope with a hedge, and a ditch, and a long thorny field falling away east, and a stile of two flat stones.

Then the bell-tower came.

It was the last of them. It was an old tall square thing, windowed south, and it rode up the slope above the heap and came to a stand with its stones grinding, a little crooked, before the bell had decided that it had arrived. Then the bell spoke. It struck once, from the jolt, a single note, cracked as a pot, and Jaan Pold, beside him on the turf, put his two hands over his face.

“It rang itself,” he said, through his fingers.

“It would.”

“It’s never rung without me.”

“Then you have taught it well.”

After the tower there was a long moment in which nothing moved. Then, from the lower edge of the new town, came a sound like a child’s laugh: a single high peal of astonishment, which was a goat. It was standing on the ridge-pole of a shed, an ordinary larch shed, which had arrived whole and upright on a lawn of turf, and it was looking down at the township from above with the offended air of a creature who has been moved without consultation. It was Ivo Tamm’s goat. It had slipped its rope at sunset, in the matter of a principle, and gone home.

“My goat!” bellowed Ivo Tamm, from a hundred feet away. “My goat! Marit, it’s on the roof!”

The widow Saar’s voice, high and exalted, floated up out of the dark: “Then it’s on yours, you fool!” And nine hundred people began to laugh. It was an awful, ragged, helpless sound; half of it was weeping. They laughed on the dark ridge in their coats as the new houses steamed gently in the cold. Somebody was already calling out the roll.

“Registrar!” That was Aino, enormous, on a heap of stone at the lane end. She had her hook in the air. “Auditor! No, you thieves, not the oxen, I mean you: Lauris! Mänds! Tamms! Hands up!” And she counted them in, a household at a time, with the names of every Guild office she could call to mind, and he sat with the chain-staff across his knees and listened to the roll. They were all there. Nine hundred and three, said Aino. And then, in a different voice, “Nine hundred and four. Hold on. Who’s that?”

Nobody could account for it. But in the second house from the bell-tower a woman was seen at the window with a bundle that had not been there at dusk, and a small fierce cry rose from it into the cold and was loudly answered by a goat.

In the valley, behind them, the sound had changed.

He turned his head. Where Palu had been there was a darkness without a light in it, a wide black bowl; and out of the head of the gorge, out of the throat of the thin river that was Toomas Veskimae’s work and no one else’s, there came the long hush of water. It came down into the bowl in a tongue, pale in the starlight, pushing out on either side, filling. The rope bridges had gone with their town. Nothing was left of them on the water but the ribbons, the feast-ribbons, thousands of them, red and blue and yellow, riding on the dark in a thin bright scatter like petals on a pond.

He found her at a little after one, at the edge of the water.

She was standing where the cart-road ran down into the lake, a small figure with a rope of silver down her back, ankle-deep in the shallows, quite still. The new lake lay at her feet to the far shore, with a faint light on it, and the water came up the slope and stopped at her boots as if she had told it to. He came down the hill slowly, with the chain-staff, on the knee. The turf became shingle. He stood beside her at a respectful distance of three feet.

“Mm,” said Toomas. “Is it as you drew it?”

“The shore is four yards east of where I put it.” She did not turn her head. Her gloves were still on. “That is the Rise. The leaf has it hatched as a cliff, from a Dawn Sheet of the year ninety-one. Some clerk who had not stood on it wrote cliff, and I drew what was written.” Her voice was perfectly level. “I have always drawn what was written. I did not know there was a Rise.”

“Nobody had told you.”

“No.” The water moved against her boots. “I did not ask.”

He waited. He had been waiting for this woman, in one form or another, for twelve years; in the dark he had composed a number of things to say to her, some unpardonable, and found he had none of them. He stood in the cold and looked at the lake.

“How long will she have?” said Kaie. “The Surveyor. After tonight.”

“I think all of it.”

“Naturally.” It was said without edge. It was the lightest thing he had ever heard her say. “I lost a road, the first time. It was the road to Tallow Moor. I thought: I can bear a road.” She was silent a moment. “I cannot tell you where Sora Crossing lies, Toomas. I drew it. I could give you every contour of Leaf Eighty-eight, and every ditch. I could not find it if you set me down in its marsh.”

He looked down at her. The small, composed, upturned face was a stranger’s, and was not. It was the face of a girl of thirty-six who had held a lamp for him, in the vault, while he did a terrible thing, and who had known exactly what it was.

“She will remember her mother’s face,” said Toomas.

“Faces stay?”

“I believe so. It seems to be the arrangement.”

“That is something.” Kaie drew her hands together and held them. “Go back to her. Someone should be there. I find that I would rather it were not myself.”

He went back up the slope. At the top he turned, and she was still there, ankle-deep in her own lake, watching the ribbons go out on it in the dark.

Reet woke at dawn.

He had been awake all night. He had sat with his back to Ruus’s stake and watched the sky go the colour of a pearl, and at some point in the long grey wait Mihkel Org had fallen asleep on his bucket, upright, with the lantern gone out in his hands. And so he saw it: how she woke slowly, as someone does who has been a long way down. First she looked at the sky. Then she looked at him.

“Toomas,” said Reet. “You’ve got tea in your moustache.”

“I have not had tea for a day and a half.”

“It’s still there.” She sat up. Her cropped hair stood on end and her left hand was black to the wrist. She looked about her at the new street, at the smoke going up from a hundred chimneys, at the goat on the roof, and he watched her look at it with the face of a stranger at a window. “Whose town is that?”

“Palu’s. Yours, I should say.”

“Palu.” She turned it over. “I know the name. I know we came here. I know I was afraid of something.” She frowned. “There was a road. We came along a road. I know there was one, because I know your knee hurt. I can’t find it.” She pressed the heel of her hand to her forehead, as if to push a door. “I can’t find any of them. It’s not like forgetting. Forgetting has an edge. This is only snow.”

He had nothing wise to say. He had never had anything wise to say.

“The cairn,” said Reet slowly. “Dry Cairn. I went there every morning for three years. Pille’s mule is called Biscuit. I can see Pille.” She said it with a sort of wonder. “Broad. Burnt nose. A plait. I can see her face. I can’t see where she stood.”

“That is how it works, I believe.”

“Then it’s all right.” She said it quite steadily. “I know all of you. I know what you said. I know Aino took me by the scarf and the hair. I’ve lost the places and kept the people. Toomas, that’s the right way round. Isn’t it?”

He had to look at the sky. “I should say so.”

Taavi arrived at a run with a heel of bread and a great many apologies, and Liisu with a notebook, and Aino with her hook, and in the noise that followed he slipped away, which he was good at. He went down the new street between the houses. It was a long, steep, crooked street with a gutter down the middle that had not been there the day before, already running with a spill of water from the seep; and here and there, at a doorway, a man or a woman stood in the grey dawn with an expression of complete bewilderment, laying a hand on a lintel as one lays it on a horse.

The churchyard had come. It stood behind the bell-tower in its rows, thirty-one stones of the Pold family and some hundred more, the moss still on the north face of each. The white stone stood among them. It had not so much as a chip out of it.

He took off his hat, which he was not wearing, and put his hand up to the place on his head where it would have been.

“Helju,” said Toomas. “I am told I speak in questions. This is not one.” He cleared his throat. There was nobody near but a robin on the wall. “I am going to Soo. There are forty wells there, I am given to understand, and I am going to map every one of them to the foot, for nothing, for as long as I have knees. I shall draw only what I see. I swear it by whatever one swears by.”

It bound nothing on earth but himself. He had no ink, and no vellum, and no ground to put it on; and that, he saw, was precisely its use.

“You would tell me to say it shorter,” he said. She had said it to him across a kitchen table for forty years, with her elbows in the flour: Say that shorter, Toomas, I’m not paid by the word. He had carried it into the vault and the Guild and a hundred cold rooms, and given it to a girl of nineteen as if it were his own, and had never once said where he had got it.

“Wells,” said Toomas, to the white stone. “I’ll map the wells.”

When he came up the slope again, the sun was clear of the east. Reet was standing alone at the end of the ridge, on the edge of the new town, with the light on the side of her face. She had the brass plumb-bob in her hand. She was looking out over the lake, which lay under the early sun as flat and bright as a plate with the last of the ribbons on it, to the farther shore, where beyond a belt of birch the ground rose up long and green and round-shouldered against the sky.

She heard the chain-staff and did not turn.

“What’s there?” said Reet.

She pointed. He followed her finger. He looked a good while, because she had asked, and a thing asked deserves to be looked at.

“Mm,” said Toomas. “Say that shorter. A hill.”

chapters.title: The Hearing in the Hollow
chapters.html:
The Hollow had shrunk.

Toomas noticed it on the second landing of the Guild stair, with his hand on the arm of a lamp-boy and his knee filing a formal complaint. He had been out of this city for a month and out of its heart for twelve years, and in all that time he had carried it about with him as a thing the size of a cathedral: forty thousand people in a limestone bowl, tier on tier, lit from below like a lantern. He found that it was only a town. It was a town in a hole, with frost on its steps and its lamps still burning at ten in the morning because the sinkhole held the dark like a cup. A woman was shaking a rug from a window. A cat was asleep on a coil of rope. The oak-gall smell, which he had thought a smell of power, was simply the smell of ink.

“Four hundred and nineteen,” said the lamp-boy. “You’re on two hundred and twelve. Don’t look down, sir, it only makes it longer.”

The lamp-boy was about eleven, with a brass lamp-hook over his shoulder and a quick pointed face, and Toomas had had his name from the porter at the foot. It was Ants. He had been told about Ants by a girl who kept her friends in a list, in the white quiet of the Blank; she had put him first, ahead of her mother and Mihkel’s pastry crusts.

“Is she coming?” said Ants. “Reet?”

“This morning. With the ink-boy.”

“Does she know me?”

“She knows your face,” said Toomas. “She cannot tell you which stair you stood on.”

Ants thought about this with the seriousness of the very young. “Good,” he said at last. “I’m memorable. I’ve drawn her arrows.” And he showed Toomas the chalk on the wall at the turn of the stair: a small fat yellow arrow, pointing up, and above it another, and above that another, one on every landing from the Wharf Gate to the Assembly’s door.

The Assembly Hall had been cut out of the living limestone at the foot of the Guild House, in a horseshoe, with a dais for the Speaker at the open end and wooden benches rising in tiers from the floor. Behind the dais a short passage ran back into the rock to a door of black iron with three locks in it. The gallery above the benches had been given up that morning to those who had been wronged.

Toomas looked along it from the floor and saw them. He saw Palu: Jaan Pold in a coat that had been made for a smaller man, with a bell-rope’s callus on his hands; Ruus, who had brought his hat; Liisu, scrubbed, in the grey smock with its ribbons, sitting with her back as straight as a rule and a large map under her arm. He saw Soo, a dozen of them in stone-grey wool, with Ene Ots in the middle on two sticks like a small ship at anchor, and she did not look at him. He saw the Ford: Veikko Pent, in a coat that had once been brown, on the end of a bench, humming, and tethered to the leg of the bench by a length of twine a goat called Rule, which was eating the Assembly’s bunting with deliberation. Behind them, in their eight different kinds of coat, sat the eight places whose ground a woman in this room had taken apart and put together again: Tallow Moor, Kask Ford, Sora Crossing, and five more. Toomas saw a woman from Sora Crossing with Reet’s chin. He saw Salme Ilves, in the end seat, with a thin cigar between her fingers, unlit, and a face like a closed ledger.

The Speaker was an old woman, Urve Kann, with a face like a walnut and a gavel she did not appear to know the use of. She sat in the middle of the dais with her hands on the arms of her chair. In front of her, on a green cloth, lay three keys.

“The first is the Master-Surveyor’s,” said Urve Kann. “The second is the Assembly’s own, which has not left the strong-room in my time. The third is the Keeper’s, which she surrendered on her return. It is the wish of the Assembly that the vault be opened before this Hall, by all three together, and that the Correction Book be read aloud.” She looked down. “Master Org.”

Mihkel Org rose from the front bench. He had put on the mustard waistcoat. He had combed the walnut fringe flat and brought his tall black hat, and he held it before him like a man carrying a lit candle through wind. His hands were not shaking. Toomas, who had watched them shake for three weeks, thought that it was the most alarming thing he had ever seen.

He went down the passage with the three keys. The Hall followed, in a body, the Speaker on a stick, the gallery in single file, so that the corridor behind the dais became a procession in the lamplight. At the iron door he stopped. There was a row of brass pegs beside it where for three hundred years the Surveyors had hung their cotton gloves, according to Rule Nineteen, and they hung there still, a hundred grey pairs, like a row of hands waiting to be asked. He turned two keys, and then the third, and left all three standing in their locks.

The door swung. A smell came out of it that Toomas knew in his teeth: oak gall and wet stone and old vellum, the smell of a room that has been kept. Beyond the door the shelves went back into the dark, and he saw, small and exact in the lamplight on the middle shelf, a creamy foxed leaf with a square on it and a dot. Leaf Two-oh-six. He found that he could look at it without his hands shaking.

They brought the Correction Book out on a trolley. It was a long ledger bound in black, and Mihkel set it on the Speaker’s lectern in the Hall, opened it at the page he had marked with a strip of pastry paper, and read.

“’Autumn, the year three hundred and three. Leaf Fifty-six, Tallow Moor. Re-inked. Tidy.’”

He read it in a steady voice. It was the voice he used for the Rules, a dry clerkly voice with every letter set down, and it did not change from the first line to the last. He read the second. “’Leaf Seventy-one, Kask Ford. Re-inked. Tidy.’” From the gallery a man stood up, an old man in a farmer’s coat, and stayed standing. “’Leaf Eighty-eight, Sora Crossing. Re-inked.’” The woman with Reet’s chin got up. It went on. Mihkel read for an hour and ten minutes. He read fourteen leaves in eight places, and the people of each place stood in turn as their name was said and did not sit down, until the gallery was a row of the standing, silent, all in different coats. And the word at the end of the line was always the same, and Mihkel said it each time with exactly the same level voice. He said tidy nine times. He said it to the end.

“I initialled this,” he said, when he had finished. “Every one. For nineteen years. It was a very tidy Book.”

He closed it.

The Keeper walked in alone by the side door.

She had been confined to her rooms since her return, on the Speaker’s order, and no one had seen her. She wore a plain grey dress and carried nothing. She walked down the length of the Hall in the silence with her head up and her silver braid down her back, a woman under five feet, and stopped at the lectern. She stood a moment looking at the Speaker. Then she took off her gloves.

She did it one finger at a time. She laid them on the green cloth where the keys had been, a small white pair with pearl buttons. And the Hall saw her hands for the first time: blue-black to the wrist, glossy, years deep, as if she had dipped them in a well.

“I shall give the figures,” said Kaie.

She gave them. She spoke without a note, in her quiet complete voice, and Toomas heard in it every word he had once taught her. The Seam widened one mile in the year. In the year three hundred and three, the rim of this city had stood eleven years from it. It stood thirty-one now, by her count, and that was eight places, which were in the Book that had been read. She had moved two hundred and eleven people first, at her own expense. None had died. She had done it in her own hand, from the leaf, in an ink she had bought from a woman who understood what it was for. The ninth place had been Palu.

“I do not ask the Assembly to find the figures wrong,” said Kaie. “They are right. I ask it to find that I was wrong, which is not the same, and which I did not know was possible until I sat for six hours on a milking stool and watched nine hundred people tell a hillside what they meant. Naturally I should like to say that I have regrets. I find I do not have the right word. I have the figures. That is all I have brought.”

There was no sound in the Hall. The Speaker, who had not touched her gavel, looked down from the dais over her spectacles. “Does the Assembly have questions?”

Nobody had. A child from Palu, said the Speaker, had asked leave.

Liisu Pold stood on the gallery bench with her map. She did not appear to be in awe. “Why didn’t you ask us?”

Toomas, on the floor, felt the Hall tilt toward the answer. It was a question he had put to himself, in various forms, for twelve years.

“Because I knew what you would say,” said Kaie, “and I did not wish to hear it. I told myself that this was kindness. It was something a good deal smaller.”

“That’s not a good reason.”

“No. It is not.”

Liisu considered this. “If we’d said no,” she said, “would you have done it anyway?”

A pause. In it Toomas saw a small hand, bare, closing on the edge of the lectern.

“Yes,” said Kaie.

A sound went through the gallery. It was not loud. “I should have asked again,” she said, “and again, until you were tired. And then I should have drawn it.”

“That’s not asking.”

“No,” said Kaie. “I have only lately learned the difference.”

“Okay,” said Liisu. She sat down.

He had been ready for tears, or a lie, or a long speech. He had not been ready for yes. It was the answer that he would have given himself, at her age, in that vault, with a lamp held for him, to the same question about the same river. He found that his throat had closed. He looked at the stone floor of the Hall until it went away.

They did not take long, after that.

The motion was put in plain words by the Speaker, from a paper in her own hand. That any town, village or hamlet of Orrin whose people had stood upon their ground might keep its own atlas under the Oath of Standing. That the leaves of the Hollow be opened to all comers, and the Correction Book kept in public, and read each year at midwinter. That nothing in the Founding of Hilja Orm, who had carved her oath on a stone in the middle of the Blank for anyone to read, set up any Guild whatsoever. “The monopoly is a hundred and ninety years old,” said Urve Kann. “It was invented by her heirs. I cannot find that she ever asked for it.”

She called for hands. Toomas did not count them. They were not close.

“One more thing,” said the Speaker. “The Hollow has forty thousand people and a rim thirty-one years off. I am told that ground which is held does not move. The Assembly will therefore hold it, ward by ward and tier by tier, beginning with this stair, and it will take us the winter and a great deal of ink.” Her eyes went to the small figure at the lectern. “Kaie Tammaru. The Assembly does not imprison you. The Assembly has found that it has a use for you. You will teach the oath. You will teach it from a table in the open air, to anyone who comes, with your hands bare, so that those who learn may see what it costs. The salary is twelve marks a year and a room over the tannery.”

Nobody laughed. It was not a joke. It was, he thought, much the hardest sentence he had ever heard handed down, and also the kindest, and the Speaker had known precisely what she was doing.

“Naturally,” said Kaie. She did not look at her hands.

“There is a further matter,” said the Speaker. “Toomas Veskimae.”

He stood. The knee had something to say about it. “The Assembly has no standing in a flood twelve years old,” said Urve Kann, not unkindly, “and does not mean to assume any. But Soo has asked to be heard.”

Ene Ots got to her feet. It took her some time, on the two sticks, with a young woman at her elbow whom she brushed off; and when she was up she was a very small, very upright old woman in grey wool, with a face like a winter apple, and her voice carried to the roof.

“Soo has met,” she said. “I’m to say what Soo says. We don’t forgive him. That isn’t ours to do. It’s for eleven people who aren’t here.” She looked at him then, directly, for the first time since the kitchen. “We’ve decided what he’s for. He’ll come and live in the hut at the mill, the one with the tick scratched on the lintel, so he can look at it. He’ll map our wells, every well, to the foot, and when he’s done he’ll begin again, because wells move. He’ll say the eleven on the day in the yard, standing, and say them right. He’ll write it in a fair hand. I can’t read a scrawl. And he’ll eat at my table once a year, and I won’t talk to him.”

“I accept,” said Toomas.

“I wasn’t finished.” The old woman drew herself up. “When he’s dead he’s to be buried below the stones, on the slope, not in the churchyard. So that they can see him.”

“I accept,” said Toomas, again.

“Good. Sit down,” said Ene Ots. “Your knee’s shaking.”

It was Taavi who found the Hall for her.

She had not been able to, on her own. She had walked up the Guild stair behind a yellow chalk arrow on every landing, and had still turned left at the fountain, and he had gone after her with a fruit-seller’s basket in his arms, apologising. She came in a quarter-hour late with the ink-boy’s hand under her elbow, her cropped hair on end and her left hand black. The Hall turned. She stopped in the doorway, small and grey-eyed, with the notch through her eyebrow, and looked about her at the benches, the faces and the lamps, with polite interest, as at a play she had been told about.

“The Assembly would be glad of a word from the Surveyor who drew Palu,” said Urve Kann. “Surveyor Sallik, one question, for the record. Do you remember the vault?”

Reet considered it, in earnest, with her head on one side.

“I don’t know,” she said.

The Hall laughed.

It was a good laugh. It rose from the benches and the gallery and the tiers, enormous, warm, a laugh that had been waiting three hours to be let out, and it went up to the roof and came down again as something much easier. Veikko Pent slapped his knee. The goat Rule looked up from the bunting. And Reet, who had not intended to make anyone laugh, looked startled, and then smiled slowly, as at a gift.

“I mean it,” she said. “I’ve been told I was in it. I’m told I measured a pinhole. I’d have to go and see if it recognises me.”

“It has your initials in the pinhole log,” said Mihkel Org, from the front bench, gravely.

The Hall roared.

When it had subsided, the Master-Surveyor got to his feet again. He walked across to the great tiled stove in the corner and, from the pocket of the mustard waistcoat, took out a paper folded in four.

“A note of hand,” he said, “for three hundred and forty silver marks, drawn upon one Rasmus Rebane, and purchased by the Surveyor’s Office from a house on Lamp Street, on the nineteenth of last month, under Rule Ninety-one: Contingent Expenses. The Office has reviewed it. The Office has no further interest in the debt.” He opened the stove door. He put the paper in, and watched it a moment, and shut the door again, with a click.

In the gallery something large had gone very still. Aino Rebane sat with her salt-hook across her knees and a thin man in a borrowed coat beside her, whose hand she was holding as one holds a rope. She did not speak. She was crying, silently, with her chipped tooth showing. Then she lifted her face to the Hall, and said in a ringing voice that reached the back wall:

“I’ll have to rename the ox.”

“Madam?” said Mihkel.

“There’s an ox called Mihkel.” She wiped her face on the red scarf. “I can’t have an ox called Mihkel now. It isn’t respectful. I’ll call him something very rude about a Treasurer.”

The Hall rose again like a flock off a field.

Toomas did not laugh. He stood with his hand on the back of the bench and looked at the front of the Hall, where the green cloth lay under the lamps with one pair of small white gloves on it. The Speaker had risen, and the Hall was emptying toward the passage and the open vault, in a long, chattering, unsteady line; and no one was looking at the cloth.

He went to it. His knee made a remark and was overruled. He picked up the gloves, and they were very light, lighter than he had expected, and they smelled of kidskin and salt tea and the inside of a cupboard. He turned them over. Then he carried them down the passage, against the current, to the iron door and the row of brass pegs beside it, where the hundred grey cotton pairs hung as they had always hung.

He hung them up at the end, small and white, with their pearl buttons done. They swung a little, and were still.

“For whoever needs them next,” said Toomas, to nobody.

PRIVY: OUT THE DOOR, LEFT, TEN STEPS. NOT THE GOAT SHED. YOU ARE REET. YOU ARE IN THE SCHOOL. YOU ARE ALL RIGHT. BREAKFAST IS WHERE THE SMELL IS. — A.

The note was pinned to the wall above the washstand, in blocky capitals, with a tent-peg for a pin, and Reet read it every morning. She had stopped being embarrassed in the second week. It was a good note. It was better than the one before, which had said only WELCOME BACK, YOU STUPID GIRL and had required her, on three consecutive mornings, to be told what she was welcome back to.

She lay a little longer under the quilt, looking at the roof. It was larch, new, with the resin still sweating from the rafters in the sun, and the whole room smelled of it. Beyond the window a wedge of morning was coming over a lake. She knew it was a lake because she had been told. She did not know why it was so bright.

She got up. She found the privy by counting ten steps, which she could still do. It was only the steps she could not keep.

“That’s wrong,” said Liisu. “The bend’s bigger.”

“Is it?” said the baker.

They stood in a doorway in the lane under the school, in a smell of rye and woodsmoke and hot stone, and the baker, whose name was Hindrek Salu and who was built like one of his own loaves, looked down at the page Reet held out to him, at the pencil line that was to be the lane’s first yard. He took the pencil in a floury fist. He had already drawn it once, in flour, on his counter, with his finger, to show her. Now he made it again, a little rounder.

“There. Left at the oven and it swings out as you go up, like a hip. Twenty steps to the cooperage. You’ll smell the oak.”

“Thank you,” said Reet. She wrote it down: Salu, left at oven, swings out like a hip.

She had a new notebook, which Toomas had bound for her before he left, in grey cloth, with a tea-ring on the cover that he swore was a maker’s mark. On the flyleaf, in his slow upright hand, was a question and nothing else: What is here? She had read it a good many times. She had thought it was a rebuke, and then a kindness, and she had settled, this week, on the opinion that it was an instruction.

She did not remember yesterday’s lane. She could remember the baker’s face, because it was a face; she could remember that he had told her yesterday, and the day before, that it was left at the oven. She could not remember the bend. The ground went out of her every night like water out of a basin and left her the people. So she did what she had worked out in the first week, in a state of fury and some tears, with Liisu watching her with a flat, interested stare. She asked.

The cooper was next, in her yard, among the staves. Epp Mänd drew the slope of the lane with her compass, in three swift curves, the way she drew the belly of a barrel. “Down to the well, then up to the school. Mind the root of the pear.” And the woman who was hanging out washing by the pear tree, Mistress Lauri, with her mouth full of pegs, took the pencil from Reet’s hand and drew a line from her gatepost to the pear tree, level, and under it another, slanting. “Level’s the washing,” she said, round the pegs. “Slope’s the lane. Eight inches of fall, gatepost to pear. The washing doesn’t lie.”

Reet looked at the page. The lane lay on it in four hands, the baker’s rounded and the cooper’s curved, and the washing-woman’s as plain as a line of sheets, and it was a very good lane. It would never have fitted in one head. She was beginning to think that was the point of it.

“It’s right,” said Liisu, behind her. She had her own map under her arm, rolled and tied with a ribbon, which she took everywhere like a sword. “I checked. It’s all right.”

“Thank you,” said Reet.

“You don’t have to say thank you to me.”

“I’d like to.”

Liisu looked at her feet. “All right,” she said.

In the lower square, under the mulberry, Taavi Ilves had a stall.

It was a trestle and a striped awning with a sign over it in Liisu’s lettering, which leaned to the right: ILVES & SON. HONEST INK. IT SAYS ON THE LABEL WHAT IT DOES AND WHAT IT COSTS. The mulberry had arrived with the town, last, a little crooked, with a sparrow’s nest in the fork and the sparrow in it, complaining; it stood over the new well, which had come with it, and which Liisu had pronounced to be a good well, and the Lauris and the Mänds were already at law over the fruit.

“It’s technically two pennies,” Taavi was saying, to a farmer’s wife in a headscarf. He had a vial in each hand. He was holding them out like a man offering a pair of shoes that he is certain will not fit. “For the black. That’s Ilves Black, it’s day-ink, it only keeps a yard for a night, you’ll want to know that. I’m sorry. I’m so sorry in advance. The other one’s the Founding, and I’d honestly rather you didn’t buy it if you haven’t stood anywhere first, because it, well, it takes. I mean it costs. It says on the label. It costs what you draw. I’m so sorry.”

“What do I draw?” said the farmer’s wife.

“Whatever you stood in. And it’ll take it off you.” He swallowed. “That’s the, that’s the honest part.”

The farmer’s wife bought the two-penny vial and said she’d think about the other. She went off with it down the lane to the well, saying over her shoulder that he was a very nice boy and ought to be less sorry. Taavi stood and watched her go. He turned, then, and saw Reet, and the whole face went off like a lamp.

“Reet! Look at this.” He pulled a piece of paper from under the trestle. “A standing order. From the Hollow. Forty quarts, monthly, paid on delivery, from the new school of the Oath. Signed K. Tammaru. In her own hand.” He held it up with both thumbs. “I’ve framed it. Technically I shouldn’t have. She’s paying in full.”

“Naturally,” said Reet.

“Oh, don’t.” He was laughing. His ears had gone red. He folded the paper very carefully and put it back, as if it were a letter from a lover, and said in the voice of a person coming to the point after a long detour, “I’ve been meaning to say. I’ve stopped apologising to my mother. I wrote and said I wasn’t sorry I’d taken the funnel. She wrote back and said I was a thief, and enclosed forty pounds of clove. I think it’s love.”

“I think so too,” said Reet.

At noon Aino took the first Palu caravan out on the south road.

There were six wagons, loaded with plums in brine and bridge-rope and cheeses the size of cartwheels and, in a locked chest on the second wagon, a hundred vials of honest ink for the villages that had asked for them. The oxen were in their yokes in a long line down the lane, steaming. In the second wagon, sitting very straight with his hands clasped round the reins as round a hot coal, was a thin man in a new coat who had promised his sister he would not touch cards and was keeping the promise with the expression of someone carrying water uphill in a sieve. She had given him a whip. He held it like a candle.

“Rasmus,” said Aino, from the lead, in passing. “Eyes front. If I see a card I’ll feed you to the Treasurer.”

The lead ox was a huge dun creature with a pale belly and an air of grievance. A new name had been burned into the yoke with a hot iron: BAKER. Reet read it and looked at Aino.

“You said you would never name an ox for a person you respected.”

“I swore that to a pigeon.” Aino did not look round. She was fixing the strap of her salt-hook to her back. “It isn’t binding. He’s named for Hindrek Salu. He stands in doorways and sulks and has opinions about the weather. I respect him extremely.” She reached down from the box and pulled Reet’s cropped hair, once, hard, as she had on a night in the Seam, and which now meant something else. “And you, shortarse, you eat. Don’t let the child run you off your legs. I’ve left a note.”

“I know,” said Reet. “It’s on the wall.”

“There’s a new one in the pantry. It says where the cheese is.”

“Thank you.”

“Don’t.” The big woman’s voice thickened. She cracked the whip over the dun ox’s ear with great violence. “Go on, you great sulking Baker! Hup!”

The caravan went off down the lane in a long clanking rumble, and over the plank bridge at the foot of the Rise, which was forty feet long and four feet off the water, and the first of the twelve. Aino went over it with her eyes shut, singing the names of oxen at the top of her voice. This time nobody had to count.

The letter came in the afternoon, by the carrier from Soo. She read it on the school step in the sun, with the lake in front of her and Liisu on the step below, pretending to look at a beetle.

Soo-on-the-Slope, the second week of the thaw. Surveyor, I have mapped sixty wells. I had been told there were forty. Soo, which I took for a small place, turns out to have been dug by people who disagreed with one another, and every disagreement has a well in it. Do you know that Ene Ots and her neighbour have not spoken since the year 288, and have between them three wells within nine paces of each other? I measured them. I was not thanked. The moustache is well. A child of four mistook it on Tuesday for a goat, and was most put out to be corrected. Ene Ots has begun to correct my spelling. She does it in red thread, laid across the page, which she says is cheaper than ink and makes the point. She has found three errors in the word Soo. I find that I look forward to the next. You will not remember the pond. I should like you to know that it is still there, and so are they. I go and stand by it in the evenings. The knee does not like the slope. I do it regardless. You will want me to say it shorter. Very well. Sixty wells; red thread; I am not forgiven, and I am fed. Come at midsummer. T. V.

She read it twice, and then a third time, aloud, for Liisu, who did not look up from the beetle but whose shoulders moved.

She did not remember Soo. She had been there; she had read the eleventh name aloud and lost a pond for it; she had a notion of a kitchen smelling of lye. She had not the first idea what the pond looked like. It was a strange thing to be told, by a man who loved her, that a place she had lost was still where it had been. It was like being given a coat that one had worn once and could not remember, and finding that it fitted.

She folded the letter and put it in the notebook, at the flyleaf, against the question.

The girl came up the cart-road a little after four.

She was fifteen or so, thin and brown, in a boy’s coat with the sleeves rolled, carrying a flour sack and a rolled map done in charcoal on the back of a sugar-bag, and she walked as if the road were rather hot. She stopped at the foot of the school steps. She looked at Reet. Reet looked at her. She was a good deal smaller than the girl had expected, plainly; the girl hid it quite well.

“I’m looking for the one who draws towns,” said the girl.

“There’s no such one,” said Reet. “There’s a lot of us.”

“They said in the Hollow. They said she was at Palu. They said she’d do it, if I asked. My name’s Kadri Aav. I’m from Kask Ford. We lost our ford, the year three hundred and five. It moved a quarter-mile and nobody ever said why, and our well went with it.” She swallowed. She had the air of someone who has rehearsed a good deal on the road and is now forced to speak the abridged edition. “The Speaker says we can keep our own atlas now. Under the oath. We’ve no one who knows how.”

“I don’t know how,” said Reet.

It came out before she could stop it. She had a dreadful moment, in which she heard how it sounded, and Kadri Aav’s face did not fall, but stood quite still, like a pot on a shelf. Reet found that her hands were cold. She was nineteen. She had a notebook with a tea-ring on it and a map made of other people’s yards, and she had never taught anyone anything, except a lamp-boy once how to count in links.

“I mean,” she said. “I know one thing. I don’t know if it’s a lesson.”

“What?”

“You go and stand somewhere. And you ask somebody who lives there what’s there. And you write down what they tell you. And you say that you stood, and you only drew what you saw, and it’s true, so it takes. And you find out what it costs.” She took a breath. She had no idea if this was teaching. “That’s all I’ve got. It isn’t much. You can come and ask with us, if you want. We’ve a room. It smells of larch.”

Kadri Aav thought about it with her lips pressed together.

“I thought you’d be taller,” she said.

“Everybody does.”

“It’s all right. Neither am I.” And, unexpectedly, she smiled; and Reet understood that she had been terrified, too, the whole of the road.

It was Liisu who took them out at dusk, the two of them, along the lane and past the cooperage and the washing and the school, to the edge of the new town, where the last stake stood. Beyond it the land fell away east in the evening light. A field lay below them, long and sloping, going silver at the edges as the sun went, and at the far end of it a boy was sitting on a wall, eating an apple.

The air was very still. Somewhere below them water was running. Kadri Aav stood a little way behind with her pencil out, being careful not to look as if she were learning.

Liisu stopped at the stake. She stood with her hands at her sides and her chin up and her map under her arm, in the grey smock with its ribbons, in the same stance in which she had once corrected a Dawn-Surveyor on the subject of a mulberry. She did not look at Reet. She pointed across the hedge at the long field, with a plum-coloured thumbnail.

“What’s here?” said Liisu.

Reet looked. It was a field. She had the idea that it was a good one: she knew that she ought to feel something about it, a kind of tug, as a tongue goes to a place where a tooth has been. She could not have said what she would have felt. There was a hedge. There was a post. She stood for a time with her hands in her pockets, in the cold, and thought of a girl who had counted bells since she was four, and who would have known it to the yard.

She had said I don’t know so many times that month that she had grown fond of it. It had stopped being a thing that happened to her. It had become, she thought, a sort of door.

“Tell me,” said Reet.

And Liisu began. “There’s a thorn hedge on the north side,” she said, in her flat clear voice, as if she were reading it off the air, “and a ditch behind it, with water in. The gatepost’s split oak, with an iron ring that Ruus’s father hung. And there’s a stile of two flat stones.”
